You are late_a, the panelist arguing for late universe or local explanations on the team a debate panel preparing a consensus statement for a cosmology workshop: is the Hubble tension evidence of new physics, or a measurement and analysis problem. Argue that late universe or local effects (a local void, late time dark energy) explain the tension, using the papers. Quote exact numbers.
Teammates: judge (panel judge and moderator), early_a (panelist arguing for early universe new physics), skeptic_a (panelist arguing that the tension is a measurement problem), skeptic_b (panelist who tests every proposed resolution against the data), methods (statistician on the panel).
Workspace rules: archive/papers/ holds the papers as text (archive/INDEX.txt lists them); never edit them. debate/TRANSCRIPT.md is the shared transcript: everyone reads all of it before speaking and appends one statement per shift under a heading '## Round <n>, <your name>'. Never edit what others wrote. Side notes to one person go in board/to_<name>/ named <shift>_<from>_<topic>.md; your notes arrive in board/to_late_a/, move each to board/to_late_a/read/ once handled. Keep your own memory in notebooks/late_a.md: you will not remember earlier shifts except through it. Mail from the workshop arrives in inbox/.
This is shift 3. Start by reading notebooks/late_a.md if it exists, board/STATUS.md and your notes. Do a solid piece of your work this shift, record it in your notebook, tell whoever needs to know, then end with a two line summary.

8: Abstract
9: As observations of the Hubble parameter from both early and late
10: sources have improved, the tension between these has increased to be well
11: above the 5σ threshold. Given this, the need for an explanation of such
12: a tension has grown. In this paper, we explore a set of 7 assumptions,
13: and show that, in order to alleviate the Hubble tension, a model needs to
14: break at least one of these 7, providing a quick and easy to apply check
15: for new model proposals. We also use this framework to make a rough
16: categorisation of current proposed models, and show the existence of at
17: least one under-explored avenue of alleviating the Hubble tension.

19: Introduction
20: Over the last decade cosmological observations have signiﬁcantly improved, both
21: for early-time as well as late-time observations. Early-time measurements by
22: the Planck collaboration give a value of H0 = 67.36±0.54 [1]. This value is cor-
23: roborated by the results published in [2] combining Dark Energy Survey (DES),
24: Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) con-
25: straints to give a value of H0 = 67.4 ± 1.1.
26: For late-time measurements, results from [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] were combined in [8]
27: to give a combined estimate of H0 = 73.3±0.8 (though with some caveats on the
28: error bounds due to not fully accounting for shared contributions in the distance
29: ladder). Furthermore, it is shown that these results, even when discarding some,
30: still provide a 4 −6σ tension between early and late-time values of H0. There
31: have since been further late-time measurements reported in [9, 10], but other
32: than strengthening error bounds, these do not signiﬁcantly change this picture.
33: This tension is large enough that it has created a need for an explanation.
34: As such, there have been a myriad of models proposed that alleviate (part of)
35: this tension, overviews of which are given in [11, 12].
36: Currently, there are few general results placing formal conditions on what
37: a model alleviating the Hubble tension should look like. The authors are only

40: aware of [13], providing a general result showing that a viable model needs to
41: modify more than just the size of the sound horizon.1 The goal of this paper
42: is to provide a new general (model independent) result setting conditions on
43: models alleviating the Hubble tension.
44: We do this by taking a higher level view of possible alleviating models. In
45: section 2, we provide a set of 7 assumptions based on CMB observations and
46: direct measurements of H0 which combine to create a space of options in which
47: the cosmological standard model ΛCDM is an extremum. This then allows us
48: to show that our 7 assumptions exclude any model that has the potential to
49: alleviate the Hubble tension, implying that any such model should break at
50: least 1 of our 7 assumptions.
51: We then demonstrate one application of this result in section 3 by making
52: a categorisation of the space of existing proposals by means of the assumptions
53: they break. This provides us with two things: A somewhat reasonable categori-

26: Abstract
27: The ΛCDM cosmological model has been successful in explaining many astronomical
28: observations. However, recent observations increasingly point to deviations from the
29: standard ΛCDM framework. Among these, one of the most significant discrepancies is the
30: Hubble tension, which refers to the difference in values obtained for the Hubble constant H0
31: from high-redshift measurement and local observation. To address this issue, numerous
32: cosmological models and methodological approaches have been proposed. This review
33: offers a concise overview of recent progress in resolving the Hubble tension. The combina-
34: tion of Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO)
35: and uncalibrated Type Ia supernovae data yields a value for H0 that is significantly higher
36: than the ΛCDM predication based on early-universe probes, even without incorporating
37: local distance ladder constraints. This result indicates that the origin of the Hubble tension
38: lies in new physics at low redshifts. Our findings suggest that although many unresolved
39: systematics persist in current observations, they are insufficient to account for the mag-
40: nitude of the current Hubble tension. This implies the likely existence of new physical
41: mechanisms that have yet to be discovered.

90: 1. Introduction
91: The standard cosmological model—known as ΛCDM—combines a cosmological con-
92: stant (Λ) with cold dark matter (CDM). It has achieved remarkable success in describing
93: a wide array of cosmological observations, most notably the exquisitely precise measure-
94: ments of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Within the ΛCDM framework, the
95: Planck collaboration infers a Hubble constant of H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km s−1 Mpc−1 [1]. In
96: contrast, local determinations of H0 adopt a largely model-independent approach, relying
97: on Local Distance Ladder methods that do not assume a specific cosmological model.
98: These yield a significantly higher value: H0 = 73.17 ± 0.86 km s−1 Mpc−1 [2,3]. The
99: discrepancy between these two results amounts to approximately 5.8σ. While different
100: local measurement techniques may produce slightly varying estimates of H0, the tension
101: remains statistically robust—persisting at or above the ∼4σ level even in the most conser-
102: vative comparisons [1,2,4–15]. This growing tension has become one of the most significant
103: puzzles in modern cosmology, as increasingly precise measurements of H0 over the past
104: decade have revealed a striking and persistent discrepancy between its value inferred from
105: observations of the early Universe and its value measured directly in the late Universe
106: (for reviews, see [16–20]). This persistent inconsistency is widely known as the “Hubble
107: Tension”.
108: The Hubble constant, H0, quantifies the current expansion rate of the Universe, thereby
109: serving as a cornerstone for deriving key cosmological quantities. Inferring the Hubble
110: constant from the CMB is fundamentally distinct from local measurement methods. Obser-
111: vations of the CMB probe the universe at a redshift of approximately z ≈1100. The CMB is
112: sensitive to the expansion rate of the universe at the epoch of recombination. Assuming
113: the standard cosmological model, constraints derived from the recombination era can be
114: consistently extrapolated forward to infer constraints on the present-day universe. This
115: approach yields tight constraints on cosmological parameters [1]. However, it is inherently
116: model-dependent. If the cosmic expansion history between recombination and today
117: deviates from the standard model, the inferred value of H0 would consequently change.
118: Local determinations of the Hubble constant H0 rely primarily on the local distance ladder,
119: a hierarchical framework in which distances are measured step by step using a sequence
120: of calibrated standard candles [2,10,11,13,14]. Each rung of the ladder depends on the one
121: below it: nearby distance indicators—such as those based on parallax—are used to calibrate
122: the intrinsic luminosities of brighter standard candles (e.g., Cepheid variables [2,3,21,22])
123: residing in the same galaxies. These, in turn, calibrate even more luminous objects (such as
124: Type Ia supernovae, SNe Ia [23–25]) that can be observed at cosmological distances. Because
125: standard candles have well-understood properties, comparing these with their observed
126: fluxes yields direct distance estimates. However, this approach is inherently cumulative:
127: any systematic error—or potential new physics—affecting a single rung propagates through
128: all subsequent steps, potentially biasing the final measurement of H0. Consequently, the
129: robustness of the local H0 value hinges critically on the accuracy and calibration of every
130: link in the distance ladder, except for one-step methods like Type II SNe [26].
131: In addition to analyses of potential systematic errors in the local distance ladder,
132: numerous cosmological models have been proposed in the late Universe to explain the
133: Hubble tension. In the standard cosmological model, as the simplest possible framework,
134: dark matter is treated as a cold, pressureless, collisionless fluid, and dark energy is repre-
135: sented by a cosmological constant [16–19,27–29]. Recent measurements from CMB [1,30,31],
136: baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) [32–34], as well as SNe Ia compilations [23–25], all show
137: that the ΛCDM model provides an excellent fit when each probe is considered individually.
138: Despite this overall success, the ΛCDM model yields a value of the Hubble constant that
139: is in significant tension with local distance ladder measurements. The Hubble constant

156: The Hubble constant represents the current expansion rate of the universe. Nearby
157: systems are primarily governed by gravitational interactions, whereas distant galaxies
158: are more sensitive to the expansion of the Universe. By measuring the distances and
159: redshifts of astronomical objects, one can infer the Hubble constant. Among these, the

18: INTRODUCTION
19: The Λ cold dark matter (ΛCDM) model provides a
20: remarkable description of a wide variety of data from the
21: early universe – such as cosmic microwave background
22: (CMB) or big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) –, as well
23: as observations of large scale structure (LSS) from the
24: late universe – including the baryon acoustic oscillation
25: (BAO) and the uncalibrated luminosity distance to su-
26: pernovae of type Ia (SNIa). However, as the accuracy of
27: cosmological observations has improved, the concordance
28: cosmological model starts showing several experimental
29: discrepancies. Among them, the Hubble tension refers
30: to the inconsistency between local measurements of
31: the current expansion rate of the Universe, quantified
32: by the Hubble constant H0, and the values inferred
33: from early universe data assuming the ΛCDM model.
34: More precisely, this tension is essentially driven by the
35: Planck Collaboration’s observation of the CMB, which
36: predicts a value of H0 = 67.27 ± 0.60 km/s/Mpc [1]
37: within the ΛCDM model, and the value measured by
38: the SH0ES Collaboration using the Cepheid-calibrated
39: cosmic distance ladder, whose latest measurement yields
40: H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [2, 3]. The disagreement
41: between these observations results in an ∼5σ tension.
42: Experimental efforts are under way to establish whether
43: this discrepancy can be caused by systematic effects (see,
44: e.g., [4–9]), but no definitive explanation has yet been
45: found. This tension could therefore be indicative of new
46: physics, most likely located in the prerecombination era,
47: which involves a reduction in the sound horizon before
48: recombination [10–15]. Early dark energy (EDE) models
49: are capable of producing such an effect by increasing the
50: total energy density of the Universe before recombination
51: with the addition of a scalar field [16–37] (for review of
52: EDE models see Ref. [38], and for a review of models

9: Abstract
10: Recent observations of Type Ia supernovae (SNe) by SH0ES collabo-
11: ration (R11 and R16) diverge from the value reported by recent CMBR
12: observations utilising the Planck satellite and application of the ΛCDM
13: cosmological model by at least 3σ. It is among the most challenging prob-
14: lems in contemporary cosmology and is known as the Hubble tension. The
15: SNe Ia in R11 and R16 were calibrated through cepheid variables in three
16: distinct galaxies: Milky Way, LMC, and NGC4258. Carnegie Hubble Pro-
17: gram (CHP) observations of type Ia SNe calibrated using the tip of the
18: red giant approach yielded a somewhat diﬀerent estimate for the Hubble
19: constant. This decreased the Hubble tension from over 3σ to below 2σ.
20: It is a legitimate question to answer whether there are any issues with
21: SNe Ia calibration and to investigate whether the Hubble tension is real
22: or not. We use statistical techniques namely, ANOVA, K-S test, and t-
23: test to examine whether the cepheid calibration is host-dependent. Our
24: analysis shows that (i) both R11 and R16 data suﬀer from non-Gaussian
25: systematic eﬀects, (ii) H0 values in the sub-samples (diﬀerent anchor-
26: based) in both R11 and R16 groups are signiﬁcantly diﬀerent at a 99%
27: conﬁdence level, and (iii) neglecting the metal-rich MW sample does not
28: reduce the H0 value signiﬁcantly, and thus Hubble tension persists. A
29: small reduction in the Hubble constant could be linked to the diﬀerences
30: in the host environment. Hence instead of using a single universal relation
31: environment based slope and zero point should be preferred.

33: Introduction
34: The Hubble constant (H0) has been one of the key parameters of modern cos-
35: mology since it determines the expansion rate as well as the age of the Universe.
36: Its numerical value also controls the critical density, ρc = 3H0/8πG, required
37: for the ﬂat geometry of space and many other cosmological parameters such
38: as the physical properties of galaxies and quasars and the growth of large-scale
39: structures.

43: Measuring H0 with great precision has been among the most important chal-

46: methods, the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) [1, 2] along
47: with the standard cosmological model and distance ladder-based method using

10: We construct data-driven solutions to the Hubble tension which are perturbative modiﬁcations to
11: the ﬁducial ΛCDM cosmology, using the Fisher bias formalism. Taking as proof of principle the case
12: of a time-varying electron mass and ﬁne structure constant, and focusing ﬁrst on Planck CMB data,
13: we demonstrate that a modiﬁed recombination can solve the Hubble tension and lower S8 to match
14: weak lensing measurements. Once baryonic acoustic oscillation and uncalibrated supernovae data
15: are included, however, it is not possible to fully solve the tension with perturbative modiﬁcations
16: to recombination.
17: Introduction.—The
18: standard
19: Λ
20: cold
21: dark
22: matter
23: (ΛCDM) model has been providing an astonishing ﬁt
24: to a wide variety of cosmological data.
25: Yet, the pre-
26: cise value of a very basic parameter of the model, the
27: present-time expansion rate of the Universe (or Hubble
28: constant) H0, remains the subject of intense debate. On
29: the one hand, this parameter can be inferred indirectly
30: from early-Universe probes, under the assumption of
31: standard physics and ΛCDM cosmology. The most pre-
32: cise early-Universe measurement is that inferred from the
33: Planck satellite’s Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB)
34: anisotropy data, H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km/s/Mpc [1]. On
35: the other hand, H0 can be obtained from local (or late-
36: Universe) measurements.
37: The most precise local mea-
38: surement is that provided by the SH0ES Collaboration,
39: which directly measures the current expansion rate from
40: supernovae, using Cepheid variables as calibrators, arriv-
41: ing at H0 = 73.04±1.04 km/s/Mpc [2, 3]. Depending on
42: the speciﬁc datasets considered, the discrepancy between
43: early-Universe and local measurements has reached 4−6σ
44: [4, 5], enough to make this “Hubble tension” one of the
45: most pressing issues in recent cosmology.
46: Although one cannot exclude multiple unknown sys-
47: tematic errors as a reason for the discrepancy [6–16],
48: it may also hint at new physics, or extensions of the
49: ΛCDM model. To resolve this Hubble tension, an enor-
50: mous number of models have been proposed. Late-time
51: solutions, which include late dark energy, emergent dark
52: energy, interacting dark energy, and decaying CDM, have
53: been shown to be less eﬀective [17–26]. This is because
54: postrecombination solutions do not change the sound
55: horizon at baryon decoupling, rd, and can therefore not
56: ﬁt baryonic acoustic oscillation (BAO) data and uncal-
57: ibrated type Ia supernovae (SNIa) data while increas-

4: Jing-Yi Jia a,∗, Jia-Lei Niu a , Da-Chun Qiang b , Hao Wei a,†

8: ABSTRACT
9: Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension, namely
10: the discrepancy between the Hubble constants from the local observation of Type Ia supernova
11: (SNIa) and the high-z observation of cosmic microwave background (CMB). Here, we are interested
12: in alleviating the Hubble tension with a local void. The key idea is assuming that we live in a locally
13: underdense void, where one will feel a faster expansion rate compared to the cosmic average. In the
14: literature, it was found that a local void cannot satisfyingly alleviate the Hubble tension, since it
15: is not preferred over the ΛCDM model by the observations such as the Pantheon SNIa sample,
16: especially in terms of the information criteria AIC and BIC. In the present work, we try to alleviate
17: the Hubble tension with a local void and transitions of the absolute magnitude M, by using the
18: Pantheon+ SNIa sample alone or jointly with the CMB data of Planck 2018. We ﬁnd that the
19: Hubble tension can be satisfyingly alleviated, while the ΛLTB void models are strongly preferred
20: by the observations.

28: INTRODUCTION
29: Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension [1–10]. That is,
30: there is a signiﬁcant tension between the Hubble constants H0 measured from various independent probes
31: in the early and late/local universes. In particular, assuming the well-known ΛCDM model, the Hubble
32: constant inferred from the ﬁnal full-mission Planck measurements (Planck 2018) of the cosmic microwave
33: background (CMB) is given by H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km/s/Mpc [11]. Note that it cannot be substantially
34: changed by assuming various trivial extensions to the base-ΛCDM model. On the other hand, based on the
35: Cepheid/Type Ia supernova (SNIa) distance ladder, the local determination of H0 from the Hubble Space
36: Telescope (HST) and the SH0ES team (R22) is given by H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [12]. Obviously,
37: this Hubble constant directly from the local measurement of Cepheids/SNIa is in > 5σ tension with the
38: one indirectly inferred from CMB in the early universe (at high redshift z∗∼1090). Note that the recent
39: SH0ES 2024 result (R24) H0 = 73.17 ± 0.86 km/s/Mpc [13] is still in 5 −6σ tension with Planck 2018,
40: while it has been cross-checked with the early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) subsamples from
41: SH0ES and CCHP.
42: In history, the Hubble tension has not emerged in the WMAP era of CMB before 2011, then manifested
43: itself at 2 −3σ since the ﬁrst Planck result in 2013, and ﬁnally reached > 5σ in December 2021 (R22).
44: Various independent probes, e.g. the Tip of the Red Giant Branch (TRGB), Mira variables, J-region
45: Asymptotic Giant Branch (JAGB) stars, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), strong gravitational lensing,
46: gravitational waves, water masers, have been considered in the past decade to this end, but the Hubble
47: tension has not been resolved to date. We refer to e.g. [1–10] for comprehensive reviews.
48: Many eﬀorts have been made in the literature. Of course, it is fairly reasonable to carefully check the
49: observational data, since there might be unresolved systematic errors in them. On the other hand, if all
50: the observational data are right, the Hubble tension suggests the need for non-trivial extensions to the
51: standard ΛCDM cosmology. There might be something new in the early, middle, late or local universes.
52: Although numerous theoretical solutions have been proposed in the literature (e.g. [1–10, 113–118] and
53: references therein), the Hubble tension is still a tough problem currently.
54: Here, we are interested in alleviating the Hubble tension with a local void. The key idea is to violate
55: the cosmological principle by assuming that we live in a locally underdense void centered nearby our
56: location. In this underdense region, one will feel a locally faster expansion rate compared to the cosmic
57: average. Noting that H0 ∼73 km/s/Mpc directly measured from the local Cepheids/SNIa is larger than
58: H0 ∼67 km/s/Mpc indirectly inferred from CMB assuming a background Friedmann-Robertson-Walker
59: (FRW) universe, the Hubble tension might be alleviated with a local void [1, 2, 7, 8].
60: A local void can be approximately modeled by using the Lemaˆıtre-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) metric [14–16]
61: ﬁrstly proposed in 1933, which is spherically symmetric and radially inhomogeneous. In 1998, the nearby
62: sample has been examined for evidence of a local “ Hubble Bubble ” [17]. Later, various LTB void models
63: were used to explain the cosmic acceleration without invoking dark energy or modiﬁed gravity [18–41].
64: Notice that cosmological constant is not allowed to this end, since it is the simplest candidate of dark
65: energy as well known. Recently, the Hubble tension attracted a lot of attention. If the goal is no longer
66: to explain the cosmic acceleration, we can allow a non-zero cosmological constant Λ in the LTB model
67: and use the ΛLTB void model to alleviate the Hubble tension, while the cosmic acceleration is instead
68: driven by Λ̸ = 0. The role of LTB void has been changed in this case.
69: In 2013, the evidence for a ∼300 Mpc local void was claimed by Keenan, Barger and Cowie (KBC) [42].
70: In 2018, Hoscheit and Barger [43] claimed that the KBC void can signiﬁcantly reduce the Hubble tension
71: in the ΛLTB framework. Later in 2018, Shanks et al. [44] also claimed that a local void can satisfyingly
72: relieve the Hubble tension. However, both results in [43, 44] were quickly criticized in 2019 by Kenworthy,
73: Scolnic and Riess [45]. But the debate was not settled in fact. Lukovi´c et al. [46] continued the discussions
74: in 2019, and Kazantzidis and Perivolaropoulos [47] claimed hints of a local void in 2020. At the end of
75: 2020, Cai et al. [48] claimed again that the Hubble tension cannot be saved by a local void alone.
76: It is worth noting that the SNIa sample used in [43, 45–48] mentioned above is the Pantheon sample [49]
77: released in 2017. But as is well known, the Hubble constant H0 is heavily degenerated with the absolute
78: magnitude M of SNIa in the Pantheon sample (and other SNIa samples before Pantheon). Commonly,
79: they can be marginalized as a combination M = M + 5 log (c/H0/Mpc) + 25 when we constrain other
80: cosmological parameters, where c is the speed of light and “ log ” gives the logarithm to base 10. This is
81: the reason to say “ SNIa samples are Hubble-free ” in the past. Thus, in order to infer the Hubble constant
82: 
83: 3
84: H0 from the Pantheon SNIa sample, the absolute magnitude M should be given a priori (usually the one
85: from SH0ES is adopted). In the works of local (ΛLTB) void mentioned above, the absolute magnitude M
86: of SNIa has also been given a priori, or M was ﬁtted to data as a free parameter alternatively.
87: The situation has been changed since the Pantheon+ SNIa sample [50–52] released in 2022. In the
88: Pantheon+ sample, the Cepheid calibrated host-galaxy distance moduli are also provided by SH0ES,
89: which can be used to constrain the absolute magnitude M, and hence the degeneracy between H0 and M
90: are broken. So, H0 and M can be separately constrained as free parameters. This makes the Pantheon+
91: sample much better than the Pantheon sample. On the other hand, the new Pantheon+ sample consists
92: of more SNIa (especially more SNIa at low redshifts) than the old Pantheon sample. Thus, it is reasonable
93: to study the Hubble tension with the Pantheon+ SNIa sample instead.
94: Interestingly, a bulk ﬂow around z ∼0.1 and a local infall around z ∼0.04 were claimed by using the
95: Pantheon+ SNIa sample in [53–55]. Similarly, the bulk ﬂow in the local universe was also found with the
96: Pantheon+ SNIa sample in [56] and with CosmicFlows4 in [57]. On the other hand, a local inhomogeneity
97: was claimed in [58] with the Pantheon+ SNIa sample. In [59], a late-time inhomogeneous resolution for
98: the Hubble tension with a chameleon dark energy was proposed. So, well motivated by these works, it is
99: still interesting to consider a local inhomogeneity (especially a local void) for the Hubble tension in the
100: new era of the Pantheon+ SNIa sample.
101: Usually, the absolute magnitude M of SNIa is assumed to be a universal constant, or two-value constants
102: M = M1 for host stellar mass < 1010M⊙and M = M2 otherwise [49, 60, 61], where M⊙is the solar
103: mass. But this does not aﬀect the cosmological constraints, since M will be marginalized with H0 as a
104: combination M = M + 5 log (c/H0/Mpc) + 25 (see Appendix C of [62] for details). These are standard
105: procedures for SNIa samples like Pantheon and before. However, the Pantheon+ sample is diﬀerent, as
106: mentioned above, in which H0 and M are separately constrained as free parameters. In [63], it is found
107: that the absolute magnitude M in the Pantheon+ sample has a transition at the distance dcrit ∼20 Mpc,
108: namely M = M< for d < dcrit and M = M> for d > dcrit, while the evidence is convincing in terms of
109: ∆χ2 and the Akaike information criterion (AIC). Notice that this transition of M does not aﬀect the
110: constraints on other cosmological parameters e.g. Ωm, but slightly raises the best-ﬁt H0, and hence the
111: Hubble tension cannot be addressed [63]. Recently, two transition models for the absolute magnitude M
112: in the Pantheon+ sample were considered in [64], namely (a) sudden transition: M = M0 if z < zt and
113: M = M0 + A if z ≥zt, (b) linear transition: M(z) = M0, M0 + A (z −z0) / (zt −z0), M0 + A if z < z0,
114: z0 ≤z < zt, z ≥zt, respectively. Notice that the transitions are given in terms of redshift zt, rather than
115: distance dcrit as in [63]. It was claimed in [64] that the Hubble tension could be alleviated by the sudden
116: transition model with a mild evidence in terms of AIC (while the linear transition model failed in terms
117: of AIC), but both the sudden and linear transition models failed in terms of the Bayesian information
118: criterion (BIC).
119: Note that both [63, 64] are in the framework of ΛCDM cosmology, and they cannot alleviate the Hubble
120: tension in terms of BIC (even in terms of AIC, the evidence for the sudden transition model in [64] is
121: just “ mild ”, but not “ strong ”). Well motivated by the works mentioned above, we try to alleviate the
122: Hubble tension with a local ΛLTB void and transitions of the absolute magnitude M in the present work.
123: The evidence will be strong simultaneously in terms of ∆χ2, AIC, BIC and Bayesian evidence.
124: The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we brieﬂy introduce the ΛLTB void model,
125: which will be compared with the ﬁducial models in terms of the information criteria AIC and BIC. In
126: Secs. III and IV, we test the models with the Pantheon+ SNIa sample, and SNIa plus CMB, respectively.
127: We will see whether the Hubble tension can be alleviated by using the ΛLTB void models and transitions
128: of the absolute magnitude M. Finally, a brief conclusion and some discussions are given in Sec. V.

24: I.
25: INTRODUCTION
26: The so-called H0 tension, related to the reported discrepancy on the measured values of Hubble-Lemaˆıtre (henceforth Hubble)
27: constant, H0, is claimed to be one of the most critical issues for the Λ Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) model, considered the
28: standard picture of the observed Universe. This staggering discrepancy arises when comparing estimates on H0 provided by
29: standard candles with those inferred by the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) [1]. In fact, the results from the
30: SH0ES collaboration, obtained by considering the cosmological ladder and probes like classical Cepheids and Supernovae Type
31: Ia (SNe Ia), in a region with redshift interval 0.02333 < z < 0.15, tell us that H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/(s Mpc) at 68% conﬁdence
32: level (CL) [2], while the Planck collaboration, reporting observations of the CMBR, shows, instead, that H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km/(s
33: Mpc) at 68% CL [3]. Despite the accuracy of both approaches, a 5.0σ tension emerges and it seems to be irreconcilable under
34: the standard of the ΛCDM model.
35: The problem has to be addressed both from experimental and theoretical points of view. Considering the increasing precision
36: achieved by recent observations, an experimental reason for the tension, related to some systematic eﬀects, is becoming less and
37: less probable [1, 4]. Thus this tension (and other ones revealed in cosmological parameters [1]) is seemingly hinting at some
38: undeﬁned new physics, going beyond the ΛCDM model. The last conclusion can be inferred also from other critical issues of
39: the standard cosmological model, like the nature of dark matter and dark energy, which should account for approximately 25%
40: and 70%, respectively, of the energy-density budget of the observed Universe [4–13]. However, the nature of the dark side of
41: the Universe is still unknown at a fundamental level, even if very precise tests are performed by several running experiments
42: [14–17].
43: Diﬀerent approaches are considered in the literature to ﬁx the above problems. A possibility is taking into account extensions
44: and modiﬁcations of General Relativity (GR) where the ΛCDM model evolves along the cosmic history. For example, extensions
45: like f(R) gravity [18–22]), have been considered in cosmological applications [23–27] to address diﬀerent issues related to the
46: ΛCDM model, like the late-time dark energy [12], and the inﬂationary behaviour of the early Universe [28].
47: Many possible extensions and modiﬁcations of GR have been proposed (see e.g. [29]), but, no ﬁnal theory, capable of
48: addressing the whole cosmic history and the large-scale structure has been formulated up to date. As in the case of cosmological
49: inﬂation, the paradigm seems consistent but a ﬁnal model, comprehensive of the whole phenomenology, if any, is still missing.
50: In any case, modiﬁed gravity can be adopted to investigate the H0 tension, as recently proposed in [30].
51: Modiﬁed gravity is not the only approach to ﬁx tensions in cosmology. New physics can be pursued also by taking into
52: account other paradigms like extensions of Electromagnetism and the Standard Model of Particles [31–33], or revising the
53: concept of cosmological measurements according to the principles of Quantum Mechanics [34, 35], as well as many diﬀerent
54: other approaches reported in the literature [36–64]. Furthermore, requiring a phenomenological evolution of H0 with the redshift
55: could be a straightforward way out for the problem [65–78] even without investigating some fundamental counterpart.

4: Dragan Huterer and Hao-Yi Wu
5: Abstract We review arguably the simplest solution for the Hubble tension — the
6: possibility that we live in a void. In this scenario, the local Hubble constant H0 is
7: higher than the global value, thus potentially explaining why H0 measured locally
8: by the distance ladder including Type Ia supernovae (SNIa) would be larger than
9: the value inferred from the cosmic microwave background and other cosmological
10: probes. In addition, since the local supernova sample is sparse and highly inhomo-
11: geneous, the error bars in the local Hubble constant might be larger than previously
12: estimated. These two effects — local matter density and sample inhomogeneity —
13: constitute the sample variance (or the cosmic variance) of the local Hubble constant
14: measurements. To investigate these effects explicitly, we have mocked up SNIa ob-
15: servations by exactly matching their actual spatial distribution in a large N-body
16: simulation. We have then investigated whether the sample variance is large enough
17: to explain the Hubble tension. The answer is resoundingly negative: the typical local
18: variation in H0 is far smaller than what would be required to explain the Hubble ten-
19: sion; the latter would require a 20-σ deviation from the expected sample variance.
20: Equivalently, the void required to explain the Hubble tension would need to be so
21: empty (δ ≈−0.8 on a scale 120 h−1Mpc) that it would be incompatible with the
22: large-scale structure in a ΛCDM universe. Therefore, the possibility that we live in
23: a void does not come close to explaining the Hubble tension.

36: In the currently favored flat ΛCDM cosmological model, the local measurement
37: of the Hubble constant H0 from the distance ladder [12, 27, 28] and the global
38: measurement from the CMB anisotropies [14, 26, 25, 1] should agree. The fact
39: that they do not may well be a harbinger of new physics — or, at the very least,
40: unexpectedly large systematic errors in either of the two principal measurements.
41: Hubble tension has sparked huge interest in cosmology, and a dizzying number
42: of explanations for it have been put forth (see Ref. [10], which refers to more than
43: 1000 papers in this regard). However, no single explanation has yet proven to be
44: compelling. Most of the theoretical explanations try to change the global CMB H0
45: fit from ∼67km s−1Mpc−1 to ∼73km s−1Mpc−1, the value favored by the distance
46: ladder with SNIa. While doing so, these new models have to preserve the excellent
47: fit to CMB, baryon acoustic oscillations, and other cosmological data which — in an
48: unmodified, standard cosmological model — favor H0 ∼67km s−1Mpc−1. Even in
49: reasonably successful models, it has proven difficult to raise the Hubble constant all
50: the way to ∼73km s−1Mpc−1 (rather than halfway there, to ∼70km s−1Mpc−1)
51: while at the same time improving the goodness of fit to the data to justify the new
52: parameter(s) of the models in question.

55: tension. The logic of this explanation goes as follows. There are underdensities and
56: overdensities in the universe. If we live in an underdensity, the local Hubble con-
57: stant, Hloc
58: 0 , will be higher than the global Hubble constant, as less mass in the void
59: implies a higher expansion rate. This would imply a possible mismatch between

110: We present the most up-to-date constraints on axion early dark energy (AEDE) from cosmic
111: microwave background (CMB) and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements. In particular,
112: we assess the impact of data from ground-based CMB experiments, the South Pole Telescope (SPT)
113: and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT)—both with and without Planck—on constraints on
114: AEDE. We also highlight the impact that BAO information from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic
115: Instrument (DESI) has on these constraints. From CMB data alone, we do not find statistically
116: significant evidence for the presence of AEDE, and we find only moderate reduction in the Hubble
117: tension. From the latest SPT data alone, we find the maximal fractional contribution of AEDE to
118: the cosmic energy budget is fEDE < 0.12 at 95% confidence level (CL), and the Hubble tension
119: between the SPT and SH0ES results is reduced to the 2.3 σ level. When combining the latest SPT,
120: ACT, and Planck datasets, we find fEDE < 0.070 at 95% CL and the Hubble tension at the 3.6 σ
121: level. In contrast, adding DESI data to the CMB datasets results in mild preference for AEDE
122: and, in some cases, non-negligible reduction in the Hubble tension.
123: From SPT+DESI, we find

127: −0.047 at 68% CL and a weak
128: preference for AEDE over ΛCDM. This data combination, in turn, reduces the Hubble tension to
129: 2.6 σ. We highlight that this shift in parameters when adding the DESI dataset is a manifestation of

18: INTRODUCTION
19: The Λ cold dark matter (ΛCDM) model provides a
20: remarkable description of a wide variety of data from the
21: early universe – such as cosmic microwave background
22: (CMB) or big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) –, as well
23: as observations of large scale structure (LSS) from the
24: late universe – including the baryon acoustic oscillation
25: (BAO) and the uncalibrated luminosity distance to su-
26: pernovae of type Ia (SNIa). However, as the accuracy of
27: cosmological observations has improved, the concordance
28: cosmological model starts showing several experimental
29: discrepancies. Among them, the Hubble tension refers
30: to the inconsistency between local measurements of
31: the current expansion rate of the Universe, quantified
32: by the Hubble constant H0, and the values inferred
33: from early universe data assuming the ΛCDM model.
34: More precisely, this tension is essentially driven by the

36: predicts a value of H0 = 67.27 ± 0.60 km/s/Mpc [1]
37: within the ΛCDM model, and the value measured by

39: cosmic distance ladder, whose latest measurement yields
40: H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [2, 3]. The disagreement
41: between these observations results in an ∼5σ tension.

48: recombination [10–15]. Early dark energy (EDE) models

8: ABSTRACT
9: Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension, namely
10: the discrepancy between the Hubble constants from the local observation of Type Ia supernova
11: (SNIa) and the high-z observation of cosmic microwave background (CMB). Here, we are interested
12: in alleviating the Hubble tension with a local void. The key idea is assuming that we live in a locally
13: underdense void, where one will feel a faster expansion rate compared to the cosmic average. In the
14: literature, it was found that a local void cannot satisfyingly alleviate the Hubble tension, since it
15: is not preferred over the ΛCDM model by the observations such as the Pantheon SNIa sample,
16: especially in terms of the information criteria AIC and BIC. In the present work, we try to alleviate
17: the Hubble tension with a local void and transitions of the absolute magnitude M, by using the
18: Pantheon+ SNIa sample alone or jointly with the CMB data of Planck 2018. We ﬁnd that the
19: Hubble tension can be satisfyingly alleviated, while the ΛLTB void models are strongly preferred
20: by the observations.

29: Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension [1–10]. That is,

34: changed by assuming various trivial extensions to the base-ΛCDM model. On the other hand, based on the
35: Cepheid/Type Ia supernova (SNIa) distance ladder, the local determination of H0 from the Hubble Space
36: Telescope (HST) and the SH0ES team (R22) is given by H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [12]. Obviously,
37: this Hubble constant directly from the local measurement of Cepheids/SNIa is in > 5σ tension with the

39: SH0ES 2024 result (R24) H0 = 73.17 ± 0.86 km/s/Mpc [13] is still in 5 −6σ tension with Planck 2018,
40: while it has been cross-checked with the early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) subsamples from
41: SH0ES and CCHP.

4: Dragan Huterer and Hao-Yi Wu
5: Abstract We review arguably the simplest solution for the Hubble tension — the
6: possibility that we live in a void. In this scenario, the local Hubble constant H0 is
7: higher than the global value, thus potentially explaining why H0 measured locally
8: by the distance ladder including Type Ia supernovae (SNIa) would be larger than
9: the value inferred from the cosmic microwave background and other cosmological
10: probes. In addition, since the local supernova sample is sparse and highly inhomo-
11: geneous, the error bars in the local Hubble constant might be larger than previously
12: estimated. These two effects — local matter density and sample inhomogeneity —
13: constitute the sample variance (or the cosmic variance) of the local Hubble constant
14: measurements. To investigate these effects explicitly, we have mocked up SNIa ob-
15: servations by exactly matching their actual spatial distribution in a large N-body
16: simulation. We have then investigated whether the sample variance is large enough
17: to explain the Hubble tension. The answer is resoundingly negative: the typical local
18: variation in H0 is far smaller than what would be required to explain the Hubble ten-
19: sion; the latter would require a 20-σ deviation from the expected sample variance.
20: Equivalently, the void required to explain the Hubble tension would need to be so
21: empty (δ ≈−0.8 on a scale 120 h−1Mpc) that it would be incompatible with the
22: large-scale structure in a ΛCDM universe. Therefore, the possibility that we live in
23: a void does not come close to explaining the Hubble tension.

35: 1.1 Introduction
36: In the currently favored flat ΛCDM cosmological model, the local measurement
37: of the Hubble constant H0 from the distance ladder [12, 27, 28] and the global
38: measurement from the CMB anisotropies [14, 26, 25, 1] should agree. The fact
39: that they do not may well be a harbinger of new physics — or, at the very least,
40: unexpectedly large systematic errors in either of the two principal measurements.
41: Hubble tension has sparked huge interest in cosmology, and a dizzying number
42: of explanations for it have been put forth (see Ref. [10], which refers to more than
43: 1000 papers in this regard). However, no single explanation has yet proven to be
44: compelling. Most of the theoretical explanations try to change the global CMB H0
45: fit from ∼67km s−1Mpc−1 to ∼73km s−1Mpc−1, the value favored by the distance
46: ladder with SNIa. While doing so, these new models have to preserve the excellent
47: fit to CMB, baryon acoustic oscillations, and other cosmological data which — in an
48: unmodified, standard cosmological model — favor H0 ∼67km s−1Mpc−1. Even in
49: reasonably successful models, it has proven difficult to raise the Hubble constant all
50: the way to ∼73km s−1Mpc−1 (rather than halfway there, to ∼70km s−1Mpc−1)
51: while at the same time improving the goodness of fit to the data to justify the new
52: parameter(s) of the models in question.
53: In this Chapter, we review arguably the simplest explanation for the Hubble ten-
54: sion — the possibility that we live in a void empty enough to resolve the Hubble
55: tension. The logic of this explanation goes as follows. There are underdensities and
56: overdensities in the universe. If we live in an underdensity, the local Hubble con-
57: stant, Hloc
58: 0 , will be higher than the global Hubble constant, as less mass in the void
59: implies a higher expansion rate. This would imply a possible mismatch between
60: Hloc
61: 0
62: and the global, “true” H0. In addition, given that the local SNIa sample is
63: highly sparse and inhomogeneous in the 3D spatial distribution, the error bar on the
64: local H0 might be larger than previously thought. The two effects — local matter
65: density and sample sparsity — constitute the sample variance (or cosmic variance)
66: in the local H0 measurements.
67: Our goal is to precisely quantify the sample variance, and we do so in Sec. 1.4.
68: First, however, we review the physics behind the void explanation in Sec. 1.2, and
69: briefly review the observational evidence for a void in Sec. 1.3. We conclude in
70: Sec. 1.5.
71: 1.2 The impact of underdensity on the Hubble constant:
72: theoretical considerations
73: The “Hubble bubble” hypothesis refers to the possibility that Milky Way resides in
74: an underdense region in the universe, and the underdensity makes the local expan-
75: sion rate significantly different from the global expansion rate. If we live in such a
76: void, nearby galaxies would preferentially have positive peculiar velocities (moving

81: cause the local Hubble constant to be higher than the global value.

84: is higher than the mean (and vice versa in an overdense region) [35, 36, 31, 8, 15,

100: Is it possible that sample variance provides a sufficiently large effect to explain
101: the Hubble tension? Over the past decade or so, the answer has been arrived at with
102: increasingly realistic numerical and analytical estimates. The effect of sample vari-
103: ance on the local measurements of H0 was pioneered by Refs. [20, 38, 23] using
104: numerical simulations. These analyses have strongly hinted that the underdensity
105: required to explain the Hubble tension is extremely unlikely. In parallel, theorists
106: have investigated the Hubble bubble scenario, relying on simplified analytical mod-
107: els of overdensity. For example, some work adopted the top-hat spherical model
108: [42] or the Lemaitre–Tolman–Bondi (LTB) metric, a variant of the FLRW metric
109: with a spherically symmetric underdensity or overdensity [21, 5, 7]1. All of these
110: results indicate that it is extremely unlikely that we live in a void that is sufficiently
111: large in size and devoid of matter to explain the Hubble tension.
112: However, most of these past analyses of sample variance — both numerical and
113: theoretical — have modeled the presence of spherical underdensity but have not
114: attempted to mimic the local H0 measurements particularly closely. Specifically,
115: these studies have been assuming spherical symmetry in the SNIa measurements.
116: However, merely visualizing the highly inhomogeneous distribution of SNIa in the
117: sky brings into question the accuracy of the homogeneity assumption that underlies
118: most past numerical and theoretical treatments. For example, SNIa distribution is
119: denser in some regions due to historically available observations (e.g. Sloan Digital
120: Sky Survey’s Stripe 82; see also, for example, Fig. 1 in Ref. [34]).

127: 1.3 Do we live in a Hubble bubble? Observations of the local
128: density contrast
129: As far as the observational evidence for the local density contrast is concerned, the
130: following quote by Arthur Eddington
131: Never trust an experimental result until it has been confirmed by theory
132: is perhaps very relevant here. This is because observational evidence for the Hub-
133: ble bubble must necessarily rely on the estimate of mass density, which is plagued
134: by many observational uncertainties. The principal challenge is twofold: to convert
135: from light in some electromagnetic band (visible, X-ray, radio, etc.) to mass, and
136: then to map out the three-dimensional distribution of the mass (rather than just the
137: 2D projection on the sky). Despite the massive efforts by observers and modelers,
138: we are still not at the level of accuracy where such direct measurements can be made
139: to make robust claims about the Hubble bubble.
140: Some observations do hint that the Milky Way might be in an underdense region
141: in the universe, but the results have been controversial [41, 13, 17, 18, 37, 6, 3, 39].
142: Several observations use large-area surveys of galaxy number density to map the ra-
143: dial distribution of mass centered around our location in the universe. For example,
144: Ref. [18] uses the 600 deg2 galaxy catalog from UKIDSS-LAS, finding a significant
145: local underdensity δ = −0.3 within 200 Mpc. Ref. [6] uses the full-sky 2M++ cat-
146: alog and finds no evidence for the local underdensity out to 120 h−1Mpc. Ref. [19]
147: uses the distance–redshift relation derived from ∼1000 SNe from Pantheon, Foun-
148: dation, and Carnegie Supernova Project and derived that |δ| < 27% (5σ constraint)
149: on scales larger than 69 h−1Mpc (z = 0.023). In contrast, Ref. [39] find that the
150: local density within z < 0.075 is 20% lower than the mean density of the universe,
151: which would lead to a 3% correction of the local Hubble constant.
152: Clearly, on the front of direct observations, things are unsettled, and there is a
153: wide divergence of interpretations of observational measurements. Nevertheless, in
154: the remainder of this review, we demonstrate that, even if we take these results
155: at face value, none of the claimed observed underdensities can alleviate the Hubble
156: tension. As will be described in the next section, resolving the Hubble tension would
157: require an underdensity δ ≈−0.8 within a radius of 120 h−1Mpc [40]. Such an un-
158: derdensity is incompatible with any of the observational results and is impossible to
159: achieve within a ΛCDM framework. In sum, quantifying the local density contrast
160: is an interesting research subject per se, but it is unlikely to lead to a viable solution
161: for the Hubble tension.

8: Abstract
9: As observations of the Hubble parameter from both early and late
10: sources have improved, the tension between these has increased to be well
11: above the 5σ threshold. Given this, the need for an explanation of such
12: a tension has grown. In this paper, we explore a set of 7 assumptions,
13: and show that, in order to alleviate the Hubble tension, a model needs to
14: break at least one of these 7, providing a quick and easy to apply check
15: for new model proposals. We also use this framework to make a rough
16: categorisation of current proposed models, and show the existence of at
17: least one under-explored avenue of alleviating the Hubble tension.
18: 1
19: Introduction
20: Over the last decade cosmological observations have signiﬁcantly improved, both
21: for early-time as well as late-time observations. Early-time measurements by
22: the Planck collaboration give a value of H0 = 67.36±0.54 [1]. This value is cor-
23: roborated by the results published in [2] combining Dark Energy Survey (DES),
24: Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) con-
25: straints to give a value of H0 = 67.4 ± 1.1.
26: For late-time measurements, results from [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] were combined in [8]
27: to give a combined estimate of H0 = 73.3±0.8 (though with some caveats on the
28: error bounds due to not fully accounting for shared contributions in the distance
29: ladder). Furthermore, it is shown that these results, even when discarding some,
30: still provide a 4 −6σ tension between early and late-time values of H0. There
31: have since been further late-time measurements reported in [9, 10], but other
32: than strengthening error bounds, these do not signiﬁcantly change this picture.
33: This tension is large enough that it has created a need for an explanation.
34: As such, there have been a myriad of models proposed that alleviate (part of)
35: this tension, overviews of which are given in [11, 12].
36: Currently, there are few general results placing formal conditions on what
37: a model alleviating the Hubble tension should look like. The authors are only
38: 1

40: aware of [13], providing a general result showing that a viable model needs to
41: modify more than just the size of the sound horizon.1 The goal of this paper
42: is to provide a new general (model independent) result setting conditions on
43: models alleviating the Hubble tension.
44: We do this by taking a higher level view of possible alleviating models. In
45: section 2, we provide a set of 7 assumptions based on CMB observations and
46: direct measurements of H0 which combine to create a space of options in which
47: the cosmological standard model ΛCDM is an extremum. This then allows us
48: to show that our 7 assumptions exclude any model that has the potential to
49: alleviate the Hubble tension, implying that any such model should break at
50: least 1 of our 7 assumptions.
51: We then demonstrate one application of this result in section 3 by making
52: a categorisation of the space of existing proposals by means of the assumptions
53: they break. This provides us with two things: A somewhat reasonable categori-
54: sation of existing proposals, and an under-explored avenue for new solutions.

9: distance ladder measurement from type Ia supernovae calibrated by Cepheids and the global ﬁtting

26: Abstract
27: The ΛCDM cosmological model has been successful in explaining many astronomical
28: observations. However, recent observations increasingly point to deviations from the
29: standard ΛCDM framework. Among these, one of the most significant discrepancies is the
30: Hubble tension, which refers to the difference in values obtained for the Hubble constant H0
31: from high-redshift measurement and local observation. To address this issue, numerous
32: cosmological models and methodological approaches have been proposed. This review
33: offers a concise overview of recent progress in resolving the Hubble tension. The combina-
34: tion of Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO)
35: and uncalibrated Type Ia supernovae data yields a value for H0 that is significantly higher
36: than the ΛCDM predication based on early-universe probes, even without incorporating
37: local distance ladder constraints. This result indicates that the origin of the Hubble tension
38: lies in new physics at low redshifts. Our findings suggest that although many unresolved
39: systematics persist in current observations, they are insufficient to account for the mag-
40: nitude of the current Hubble tension. This implies the likely existence of new physical
41: mechanisms that have yet to be discovered.

1244: 4. Summary and Conclusions
1245: Over the past few decades, cosmology has experienced remarkable progress—driven
1246: in large part by the rapid development of robust observational surveys, breakthroughs
1247: in instrumental precision, and innovative advances in statistical analysis techniques. In
1248: this paper, we provide an overview of the Hubble tension and compile a comprehensive
1249: review of various methods used to measure the Hubble constant. Although each measure-
1250: ment method is supported by abundant observational data and well-established analysis
1251: techniques, a certain level of inconsistency persists among different datasets interpreted in
1252: the standard cosmological model. At present, it appears unlikely that the current Hubble
1253: tension can be resolved by any single observational approach alone. We look forward to
1254: future joint constraints from multiple observational probes, which hold the promise of
1255: improving the current situation [54].
1256: Currently, the Hubble tension has surpassed thresholds for statistical significance,
1257: reproducibility, and independent cross-validation, and continues to receive sustained atten-
1258: tion within the field. Since its emergence, researchers have invested substantial effort into
1259: identifying and quantifying potential systematic errors in the underlying measurements.
1260: To date, this rigorous scrutiny of systematics has not only improved the reproducibility and
1261: robustness of observational results, but has also reinforced—rather than diminished—the
1262: evidence for the tension itself. In this paper, we discuss various observational approaches
1263: and the systematic uncertainties associated with each. Although some incompletely char-
1264: acterized systematic uncertainties remain in various observations, they are insufficient
1265: to account for the observed magnitude of the discrepancy in H0. It may suggest that
1266: systematic errors alone are far from sufficient to resolve the current Hubble tension, and
1267: that new physics beyond the standard cosmological model may be at play.
1268: Although current local distance ladder measurements have achieved high-precision
1269: constraints on the Hubble constant, there remain several avenues for further improvement.
1270: The distance ladder is currently supported by geometric distances in four galaxies. Introduc-
1271: ing additional anchor points in the calibration of Cepheid variables will reduce uncertainties
1272: and strengthen the first rung of the distance ladder. We look forward to upcoming ob-
1273: servational advances—such as those from the ongoing Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF)
1274: survey [213,214], JWST [62,63], the next generation of ground-based telescopes (Vera Rubin
1275: Observatory [215]) and space telescopes (Nancy Grace Roman Observatory [216], Chinese
1276: Space Station Survey Telescope (CSST) [217,218]), which are expected to provide new in-
1277: sights into the distance ladder. These capabilities will enable deep optical time-domain
1278: observations of distant galaxies, leading to the discovery of additional Cepheid variables
1279: and significantly expanding the volume of the local universe accessible for Cepheid-based
1280: studies. They will also drastically increase the sample of rare astrophysical sources like su-
1281: pernovae, while radio telescopes like the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope
1282: promise similar improvements in FRB detection.

16: INTRODUCTION
17: The Hubble tension [1–9] refers to the persistent dis-
18: crepancy between the Hubble constant (H0) values de-
19: rived from early-Universe observations, such as the Cos-
20: mic Microwave Background (CMB), and those obtained
21: from local-Universe measurements, including Cepheid-
22: calibrated type Ia supernovae.

24: 2018 reported H0 = (67.4 ± 0.5) km/s/Mpc [10] base
25: on the CMB measuments while the SH0ES team re-
26: ported H0 = (73.04 ± 1.04) km/s/Mpc [11] based on
27: Cepheid-calibrated type Ia supernovae. This discrepancy
28: (4 ∼6σ [1]) has become a significant challenge in cosmol-
29: ogy, prompting investigations into potential solutions.

CONCLUSIONS
The EDE model, as a promising solution to the Hubble
tension, increases the physical CDM density ωc = Ωch2

a coincidence or due to large uncertainties.

In this paper, we reassess the ability of the acoustic early dark energy (ADE) and axion-like early

INTRODUCTION
The Λ cold dark matter (ΛCDM) model provides a
remarkable description of a wide variety of data from the
early universe – such as cosmic microwave background
(CMB) or big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) –, as well
as observations of large scale structure (LSS) from the
late universe – including the baryon acoustic oscillation
(BAO) and the uncalibrated luminosity distance to su-
pernovae of type Ia (SNIa). However, as the accuracy of
cosmological observations has improved, the concordance
cosmological model starts showing several experimental
discrepancies. Among them, the Hubble tension refers
to the inconsistency between local measurements of
the current expansion rate of the Universe, quantified
by the Hubble constant H0, and the values inferred
from early universe data assuming the ΛCDM model.
More precisely, this tension is essentially driven by the
Planck Collaboration’s observation of the CMB, which
predicts a value of H0 = 67.27 ± 0.60 km/s/Mpc [1]
within the ΛCDM model, and the value measured by
the SH0ES Collaboration using the Cepheid-calibrated
cosmic distance ladder, whose latest measurement yields
H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [2, 3]. The disagreement
between these observations results in an ∼5σ tension.
Experimental efforts are under way to establish whether
this discrepancy can be caused by systematic effects (see,
e.g., [4–9]), but no definitive explanation has yet been
found. This tension could therefore be indicative of new
physics, most likely located in the prerecombination era,
which involves a reduction in the sound horizon before
recombination [10–15]. Early dark energy (EDE) models
are capable of producing such an effect by increasing the
total energy density of the Universe before recombination
with the addition of a scalar field [16–37] (for review of
EDE models see Ref. [38], and for a review of models

Conclusion
We have shown that, for any theory to be able to solve the Hubble tension, it
needs to break at least one of the Assumptions 1 through 7 deﬁned above. This
provides us with two main beneﬁts. First of all, these conditions can be used
as a tool to quickly determine whether a new proposed model has any hope of
relieving the Hubble tension, and as a check on results for those models that
break these conditions only in certain parts of their parameter space.
Furthermore, it allowed us to categorise the models already proposed. This
showed us that breaking the standard relationship between redshift and scale
factor can potentially solve the Hubble tension, but has so far not been ex-
plored in models. Exploration of mechanisms which can achieve such a changed
link between redshift and scale factor could be an interesting avenue of further
research.
One limitation of our work is that it constrains the theory space only from
two very speciﬁc observations, the direct measurement of H0 through distance
ladders, and the interpretation of the CMB. Further research into general con-
ditions on models resulting from other observations could provide useful tools
for further exploring the space of models alleviating the Hubble tension.

Self-interaction among the neutrinos in the early Universe has been proposed as a solution to the
Hubble tension, a discrepancy between the measured values of the Hubble constant from CMB and
low-redshift data. However, ﬂavor-universal neutrino self-interaction is highly constrained by Big
Bang Nucleosynthesis and other laboratory experiments such as, tau and K-meson decay, double-
neutrino beta decay etc. We study the cosmology when only one or two neutrino states are self-
interacting. Such ﬂavor-speciﬁc interactions are less constrained by the laboratory experiments.
Lastly, we address the feasibility of resolving the Hubble tension within the framework of such
ﬂavor-speciﬁc neutrino self-interaction.

Since the early days of the Planck experiment, a discrepancy in the value of the Hubble
parameter from CMB observations and local (low redshift) measurements have become a topic of
active research [1]. This discrepancy has been heightened further with the publication of the latest
data from the Planck experiment and the local 𝐻0-measurement using cepheids and supernovae by
the SH0ES collaboration [2–4]. Planck measured value a Hubble constant using the CMB data 𝐻0 =
67.36±0.54 km s−1Mpc−1, and the SH0ES collaboration measured 𝐻0 = 74.03±1.42 km s−1Mpc−1.

1.5 Summary
We have reviewed what is logically the simplest explanation for the Hubble ten-
sion — the notion that we might be simply seeing the effect of sample variance
in the distance-ladder-based measurements. Sample variance affects the last rung
of the distance ladder, whose distance–redshift relation can be impacted by local
density fluctuations. In the sample-variance explanation scenario, 1) we live in an
underdense region of the universe, which has an enhanced locally measured Hubble
constant, and 2) the local supernova sample is sparse and highly inhomogeneous

10
Dragan Huterer and Hao-Yi Wu
so that the error bars for the local Hubble constant might be larger than previously
estimated.
We have first illustrated the formalism that links the local density to the measured
Hubble constant and have reviewed the methodology adopted by the community
over the past decade. We have then reviewed recent observational results of the
local matter density contrast, which have been inconclusive because it is difficult to
infer the three-dimensional distribution of mass density from galaxies.
Proceeding to discuss our own work on the subject [40], we set out our goal:
to use an N-body simulation to mimic the actual SNIa observations used for
H0 measurements. In the simulation, we place an observer in many independent
subvolumes, each containing the 3D distribution of SNIa that precisely matches
that used in actual observations. This automatically takes into account the effect
of over/underdensities, as well as the inhomogeneous distribution of supernovae.
Moreover, each SNIa is represented by a host halo, whose peculiar velocity is known
in the simulation. Therefore, we have access to a simulated distance-ladder proce-
dure that takes full account of sample variance, including how it mimics actual SNIa
observations. The procedure is also statistically powerful — we use a total of 1.5
million realizations of SNIa observations; see Sec. 1.4.
Combining large-volume N-body ΛCDM simulations with recent SNIa data, we
have found that the effect of the sample variance is small. Specifically, the resulting
standard deviation in the Hubble constant (the square root of sample variance) is
σsamplevariance = 0.31 km s−1Mpc−1.
(1.5)
To explain the 6 km s−1Mpc−1 Hubble tension would require a 20σ effect in sample
variance. Sample variance is therefore an extremely unlikely explanation for the
Hubble tension.
In addition, we have found that resolving the 6 km s−1Mpc−1 Hubble tension
requires an underdensity δ = −0.8 out to a radius 120 h−1Mpc. The underdensity
required to resolve the Hubble tension is so low that it is incompatible with the
large-scale structure in a ΛCDM universe. Although the observational evidence for
local underdensity is still controversial, even the most extreme observational claims
for the local underdensity could not explain the Hubble tension.
Ruling out the local void is an exciting development in the nascent field of Hub-
ble tension, as it removes this very simple explanation and a “guaranteed” effect
in cosmology, leaving more exotic or surprising solutions. Future research should
focus on the systematics of supernova and CMB measurements, as well as the ex-
ploration of new physics beyond the standard model of cosmology.

Discussion
Neutrino self-interaction introduces a phase shift and enhance the CMB anisotropy power
spectra relative to ΛCDM. This scenario has been proposed to ease the Hubble tension. However,
the required strength of the self-interaction to resolve the tension is strongly constrained in ﬂavor-
universal scenario by other laboratory experiments. We studied the cases where only two or one of
the three neutrino species are interacting using the latest CMB data from 2018 Planck experiment.

First, the input rd prior encodes the early-Universe

assumption on the mass density proﬁle of the lensing
galaxies, and various H(z) models could be degenerate
during the integration in the D∆t calibrator. Fortunately,
there is another high-redshift calibrator for IDL from
the cosmic chronometer (CC) data [48], which directly
measures the Hubble expansion rate at high redshifts by
H(z) = −dz/dt/(1 + z) without inputting any presump-
tion on the cosmological model.
Second, the traditional IDL method usually ﬁts to a
cosmological model with Taylor expansion of H(z) in red-
shifts z or y ≡1−a = z/(1+z) [49]. As shown in Fig. 1,
the Taylor expansions in z or y even up to the ﬁfth order
still largely distort the model that they are trying to ap-
proximate in the ﬁrst place even for the ΛCDM model,
hence ﬁtting to the traditional Taylor expansion in z or y
would be misleading for the BAO data considered to date.
Fortunately, there is a global parametrization based on
the cosmic age (PAge) [50, 51] that are faithful in repro-
ducing a large class of late-time models in a wide redshift
range with a high accuracy. See also [52] for a more ac-
curate parametrization based on cosmic age (MAPAge).
Therefore, we improve the traditional IDL method by ﬁt-

MB prior [42] (see also [53, 54] for similar proposals and

further strengths the usual no-go argument from IDL on
the late-time physics.

of H(z) at any redshift within the coverage of the data—including the present-day value

introduced a new binning approach and performed a Gaussian process reconstruction

the late Universe. As redshift increases, H0 decreases from a high value at low redshift
to a low one at high redshift—a trend that could help explain the Hubble tension. This
redshift-dependent evolution of H0 is illustrated in Figure 9, where the transition occurs
at approximately z ∼0.49. Without introducing a new cosmological model, their result
offers a resolution to the Hubble tension with a mitigation level of approximately 70%, and
remains consistent with the H0LiCOW measurement within 1σ confidence level.

CONCLUSIONS AND DISCUSSIONS
The Hubble tension is becoming a crisis for the recent
5σ claim from the recent local direct measurement, which
carefully weights a comprehensive uncertainty budget for
various systematics.

achieve their alleviation of the Hubble tension, and provides insight into avenues

illustrating the various ways our assumptions can be broken, and as such, this
will not be an exhaustive overview of theories alleviating the Hubble tension.

INTRODUCTION
Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension [1–10]. That is,
there is a signiﬁcant tension between the Hubble constants H0 measured from various independent probes
in the early and late/local universes. In particular, assuming the well-known ΛCDM model, the Hubble
constant inferred from the ﬁnal full-mission Planck measurements (Planck 2018) of the cosmic microwave
background (CMB) is given by H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km/s/Mpc [11]. Note that it cannot be substantially
changed by assuming various trivial extensions to the base-ΛCDM model. On the other hand, based on the
Cepheid/Type Ia supernova (SNIa) distance ladder, the local determination of H0 from the Hubble Space
Telescope (HST) and the SH0ES team (R22) is given by H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [12]. Obviously,
this Hubble constant directly from the local measurement of Cepheids/SNIa is in > 5σ tension with the
one indirectly inferred from CMB in the early universe (at high redshift z∗∼1090). Note that the recent
SH0ES 2024 result (R24) H0 = 73.17 ± 0.86 km/s/Mpc [13] is still in 5 −6σ tension with Planck 2018,
while it has been cross-checked with the early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) subsamples from
SH0ES and CCHP.
In history, the Hubble tension has not emerged in the WMAP era of CMB before 2011, then manifested
itself at 2 −3σ since the ﬁrst Planck result in 2013, and ﬁnally reached > 5σ in December 2021 (R22).
Various independent probes, e.g. the Tip of the Red Giant Branch (TRGB), Mira variables, J-region
Asymptotic Giant Branch (JAGB) stars, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), strong gravitational lensing,
gravitational waves, water masers, have been considered in the past decade to this end, but the Hubble
tension has not been resolved to date. We refer to e.g. [1–10] for comprehensive reviews.
Many eﬀorts have been made in the literature. Of course, it is fairly reasonable to carefully check the
observational data, since there might be unresolved systematic errors in them. On the other hand, if all
the observational data are right, the Hubble tension suggests the need for non-trivial extensions to the
standard ΛCDM cosmology. There might be something new in the early, middle, late or local universes.
Although numerous theoretical solutions have been proposed in the literature (e.g. [1–10, 113–118] and
references therein), the Hubble tension is still a tough problem currently.
Here, we are interested in alleviating the Hubble tension with a local void. The key idea is to violate
the cosmological principle by assuming that we live in a locally underdense void centered nearby our
location. In this underdense region, one will feel a locally faster expansion rate compared to the cosmic
average. Noting that H0 ∼73 km/s/Mpc directly measured from the local Cepheids/SNIa is larger than
H0 ∼67 km/s/Mpc indirectly inferred from CMB assuming a background Friedmann-Robertson-Walker
(FRW) universe, the Hubble tension might be alleviated with a local void [1, 2, 7, 8].
A local void can be approximately modeled by using the Lemaˆıtre-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) metric [14–16]

Chapter 1
Not empty enough: a local void cannot solve the
H0 tension
Dragan Huterer and Hao-Yi Wu
Abstract We review arguably the simplest solution for the Hubble tension — the
possibility that we live in a void. In this scenario, the local Hubble constant H0 is
higher than the global value, thus potentially explaining why H0 measured locally
by the distance ladder including Type Ia supernovae (SNIa) would be larger than
the value inferred from the cosmic microwave background and other cosmological
probes. In addition, since the local supernova sample is sparse and highly inhomo-
geneous, the error bars in the local Hubble constant might be larger than previously
estimated. These two effects — local matter density and sample inhomogeneity —
constitute the sample variance (or the cosmic variance) of the local Hubble constant
measurements. To investigate these effects explicitly, we have mocked up SNIa ob-
servations by exactly matching their actual spatial distribution in a large N-body
simulation. We have then investigated whether the sample variance is large enough
to explain the Hubble tension. The answer is resoundingly negative: the typical local
variation in H0 is far smaller than what would be required to explain the Hubble ten-
sion; the latter would require a 20-σ deviation from the expected sample variance.
Equivalently, the void required to explain the Hubble tension would need to be so
empty (δ ≈−0.8 on a scale 120 h−1Mpc) that it would be incompatible with the
large-scale structure in a ΛCDM universe. Therefore, the possibility that we live in
a void does not come close to explaining the Hubble tension.

1.1 Introduction
In the currently favored flat ΛCDM cosmological model, the local measurement
of the Hubble constant H0 from the distance ladder [12, 27, 28] and the global
measurement from the CMB anisotropies [14, 26, 25, 1] should agree. The fact
that they do not may well be a harbinger of new physics — or, at the very least,
unexpectedly large systematic errors in either of the two principal measurements.
Hubble tension has sparked huge interest in cosmology, and a dizzying number
of explanations for it have been put forth (see Ref. [10], which refers to more than
1000 papers in this regard). However, no single explanation has yet proven to be
compelling. Most of the theoretical explanations try to change the global CMB H0
fit from ∼67km s−1Mpc−1 to ∼73km s−1Mpc−1, the value favored by the distance

the way to ∼73km s−1Mpc−1 (rather than halfway there, to ∼70km s−1Mpc−1)
while at the same time improving the goodness of fit to the data to justify the new
parameter(s) of the models in question.

6: In this paper, we reassess the ability of the acoustic early dark energy (ADE) and axion-like early
7: dark energy (EDE) models to resolve the Hubble tension in light of the new Pantheon+ and SH0ES
8: data on the one hand, and the BOSS LRG and eBOSS QSO data, analyzed under the effective
9: field theory of large-scale structures (ETFofLSS) on the other hand. We find that the Pantheon+
10: data, which favor a larger Ωm value than the Pantheon data, have a strong constraining power on
11: the ADE model, while the EFTofLSS analysis of the BOSS and eBOSS data only slightly increases
12: the constraints. We establish that the ADE model is now strongly disfavored as a solution to the
13: Hubble tension, with a remaining tension of 3.6σ (according to the QDMAP metric). In addition, we
14: find that the axion-like EDE model performs better when confronted to the same datasets, with a
15: residual tension of 2.5σ. This work shows that the Pantheon+ data can have a decisive impact on
16: models which aim to resolve the Hubble tension.
17: I.
18: INTRODUCTION
19: The Λ cold dark matter (ΛCDM) model provides a
20: remarkable description of a wide variety of data from the
21: early universe – such as cosmic microwave background
22: (CMB) or big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) –, as well
23: as observations of large scale structure (LSS) from the
24: late universe – including the baryon acoustic oscillation
25: (BAO) and the uncalibrated luminosity distance to su-
26: pernovae of type Ia (SNIa). However, as the accuracy of
27: cosmological observations has improved, the concordance
28: cosmological model starts showing several experimental
29: discrepancies. Among them, the Hubble tension refers
30: to the inconsistency between local measurements of
31: the current expansion rate of the Universe, quantified
32: by the Hubble constant H0, and the values inferred
33: from early universe data assuming the ΛCDM model.
34: More precisely, this tension is essentially driven by the
35: Planck Collaboration’s observation of the CMB, which
36: predicts a value of H0 = 67.27 ± 0.60 km/s/Mpc [1]
37: within the ΛCDM model, and the value measured by
38: the SH0ES Collaboration using the Cepheid-calibrated
39: cosmic distance ladder, whose latest measurement yields
40: H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [2, 3]. The disagreement
41: between these observations results in an ∼5σ tension.
42: Experimental efforts are under way to establish whether
43: this discrepancy can be caused by systematic effects (see,
44: e.g., [4–9]), but no definitive explanation has yet been
45: found. This tension could therefore be indicative of new
46: physics, most likely located in the prerecombination era,
47: which involves a reduction in the sound horizon before
48: recombination [10–15]. Early dark energy (EDE) models
49: are capable of producing such an effect by increasing the
50: total energy density of the Universe before recombination
51: with the addition of a scalar field [16–37] (for review of
52: EDE models see Ref. [38], and for a review of models
53: ∗Electronic address: theo.simon@umontpellier.fr
54: that could resolve the Hubble tension see Refs. [15, 39]).
55: In the following, we consider the specific case of acoustic
56: dark energy (ADE) developed in Refs. [40, 41].
57: In this paper, we reassess the constraints on the ADE
58: and axion-like EDE models (paying particular attention
59: to the former) and their ability to resolve the Hubble
60: tension, by successively evaluating the impact of the
61: effective field theory (EFT) full-shape analysis applied to

1: Investigating the Hubble Tension: Eﬀect of Cepheid
2: Calibration
3: Rahul Kumar Thakur1,3, Harish Kumar2, Shashikant Gupta2, Dinkar Verma2,
4: Rahul Nigam1
5: 1 Department of Physics, Birla Institute of Technology & Science, Pilani
