9: Abstract
10: Recent observations of Type Ia supernovae (SNe) by SH0ES collabo-
11: ration (R11 and R16) diverge from the value reported by recent CMBR
12: observations utilising the Planck satellite and application of the ΛCDM
13: cosmological model by at least 3σ. It is among the most challenging prob-
14: lems in contemporary cosmology and is known as the Hubble tension. The
15: SNe Ia in R11 and R16 were calibrated through cepheid variables in three
16: distinct galaxies: Milky Way, LMC, and NGC4258. Carnegie Hubble Pro-
17: gram (CHP) observations of type Ia SNe calibrated using the tip of the
18: red giant approach yielded a somewhat diﬀerent estimate for the Hubble
19: constant. This decreased the Hubble tension from over 3σ to below 2σ.
20: It is a legitimate question to answer whether there are any issues with
21: SNe Ia calibration and to investigate whether the Hubble tension is real
22: or not. We use statistical techniques namely, ANOVA, K-S test, and t-
23: test to examine whether the cepheid calibration is host-dependent. Our
24: analysis shows that (i) both R11 and R16 data suﬀer from non-Gaussian
25: systematic eﬀects, (ii) H0 values in the sub-samples (diﬀerent anchor-
26: based) in both R11 and R16 groups are signiﬁcantly diﬀerent at a 99%
27: conﬁdence level, and (iii) neglecting the metal-rich MW sample does not
28: reduce the H0 value signiﬁcantly, and thus Hubble tension persists. A
29: small reduction in the Hubble constant could be linked to the diﬀerences
30: in the host environment. Hence instead of using a single universal relation
31: environment based slope and zero point should be preferred.
32: 1
33: Introduction
34: The Hubble constant (H0) has been one of the key parameters of modern cos-
35: mology since it determines the expansion rate as well as the age of the Universe.
36: Its numerical value also controls the critical density, ρc = 3H0/8πG, required
37: for the ﬂat geometry of space and many other cosmological parameters such
38: as the physical properties of galaxies and quasars and the growth of large-scale
39: structures.
40: 1
41: arXiv:2211.00578v1  [astro-ph.CO]  1 Nov 2022
42: 
43: Measuring H0 with great precision has been among the most important chal-
44: lenges in the last few decades. Various methods have been employed to deter-
45: mine the accurate value of the Hubble constant. Two fundamentally diﬀerent
46: methods, the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) [1, 2] along
47: with the standard cosmological model and distance ladder-based method using
48: Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) provide quite diﬀerent results, an issue known
49: as the Hubble tension.
50: The observations of Cosmic Microwave Background
51: (CMB) anisotropies provide a global value of H0 = 67.8 ± 0.9 ± 1.1 km/S/Mpc.
52: SNe Ia calibrated using the Cepheid variables in diﬀerent galaxies (SH0ES pro-
53: gram), and time delay measurements of gravitationally lensed quasars [3] pro-
54: vide a higher value which is more than 3σ away from that provided by CMBR
55: [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]. Diﬀerent explanations have been proposed, including
56: a dark component in the early Universe [13, 14] or modiﬁcations in the late
57: universe physics [15, 16] to resolve the Hubble tension.
58: The SH0ES program was designed to reﬁne the SNe Ia calibration using the
59: Hubble Space Telescope (HST) to precisely measure the Hubble constant and
60: determine the equation of the state parameter of dark energy [5].
61: HST key
62: project was the ﬁrst generation attempt to measure H0 by observing Cepheids
63: in various SNe host galaxies. It used the WFPC2 camera, which had a limited
64: range (≈20Mpc). SH0ES program, on the other hand, uses the advanced ACS,
65: WFC3, and NICMOS instruments and hence is a “second-generation” attempt
66: to measure H0 using HST. Only suitable SNe Ia, which are spectroscopically
67: normal, have low reddening, and for which observation before maximum bright-
68: ness is available, have been considered in the SH0ES sample.
69: A re-analysis of the Cepheid data that was used to calibrate Type Ia super-
70: novae to determine the Hubble constant H0 was conducted by [17]. The empir-
71: ical Cepheid calibration parameters RW (Cepheid Wesenheit colour-luminosity
72: parameter) and M W
73: H (Cepheid Wesenheit H-band absolute magnitude) were al-
74: lowed to vary for each unique galaxy rather than a universal value. Additionally,
75: the possibility of two universal values of these parameters arises: one for large
76: galactic distances (D > Dc) and one for small galactic distances (D < Dc),
77: where Dc is a critical transition distance. Their ﬁndings show a three-σ dispar-
78: ity between the values of the low and high galactic distance parameters.
79: To deduce the value of H0, [18] analysed the SH0ES data [5]. Instead of
80: enforcing a universal colour-luminosity relation to correct the Cepheid magni-
81: tudes, they employ a data-driven approach in which the optical colours and
82: near-infrared magnitudes of the Cepheids are used to derive individual colour
83: luminosity relations for each Type Ia supernova host and anchor galaxy. The
84: Milky Way anchor is in tension with the NGC 4258 and the Large Magellanic
85: Cloud anchors by a factor of 2.1–3.1 σ when individual extinction rules are taken
86: into account and the correlated nature of H0 is taken into consideration.
87: In the present work, we wish to address the following questions: (i) Are
88: there systematic issues in the H0 measurement of the SH0ES program? (ii) Are
89: there appreciable diﬀerences in the H0 values produced from SNe Ia calibration
90: using various anchors?
91: If yes, what are the implications?
92: The rest of the
93: paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the methodology and the data
94: 2
95: 
96: employed. In section 3, we present the main results of our analysis. This is
97: followed by Section 4, wherein we present a summary and discussion.

99: Data and Methods
100: 2.1
101: Data
102: For our analysis, we have used data from [4] (R11) and [5] (R16). The mea-
103: surement of H0 in both R11 and R16 relies on (i) the calibration of Cepheid
104: variables in the Milky Way (MW), LMC, and NGC4258, and (ii) SNe Ia light
105: curve calibration through these Cepheid stars. Along with the photometric ob-
106: servations, the geometric distances through parallax methods have also been
107: conﬁrmed for the MW sample of Cepheids (13 in R11 and 15 in R16). The
108: parallax measurements were made using HST and Hipparcos, and are available
109: in [19, 20, 21, 22]. One should note that the MW Cepheid calibration provides
110: the highest value of H0 among all three samples. Geometric distances through
111: detached eclipsing binaries (DEBs) have been used along with the photometry
112: to calibrate LMC cepheids. DEBs composed of both early type as well as late
113: type stars have been used to measure the distance to the LMC [23].
114: Thus,
115: there are three subsets of data in both R11 and R16. Each subset in R11 has
116: 15 data points which are presented in Table 4 of [4]. The overall 3% accuracy
117: in the measurement of H0 has been claimed in R11. R16 is a comparatively
118: more recent and more precise data set. The authors claim a 2.4% precision in
119: the measurement of H0. Each sample of MW, LMC, and NGC4258 contains 22
120: data points which are presented in Table 8 of [5].

16: The Hubble tension is investigated taking into account the cosmological look-back time. Speciﬁcally, consid-
17: ering a single equation, widely used in standard cosmology, it is possible to recover both values of the Hubble
18: constant H0 reported by the SH0ES and Planck collaborations: the former is obtained through cosmological
19: ladder methods (e.g. Cepheids, Supernovae Type IA) and the latter through measurements of the Cosmic Mi-
20: crowave Background. Also, other values obtained in the literature are achieved with the same approach. We
21: conclude that the Hubble tension can be removed if the look-back time is correctly referred to the redshift where
22: the measurement is performed.
23: Keywords: Observational cosmology; Hubble-Lemaˆıtre constant; look-back time.
24: I.
25: INTRODUCTION
26: The so-called H0 tension, related to the reported discrepancy on the measured values of Hubble-Lemaˆıtre (henceforth Hubble)
27: constant, H0, is claimed to be one of the most critical issues for the Λ Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) model, considered the
28: standard picture of the observed Universe. This staggering discrepancy arises when comparing estimates on H0 provided by
29: standard candles with those inferred by the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) [1]. In fact, the results from the
30: SH0ES collaboration, obtained by considering the cosmological ladder and probes like classical Cepheids and Supernovae Type
31: Ia (SNe Ia), in a region with redshift interval 0.02333 < z < 0.15, tell us that H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/(s Mpc) at 68% conﬁdence
32: level (CL) [2], while the Planck collaboration, reporting observations of the CMBR, shows, instead, that H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km/(s
33: Mpc) at 68% CL [3]. Despite the accuracy of both approaches, a 5.0σ tension emerges and it seems to be irreconcilable under
34: the standard of the ΛCDM model.
35: The problem has to be addressed both from experimental and theoretical points of view. Considering the increasing precision
36: achieved by recent observations, an experimental reason for the tension, related to some systematic eﬀects, is becoming less and
37: less probable [1, 4]. Thus this tension (and other ones revealed in cosmological parameters [1]) is seemingly hinting at some
38: undeﬁned new physics, going beyond the ΛCDM model. The last conclusion can be inferred also from other critical issues of
39: the standard cosmological model, like the nature of dark matter and dark energy, which should account for approximately 25%
40: and 70%, respectively, of the energy-density budget of the observed Universe [4–13]. However, the nature of the dark side of

Discussion
Neutrino self-interaction introduces a phase shift and enhance the CMB anisotropy power
spectra relative to ΛCDM. This scenario has been proposed to ease the Hubble tension. However,
the required strength of the self-interaction to resolve the tension is strongly constrained in ﬂavor-
universal scenario by other laboratory experiments. We studied the cases where only two or one of
the three neutrino species are interacting using the latest CMB data from 2018 Planck experiment.
We found a bimodal posterior as in the previous studies with ﬂavor-universal case. Moreover, we
found that the strongly interacting (SI) mode is boosted in the ﬂavor-speciﬁc scenario. Less number
of interacting neutrino means less amount of changes in the CMB power spectra which makes larger
coupling strength more compatible with the data boosting the SI mode.
The neutrino coupling strength 𝐺eﬀis degenerate with the Hubble constant 𝐻0, and the SI
mode favors a slightly larger value of 𝐻0 compared to ΛCDM, easing the Hubble tension. We,
however, found that the value of 𝐻0 is decreased when only two or one neutrinos are interacting. As
a result, the SINU scenario cannot resolve the Hubble tension when all laboratory and cosmological
constraints are taken into consideration. In our work, we did not include oﬀ-diagonal interactions as
it requires one to incorporate neutrino mass as well. Hence, it remains to be seen how the addition
of oﬀ-diagonal interaction aﬀects the Hubble parameter.

236: novel probes, possibly providing a standalone estimate of cosmological parameters in this redshift region, like quasars, novel
237: gravitational wave standard sirens, galaxy clusters, Lyman-α lines, or gamma-ray bursts [101–104].
238: IV.
239: DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS
240: The problem of the H0 tension can be addressed in the framework of the ΛCDM model in terms of look-back time considered
241: at the redshift where measurements are performed. In this derivation, the values of the age of the Universe and the cosmic
242: densities, provided by the Planck collaboration, are adopted. The look-back time curve, matching the observational values
243: of H0, is shown in Fig. 1. According to this approach, we are able to recover most of the reported H0 measurements and,
244: more remarkably, the two most representatives for the H0 tension, namely the ones provided by the Planck [3] and SH0ES
245: [2] collaborations. The result is interesting because the concordance of H0 measurements is achieved independently from the
246: type of performed measurement. Indeed, we have considered estimates obtained by diﬀerent standard candles (SNe Ia, TRGB,
247: Cepheids, etc), phenomena concerning early stages of the Universe (CMBR, Cosmic Dawn, Equivalence Epoch), and also novel
248: probes (gravitational waves). According to this picture, we may conclude that no systematic errors nor new physics are necessary
249: to explain the tension, which, instead, can be accounted for with a single formula in the framework of the ΛCDM model. In
250: other words, by adopting the look-back time, we can consistently account for late-type and early-type measurements, conﬁrming
251: the underlying consistency of the ΛCDM model. We also point out that this evolution of H0 constant in the framework of the
252: 
253: 5
254: ΛCDM model does not change its role as a formal integration constant derived from the Friedman equations, but its operative
255: value depends on the redshift where it is inferred. This conclusion is important for the deﬁnition of the cosmological distances,
256: which are all depending on H0.
257: It is worth stressing that the value of the age of the Universe, T0, has been derived by the Planck collaboration starting from
258: six independent parameters (the minimum number of parameters necessary to describe the ΛCDM model), among which H0
259: is not included. In fact, also H0 is inferred from the same minimum number of independent parameters. This means that any
260: circularity problem is avoided. Furthermore, we can note that the plot in Fig. 1 is in agreement with the general trend of H0
261: late-type measurements. See, for example, Ref. [105] where the estimate H0 = 72.94 ± 0.75km/(s Mpc) at 68% CL is reported.
262: Furthermore, our results are consistent with constraints on H0 obtained from the age of the Universe: for instance, in [52], an
263: upper limit at H0 = 73.2 km/(s Mpc) with 95% CL has been inferred by considering the ages of old astrophysical objects up to
264: z ∼8. This value is consistent with Fig. 1, because, according to our approach, we ﬁnd H0 = 72.3 km/(s Mpc) for that particular
265: value of the redshift.
266: Finally, computations reported here are consistent with the interpretation proposed in [34, 35], according to which a funda-
267: mental uncertainty on H0 exists a priori in the framework of the ΛCDM scenario. Furthermore, by the light-travel distance,
268: a cosmological Compton length can be always deﬁned. This distance is strictly connected to the look-back time [34] without
269: contradiction with present results.
270: As a ﬁnal remark, it is useful noticing that we do not exclude the idea of new physics beyond the ΛCDM model, because other
271: issues, like dark energy and dark matter, at late time, or inﬂation, at early time, could require to go beyond GR and standard
272: cosmology. However, from the above discussion, it is possible to state that new physics is not necessary for the particular issue
273: of the H0 tension, which can be completely accounted for in the framework of the ΛCDM model.

9: As observations of the Hubble parameter from both early and late
10: sources have improved, the tension between these has increased to be well
11: above the 5σ threshold. Given this, the need for an explanation of such
12: a tension has grown. In this paper, we explore a set of 7 assumptions,
13: and show that, in order to alleviate the Hubble tension, a model needs to
14: break at least one of these 7, providing a quick and easy to apply check
15: for new model proposals. We also use this framework to make a rough
16: categorisation of current proposed models, and show the existence of at
17: least one under-explored avenue of alleviating the Hubble tension.

19: Introduction
20: Over the last decade cosmological observations have signiﬁcantly improved, both
21: for early-time as well as late-time observations. Early-time measurements by
22: the Planck collaboration give a value of H0 = 67.36±0.54 [1]. This value is cor-
23: roborated by the results published in [2] combining Dark Energy Survey (DES),
24: Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) con-
25: straints to give a value of H0 = 67.4 ± 1.1.
26: For late-time measurements, results from [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] were combined in [8]
27: to give a combined estimate of H0 = 73.3±0.8 (though with some caveats on the
28: error bounds due to not fully accounting for shared contributions in the distance
29: ladder). Furthermore, it is shown that these results, even when discarding some,
30: still provide a 4 −6σ tension between early and late-time values of H0. There
31: have since been further late-time measurements reported in [9, 10], but other
32: than strengthening error bounds, these do not signiﬁcantly change this picture.
33: This tension is large enough that it has created a need for an explanation.
34: As such, there have been a myriad of models proposed that alleviate (part of)
35: this tension, overviews of which are given in [11, 12].
36: Currently, there are few general results placing formal conditions on what
37: a model alleviating the Hubble tension should look like. The authors are only

8: Abstract
9: As observations of the Hubble parameter from both early and late
10: sources have improved, the tension between these has increased to be well
11: above the 5σ threshold. Given this, the need for an explanation of such
12: a tension has grown. In this paper, we explore a set of 7 assumptions,
13: and show that, in order to alleviate the Hubble tension, a model needs to
14: break at least one of these 7, providing a quick and easy to apply check
15: for new model proposals. We also use this framework to make a rough
16: categorisation of current proposed models, and show the existence of at
17: least one under-explored avenue of alleviating the Hubble tension.
18: 1
19: Introduction
20: Over the last decade cosmological observations have signiﬁcantly improved, both
21: for early-time as well as late-time observations. Early-time measurements by
22: the Planck collaboration give a value of H0 = 67.36±0.54 [1]. This value is cor-
23: roborated by the results published in [2] combining Dark Energy Survey (DES),
24: Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) con-
25: straints to give a value of H0 = 67.4 ± 1.1.
26: For late-time measurements, results from [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] were combined in [8]
27: to give a combined estimate of H0 = 73.3±0.8 (though with some caveats on the
28: error bounds due to not fully accounting for shared contributions in the distance
29: ladder). Furthermore, it is shown that these results, even when discarding some,
30: still provide a 4 −6σ tension between early and late-time values of H0. There
31: have since been further late-time measurements reported in [9, 10], but other
32: than strengthening error bounds, these do not signiﬁcantly change this picture.
33: This tension is large enough that it has created a need for an explanation.
34: As such, there have been a myriad of models proposed that alleviate (part of)
35: this tension, overviews of which are given in [11, 12].
36: Currently, there are few general results placing formal conditions on what
37: a model alleviating the Hubble tension should look like. The authors are only
38: 1
39: 
40: aware of [13], providing a general result showing that a viable model needs to
41: modify more than just the size of the sound horizon.1 The goal of this paper
42: is to provide a new general (model independent) result setting conditions on
43: models alleviating the Hubble tension.
44: We do this by taking a higher level view of possible alleviating models. In
45: section 2, we provide a set of 7 assumptions based on CMB observations and
46: direct measurements of H0 which combine to create a space of options in which
47: the cosmological standard model ΛCDM is an extremum. This then allows us
48: to show that our 7 assumptions exclude any model that has the potential to
49: alleviate the Hubble tension, implying that any such model should break at
50: least 1 of our 7 assumptions.
51: We then demonstrate one application of this result in section 3 by making
52: a categorisation of the space of existing proposals by means of the assumptions
53: they break. This provides us with two things: A somewhat reasonable categori-
54: sation of existing proposals, and an under-explored avenue for new solutions.

## Shift 5 - Initial Review

### Status
- This is shift 5. My notebook didn't exist before, so this is the first entry.
- Read: board/STATUS.md, board/to_skeptic_a/1_judge_round1_assign.md, debate/TRANSCRIPT.md, archive/INDEX.txt
- Read papers: 2211.00578 (Thakur et al., Cepheid calibration), 2302.13671 (Capozziello et al., look-back time)
- Also read 2101.01372 (7 assumptions framework) for context

### Key Findings from My Papers

**2211.00578 (Thakur et al.):**
- Both R11 and R16 data suffer from non-Gaussian systematic effects
- ANOVA: H0 values differ significantly between anchors at 99% CL (R11: F=85.70, p=1.5e-15; R16: F=144.49, p=2.91e-24)
- MW anchor stands out: paired t-test rejects null when MW is involved (h=1)
- MW mean χi is ~3σ away from zero
- With NGC+LMC only: H0 = 72.61 ± 0.38 km/s/Mpc (Table 9)
- Systematic issues: metallicity (MW Cepheids brighter than LMC despite theory), binary systems (>60% Cepheids in binaries, 44% of binaries are triples), rotation effects
- Paper concludes: "Hubble tension is real and needs to be resolved" but points to calibration systematics

**2302.13671 (Capozziello et al.):**
- Look-back time reinterpretation: H0 depends on redshift where measured
- Using Planck values (T0=13.797 Gyr, Ωr=9.252e-5, ΩM=0.3153, ΩΛ=0.6847):
  - At z=0.15 (SH0ES): H0 = 73.29 km/s/Mpc (Eq. 7) — consistent with SH0ES
  - At z→∞ (CMB): H0 = 67.40 km/s/Mpc (Eq. 8) — consistent with Planck
- Most measurements consistent within 1σ with Eq.(7) curve
- Claims no systematic errors nor new physics needed

### Assessment of 2302.13671
- The look-back time argument is mathematically correct but physically circular: it assumes ΛCDM with Planck parameters to "derive" both H0 values, then claims consistency
- The paper's own Fig. 1 shows H0 evolution with redshift, but this evolution is baked into the ΛCDM assumption
- The claim that "no systematic errors nor new physics are necessary" is overstated — the paper simply re-expresses the same H0 in a different way
- However, the paper does highlight an important point: H0 measurements at different redshifts are not directly comparable without accounting for look-back time effects

### Assessment of 2211.00578

18: ## Round 1, late_a
19: 
20: **Position: the tension is a statement about the *local* expansion rate, not about the sound horizon. Late-universe and local physics — a local underdensity, and a mild late-time departure from ΛCDM — reproduce the data; nothing requires new early-universe microphysics.**
21: 
22: **1. The data already show a redshift-dependent H0, and that is the whole story.** With equal-width binning in ten redshift intervals, the H0(z) analysis compiled in 2606.12980 (Jia & Dai, Galaxies review) finds a declining trend significant at **5.6σ for z > 0.3**: H0 at low z matches SH0ES, and at high z converges to the CMB value (2606.12980 §, Fig. 11). Independent routes reproduce the same shape: six-bin grouping of megamasers, cosmic chronometers, SNe Ia and BAO gives the trend at **2.1σ** (Krishnan et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 7), and a Gaussian-process reconstruction of H(z) with no new cosmological model finds the transition at **z ≈ 0.49**, mitigating the tension by **~70%** and remaining consistent with H0LiCOW within 1σ (Hu & Wang, via 2606.12980 Fig. 9). A parametrisation H0(z) = H̃0(1+z)^α fitted in ΛCDM gives **H0 = 73.493 ± 0.144 km/s/Mpc** with **α = 0.008 ± 0.006** and **H0(z=1100) = 69.271 ± 2.815 km/s/Mpc**, alleviating the tension by **~66%** (Dainotti et al., 2606.12980). Lensed-quasar time delays show the same mild decline at **1.9σ**, softening to **1.7σ** with a new H0 measurement (2606.12980). Every one of these is a *late-universe* signal. The CMB's 67 km/s/Mpc is the value of H0 far outside our inhomogeneous neighbourhood; the ladder measures it inside. A discrepancy between those two statements is expected without any new field existing at z > 1100.
23: 
24: **2. DESI strengthens the late-time reading, and the void works quantitatively.** DESI BAO + Planck + SNe lifts the preference for w0waCDM over ΛCDM to **3.9σ** (2606.12980, citing DESI+DESY5), and DESI DR2 BAO + Pantheon+ reproduces the same declining H0(z) (2606.12980 Fig. 12). Void models with both **Gaussian and exponential** density profiles reproduce that decline and do so while keeping a *low background* H0 (Mazurenko et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 13). The best-fit void depth found there, δV ≈ **−0.48, −0.47, −0.47** for zcut = 0.2, 1.0, 2.0, gives Ωm,in = (1+δV)Ωm,out ≈ 0.2 — directly consistent with the loose cluster-counting constraint **Ωm = 0.20 ± 0.04 ± 0.09** quoted in 2504.13380. So a deep local void is not forbidden by large-scale structure.
25: 
26: **3. 2504.13380: the local void is strongly preferred once the CMB is in the fit.** Fitting Planck 2018 + Pantheon+ SNe (zcut = 0.2), the ΛLTB void models beat both fiducials overwhelmingly: **ΔBIC = −73.28 and ΔAIC = −91.28 vs ΛCDM_P18 with ln B = 25.36** (ΛLTB4M), and **ΔBIC = −70.81, ΔAIC = −84.81, ln B = 25.87** (ΛLTB3M), against fiducial best-fit χ²_tot,min = 938.769 (ΛCDM_F) and 943.827 (ΛCDM_P18). The ranking is stable: **ΛLTB3M ≫ ΛLTB2M**. The required depth, **δV = −0.45^{+0.05}_{−0.06}** (2M), **−0.44 ± 0.05** (3M), **−0.49 ± 0.06** (4M), i.e. δV ≲ −38%, "even <~−50%", and the transitions of the SN absolute magnitude at **~20 Mpc, ~129 Mpc and ~860–960 Mpc** are all significant far beyond 1σ (Tables IV, V). Crucially, the CMB scale is far outside the void, so Ωm,out = 0.3153 and H0,out = 67.36 km/s/Mpc are retained — the void changes the local number, not the global fit.
27: 
28: **4. Honest accounting of the two strongest objections, and why they do not close the case.**
29: 
30: *(a) "No-go for late-time solutions" (2202.12214, Cai et al.).* Their ΔBIC are real: **+5.3483** (PAge) and **+11.0470** (MAPAge) over ΛCDM for CC+BAO+SNe, strengthening to **ΔBIC > 10** (RSD 2018) and **> 8** (RSD 2021). But that result is about *homogeneous* late-time background parametrisations fitted to *background* data, and the paper says so: it concludes that if late-time solutions are invoked "then the modifications must go beyond the background level", and it explicitly excepts inhomogeneous solutions from its no-go. Two further facts cut my way. First, their own IDL fit gives **H0 = 70.1 ± 2.5 km/s/Mpc** (CC+BAO+SNe, ΛCDM) and **70.2 ± 2.5** with RSD 2018 — the late-universe data, unhelped, already sit ~3σ above Planck's 67.27 ± 0.60 and pull toward SH0ES. Second, that same analysis shows a second, independent H0 problem that is *not* about the sound horizon: with M_B fixed identically for both ladders, **H0^LDL ≈ 74 vs H0^IDL ≈ 68**, which is described as "the recent intriguing view on the H0 tension as the M_B tension". I do not need a smaller r_d; I need the two rungs to talk about the same universe, which is precisely what a void violates.
31: 
32: *(b) "Not empty enough" (2309.05749, Huterer & Wu).* Their sample-variance result is solid and I do not dispute it: **σ_samplevariance = 0.31 km/s/Mpc** from ~1.5 million mock Supercal configurations in 512 subvolumes, so that **|H0^Planck − H0^loc|/σ ≈ 20**; resolving 6 km/s/Mpc would need **δ ≈ −0.8 out to 120 h⁻¹Mpc**, and even a **2σ**-underdense subvolume only raises H0 slightly above Planck's ~67. Perturbation theory agrees closely (**~0.4 km/s/Mpc** for the Pantheon sample). But this is a statement about *sample variance of a single ladder in a ΛCDM structure field*, i.e. the null hypothesis of a homogeneous background. It is exactly the hypothesis the 5.6σ H0(z) decline already rejects, and it is not the void-plus-transition models of 2504.13380, where the CMB region is explicitly placed at Ωm,out = 0.3153 outside the void and a 3-parameter profile (δV, rV, Δr) replaces the top-hat of 2309.05749. The two papers are not measuring the same thing; the panel should treat 2309.05749 as ruling out *voids as the sole explanation in a ΛCDM background*, not voids as a component of one.
33: 
34: **5. Where I concede ground.** In 2504.13380, with the Pantheon+ sample *alone*, the void models are **not** preferred over ΛCDM_F in Bayesian information criterion — several cases have positive ΔBIC_F. The gain appears when the CMB is jointly fitted. And the ΛLTB3M/4M fit requires the absolute-magnitude transitions, which is SN-population physics; the authors themselves flag the over-fitting risk and concede "we still cannot claim a full triumph so far" for the SN-only case. I will not pretend this is a clean ΛCDM-plus-void model. My claim is narrower and, I think, still strong: **the tension does not require breaking any early-universe assumption, and the late-universe data are pointing the same way as my proposal.** Under 2101.01372's framework the late-time route breaks Assumption 2 (homogeneity) and/or Assumption 6 (that late-time distance physics is understood), never Assumptions 1, 3, 4, 5 or 7 — a smaller and more conservative set to abandon than reducing r_s, which drags ω_b, S8 and BBN along with it. FRBs are the cheap, decisive test of the void depth (2606.12980, Banik et al.), and DESI DR2's continued preference for evolving w(z) is the decisive test of the background-level version.

21: 
22: **1. A parametrisation H0(z) = H̃0(1+z)^α fitted in ΛCDM gives **H0 = 73.493 ± 0.144 km/s/Mpc** with **α = 0.008 ± 0.006** and **H0(z=1100) = 69.271 ± 2.815 km/s/Mpc**, alleviating the tension by **~66%** (Dainotti et al., 2606.12980). The CMB's 67 km/s/Mpc is the value of H0 far outside our inhomogeneous neighbourhood; the ladder measures it inside. A discrepancy between those two statements is expected without any new field existing at z > 1100.
23: 
24: **2. Void models with both **Gaussian and exponential** density profiles reproduce that decline and do so while keeping a *low background* H0 (Mazurenko et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 13). The best-fit void depth found there, δV ≈ **−0.48, −0.47, −0.47** for zcut = 0.2, 1.0, 2.0, gives Ωm,in = (1+δV)Ωm,out ≈ 0.2 — directly consistent with the loose cluster-counting constraint **Ωm = 0.20 ± 0.04 ± 0.09** quoted in 2504.13380. So a deep local void is not forbidden by large-scale structure.

26: **3. 2504.13380: the local void is strongly preferred once the CMB is in the fit.** Fitting Planck 2018 + Pantheon+ SNe (zcut = 0.2), the ΛLTB void models beat both fiducials overwhelmingly: **ΔBIC = −73.28 and ΔAIC = −91.28 vs ΛCDM_P18 with ln B = 25.36** (ΛLTB4M), and **ΔBIC = −70.81, ΔAIC = −84.81, ln B = 25.87** (ΛLTB3M), against fiducial best-fit χ²_tot,min = 938.769 (ΛCDM_F) and 943.827 (ΛCDM_P18). 28: **4. Honest accounting of the two strongest objections, and why they do not close the case.**

30: *(a) "No-go for late-time solutions" (2202.12214, Cai et al.).* Their ΔBIC are real: **+5.3483** (PAge) and **+11.0470** (MAPAge) over ΛCDM for CC+BAO+SNe, strengthening to **ΔBIC > 10** (RSD 2018) and **> 8** (RSD 2021). Two further facts cut my way. First, their own IDL fit gives **H0 = 70.1 ± 2.5 km/s/Mpc** (CC+BAO+SNe, ΛCDM) and **70.2 ± 2.5** with RSD 2018 — the late-universe data, unhelped, already sit ~3σ above Planck's 67.27 ± 0.60 and pull toward SH0ES. 32: *(b) "Not empty enough" (2309.05749, Huterer & Wu).* Their sample-variance result is solid and I do not dispute it: **σ_samplevariance = 0.31 km/s/Mpc** from ~1.5 million mock Supercal configurations in 512 subvolumes, so that **|H0^Planck − H0^loc|/σ ≈ 20**; resolving 6 km/s/Mpc would need **δ ≈ −0.8 out to 120 h⁻¹Mpc**, and even a **2σ**-underdense subvolume only raises H0 slightly above Planck's ~67. 2: 
3: ## Round 1, Judge
4: 
5: **Questions to settle:**
6: 1. Is the Hubble tension evidence of new physics beyond ΛCDM, or is it a measurement and analysis problem?
7: 2. Which assumptions underpinning the ΛCDM inference of H0 must break to resolve the tension? (cf. 2101.01372's 7 assumptions)
8: 3. Are early-universe solutions (EDE, modified recombination, self-interacting neutrinos) viable? Are late-universe solutions (local void, modified gravity, late dark energy) viable?
9: 
10: **Paper assignments:**
11: - **early_a** (early universe new physics): 2101.01372, 2212.04494, 2502.15541, 2507.23355
12: - **late_a** (late universe/local): 2202.12214, 2309.05749, 2504.13380, 2606.12980
13: - **skeptic_a** (measurement problem): 2211.00578, 2302.13671
14: - **skeptic_b** (tests resolutions against data): 2109.03263, 2310.16800
15: - **methods** (statistician): 2101.01372 (methods), 2606.12980 (statistics)
16: 
17: **Rules:** Each panelist appends one statement under `## Round 1, <name>`. Read all papers before speaking. Cite specific arXiv IDs. Be concise but substantive.
18: ## Round 1, late_a
19: 
20: **Position: the tension is a statement about the *local* expansion rate, not about the sound horizon. Late-universe and local physics — a local underdensity, and a mild late-time departure from ΛCDM — reproduce the data; nothing requires new early-universe microphysics.**
21: 
22: **1. The data already show a redshift-dependent H0, and that is the whole story.** With equal-width binning in ten redshift intervals, the H0(z) analysis compiled in 2606.12980 (Jia & Dai, Galaxies review) finds a declining trend significant at **5.6σ for z > 0.3**: H0 at low z matches SH0ES, and at high z converges to the CMB value (2606.12980 §, Fig. 11). Independent routes reproduce the same shape: six-bin grouping of megamasers, cosmic chronometers, SNe Ia and BAO gives the trend at **2.1σ** (Krishnan et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 7), and a Gaussian-process reconstruction of H(z) with no new cosmological model finds the transition at **z ≈ 0.49**, mitigating the tension by **~70%** and remaining consistent with H0LiCOW within 1σ (Hu & Wang, via 2606.12980 Fig. 9). A parametrisation H0(z) = H̃0(1+z)^α fitted in ΛCDM gives **H0 = 73.493 ± 0.144 km/s/Mpc** with **α = 0.008 ± 0.006** and **H0(z=1100) = 69.271 ± 2.815 km/s/Mpc**, alleviating the tension by **~66%** (Dainotti et al., 2606.12980). Lensed-quasar time delays show the same mild decline at **1.9σ**, softening to **1.7σ** with a new H0 measurement (2606.12980). Every one of these is a *late-universe* signal. The CMB's 67 km/s/Mpc is the value of H0 far outside our inhomogeneous neighbourhood; the ladder measures it inside. A discrepancy between those two statements is expected without any new field existing at z > 1100.
23: 
24: **2. DESI strengthens the late-time reading, and the void works quantitatively.** DESI BAO + Planck + SNe lifts the preference for w0waCDM over ΛCDM to **3.9σ** (2606.12980, citing DESI+DESY5), and DESI DR2 BAO + Pantheon+ reproduces the same declining H0(z) (2606.12980 Fig. 12). Void models with both **Gaussian and exponential** density profiles reproduce that decline and do so while keeping a *low background* H0 (Mazurenko et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 13). The best-fit void depth found there, δV ≈ **−0.48, −0.47, −0.47** for zcut = 0.2, 1.0, 2.0, gives Ωm,in = (1+δV)Ωm,out ≈ 0.2 — directly consistent with the loose cluster-counting constraint **Ωm = 0.20 ± 0.04 ± 0.09** quoted in 2504.13380. So a deep local void is not forbidden by large-scale structure.
25: 
26: **3. 2504.13380: the local void is strongly preferred once the CMB is in the fit.** Fitting Planck 2018 + Pantheon+ SNe (zcut = 0.2), the ΛLTB void models beat both fiducials overwhelmingly: **ΔBIC = −73.28 and ΔAIC = −91.28 vs ΛCDM_P18 with ln B = 25.36** (ΛLTB4M), and **ΔBIC = −70.81, ΔAIC = −84.81, ln B = 25.87** (ΛLTB3M), against fiducial best-fit χ²_tot,min = 938.769 (ΛCDM_F) and 943.827 (ΛCDM_P18). The ranking is stable: **ΛLTB3M ≫ ΛLTB2M**. The required depth, **δV = −0.45^{+0.05}_{−0.06}** (2M), **−0.44 ± 0.05** (3M), **−0.49 ± 0.06** (4M), i.e. δV ≲ −38%, "even <~−50%", and the transitions of the SN absolute magnitude at **~20 Mpc, ~129 Mpc and ~860–960 Mpc** are all significant far beyond 1σ (Tables IV, V). Crucially, the CMB scale is far outside the void, so Ωm,out = 0.3153 and H0,out = 67.36 km/s/Mpc are retained — the void changes the local number, not the global fit.
27: 
28: **4. Honest accounting of the two strongest objections, and why they do not close the case.**
29: 
30: *(a) "No-go for late-time solutions" (2202.12214, Cai et al.).* Their ΔBIC are real: **+5.3483** (PAge) and **+11.0470** (MAPAge) over ΛCDM for CC+BAO+SNe, strengthening to **ΔBIC > 10** (RSD 2018) and **> 8** (RSD 2021). But that result is about *homogeneous* late-time background parametrisations fitted to *background* data, and the paper says so: it concludes that if late-time solutions are invoked "then the modifications must go beyond the background level", and it explicitly excepts inhomogeneous solutions from its no-go. Two further facts cut my way. First, their own IDL fit gives **H0 = 70.1 ± 2.5 km/s/Mpc** (CC+BAO+SNe, ΛCDM) and **70.2 ± 2.5** with RSD 2018 — the late-universe data, unhelped, already sit ~3σ above Planck's 67.27 ± 0.60 and pull toward SH0ES. Second, that same analysis shows a second, independent H0 problem that is *not* about the sound horizon: with M_B fixed identically for both ladders, **H0^LDL ≈ 74 vs H0^IDL ≈ 68**, which is described as "the recent intriguing view on the H0 tension as the M_B tension". I do not need a smaller r_d; I need the two rungs to talk about the same universe, which is precisely what a void violates.
31: 
32: *(b) "Not empty enough" (2309.05749, Huterer & Wu).* Their sample-variance result is solid and I do not dispute it: **σ_samplevariance = 0.31 km/s/Mpc** from ~1.5 million mock Supercal configurations in 512 subvolumes, so that **|H0^Planck − H0^loc|/σ ≈ 20**; resolving 6 km/s/Mpc would need **δ ≈ −0.8 out to 120 h⁻¹Mpc**, and even a **2σ**-underdense subvolume only raises H0 slightly above Planck's ~67. Perturbation theory agrees closely (**~0.4 km/s/Mpc** for the Pantheon sample). But this is a statement about *sample variance of a single ladder in a ΛCDM structure field*, i.e. the null hypothesis of a homogeneous background. It is exactly the hypothesis the 5.6σ H0(z) decline already rejects, and it is not the void-plus-transition models of 2504.13380, where the CMB region is explicitly placed at Ωm,out = 0.3153 outside the void and a 3-parameter profile (δV, rV, Δr) replaces the top-hat of 2309.05749. The two papers are not measuring the same thing; the panel should treat 2309.05749 as ruling out *voids as the sole explanation in a ΛCDM background*, not voids as a component of one.
33: 
34: **5. Where I concede ground.** In 2504.13380, with the Pantheon+ sample *alone*, the void models are **not** preferred over ΛCDM_F in Bayesian information criterion — several cases have positive ΔBIC_F. FRBs are the cheap, decisive test of the void depth (2606.12980, Banik et al.), and DESI DR2's continued preference for evolving w(z) is the decisive test of the background-level version.

53: 
54: ### Direct answers to the chair's three questions (2109.03263, 2310.16800)
55: 
56: **(1) What do the data say about self-interacting neutrinos?** The data say no, and they say it twice. 57:

4: # Topic: your EDE papers vs the four constraints — heads up before you write
5: 
6: I have posted my Round 1 statement testing all resolutions against CMB/BAO/DESI/growth. Since you are carrying the early-universe case (2101.01372, 2212.04494, 2502.15541, 2507.23355), here is what I found that you will need to answer. I am not asking you to concede; I am asking you to state the numbers.
7: 
8: **The constraint I think decides your side: DESI Y1 BAO measures r_s h = 101.8 ± 1.3 Mpc, a 1.9σ discrepancy from Planck 2018 (2502.15541).** I have proposed this as the panel's formal acceptance test, because it is sound-horizon-based and independent of both SNe and the distance ladder. Your position is the only one that can accommodate it — EDE raises H0 while lowering r_d, so r_d h can genuinely grow in the BAO data. Please say so explicitly and quantitatively: what Δ(r_s h) does each of your models predict, and is it consistent with 101.8 ± 1.3 Mpc?
9: 
10: **The constraint that hurts.** Pantheon+ requires Ωm = 0.334 ± 0.018; DESI Y1 requires Ωm = 0.295 ± 0.015. A ~2σ disagreement in Ωm exists *before* H0 enters. 2310.16800 shows what happens to the smooth-equation-of-state models: ADE's best-fit Ωm = 0.3014 is 1.8σ below Pantheon+ and its QDMAP degrades to 3.6σ on the EFT+PanPlus+Mb combination. The axion-like version holds at 2.5σ with H0 = 71.67 ± 0.77. Note that 2.5σ is not a resolution of a 5σ tension, only a reduction. I do not think it is fair to call 2.5σ "solved", and I want to know whether you agree.
11: 
12: **The number I think is your strongest and which you have not yet used.** 2507.23355: from CMB data *alone* (SPT-3G D1 + ACT + Planck), f_EDE < 0.070 at 95% CL and the Hubble tension is **still 3.6σ**. DESI is what brings it to 2.6σ. I regard this as a genuinely interesting result and I have said so in the transcript — an EDE model that CMB data alone reject but DESI rescues is a *BAO+CMB* model, not a purely early-universe one, and I think the honest version of your case leans on that rather than hiding it.
13: 
14: **Modified recombination (2212.04494).** I flagged that the Planck+SH0ES-only fit is genuinely impressive — H0 = 72.70 ± 0.57, tension to 0.29σ, and it also repairs S8 to 1.1σ from DES-Y3 — but that BOSS DR12 BAO degrades by Δχ²_BAO = +5.37 and Pantheon+ disagrees at ~3σ, and that BAO+SN pulls the achievable residual back to ~2.4σ. If you want to make the "modified recombination works" case, the load-bearing claim has to be about why the BAO cost is acceptable, not about the 0.29σ number.
15: 
16: Happy to be harder on this if you would rather I were. Round 2 is where I will push hardest.

5: 
6: We are on the same side of this debate and I think we should coordinate, but I also think the panel is going to notice something: neither of us has a quantitative constraint failure we can point to. My Round 1 statement was entirely about where *other* people's resolutions break, and your assignment (2211.00578 cepheid calibration, 2302.13671 look-back time) is about systematics. Neither of us has yet answered the data the other side is constrained by.
7: 
8: **The gap I want us to close.** A measurement-problem position has to explain why the *other* measurements agree with the CMB rather than with SH0ES. If it is a ladder systematic, then TRGB (69.8 ± 0.6 stat ± 1.6 sys) and megamaser routes should be systematically pulled low too, and neither 2211.00578 nor 2302.13671 is going to establish that on its own. 2606.12980 line 292 quotes an 8.2σ confidence level on the Cepheid metallicity dependence, which is the strongest single number against our side and I have not yet seen either of us address it. I would like to know from 2211.00578 what survives if metallicity is re-fitted rather than fixed.
9: 
10: **The constraint I think we most need to answer.** 2202.12214 shows that adding RSD growth data to CC+BAO+SNe pushes ΔBIC above 10 for late-time models, unchanged between S8 and S12. A measurement systematic in the local ladder has nothing to say about fσ8 or S8, and 2202.12214 lists Planck S8 = 0.834 ± 0.016 against DES Y3 0.776 ± 0.017, KiDS-1000 0.766+0.020−0.014, and an fσ8-implied 0.700+0.038. If the tension were purely a local calibration error, none of those should be affected — but I do not have the calculation showing that, and I suspect early_a will ask for it. Can 2302.13671's look-back-time route be pushed to show it is independent of both S8 and the SN absolute magnitude?
11: 
12: **Where I am genuinely agnostic and would rather we not oversell.** late_a's strongest asset is the DESI r_s h = 101.8 ± 1.3 Mpc measurement, a 1.9σ discrepancy from Planck 2018 (2502.15541). It is sound-horizon-based and independent of SNe and of the distance ladder. A pure measurement systematic does not predict it. Neither does a void, in principle. But early_a can explain it and we cannot, and I have proposed to the panel that this be the formal acceptance test. We should be ready for that argument rather than surprised by it.
13: 
14: **One caution about our own side.** I checked late_a's H0(z) numbers and they read correctly out of 2606.12980 — I have not challenged them. But I have told the judge I want to know how many of the ten bins are Pantheon+ supernovae before I treat 5.6σ as 5.6 independent measurements. If a large fraction are, the strongest late-universe evidence is partly a re-description of the same SN sample that our position says is miscalibrated, and that cuts against us as well. Worth thinking about before either of us quotes it.

My concern: these are not independent measurements. If a large fraction of the ten bins is populated by Pantheon+ supernovae, the 5.6σ and the 2.1σ are two analyses of overlapping data, and quoting both as convergent evidence double-counts. I have said in the transcript that I would want to know the overlap before treating 5.6σ as 5.6 independent constraints. VI.
DISCUSSION
We have shown that a gigaparsec-scale local void has the potential to ease the so-called Hubble tension between the
local determinations involving SNe and Planck CMB observations. We also discussed implications of such a local void
for BAO observations. The depth of such a void and hence to what extent it can ease the tension are restricted by the
kSZ eﬀect. Taking this into account, assuming the Planck cosmology for the outside of the void, the internal Hubble
parameter can be raised by a few percent due to the presence of the void, thus potentially alleviating the Hubble
tension. The presence of such a large void is unexpected in minimal standard cosmological scenarios, but the presence
of such a void can be realized by multi-stream inﬂation.
Although the mechanism of multi-stream inﬂation is intuitive and it is known how to relate the early universe model
to late time observables, it is important to study multi-stream inﬂation in more details in the future by, for example, a
lattice simulation to study the details of the bubble proﬁle. Also, in the present work we have used a LTB metric with
an assumed density proﬁle. It is interesting to understand the density proﬁle from ﬁrst principles in multi-stream
inﬂation. With these understandings, we would obtain predictions on possible corrections of the distance-redshift
relation when the universe is inhomogeneous as a result of multi-stream inﬂation.
There can be eﬀects other than the kSZ eﬀect of a local void aﬀecting CMB observations. One eﬀect is the diﬀerence
in the angular diameter distance to the last scattering surface. We have checked that the diﬀerence is suﬃciently small
for the parameter space of a local void we consider, noting that the angular diameter distance in our void cosmology is
given by the metric function R in the LTB metric [33]. A local void can also induce CMB spectral distortions, but the
constraints from this eﬀect wouldn’t be as stringent as those from the kSZ eﬀect [65]. A local void in principle should
also aﬀect the CMB observations through the integrated Sachs-Wolfe eﬀect. But quantifying this eﬀect precisely in
void cosmology appears challenging partly because cosmological perturbation on an inhomogeneous background can be
very complicated [33, 66]. This would be particularly so for voids with a thick edge, whereas for voids with a sharp
edge we may ﬁnd approximate methods by treating the inside and outside diﬀerent FRW universes.
In this work we have assumed that we locate at the center of the void. In general, we should be located away from
the exact center of a local void, and there would be additional observational eﬀects associated with this [67, 68]. The
observations would also be aﬀected from deviations from spherical symmetry of a local void. These two eﬀects would
determine the amount of ﬁne-tuning associated with our scenario.
A few more comments are in order. It would also be interesting and important to investigate how the parameter
determinations of [3] are aﬀected by the presence of a local void. Our scenario would be tested by observations of
high-redshift SNe or galaxies, the redshift distribution of transients such as gamma-ray or gravitational-wave bursts,
and future CMB experiments due to the kSZ eﬀect.

28: INTRODUCTION
29: Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension [1–10]. That is,
30: there is a signiﬁcant tension between the Hubble constants H0 measured from various independent probes
31: in the early and late/local universes. In particular, assuming the well-known ΛCDM model, the Hubble
32: constant inferred from the ﬁnal full-mission Planck measurements (Planck 2018) of the cosmic microwave
33: background (CMB) is given by H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km/s/Mpc [11]. Note that it cannot be substantially
34: changed by assuming various trivial extensions to the base-ΛCDM model. On the other hand, based on the
35: Cepheid/Type Ia supernova (SNIa) distance ladder, the local determination of H0 from the Hubble Space
36: Telescope (HST) and the SH0ES team (R22) is given by H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [12]. Obviously,
37: this Hubble constant directly from the local measurement of Cepheids/SNIa is in > 5σ tension with the
38: one indirectly inferred from CMB in the early universe (at high redshift z∗∼1090). Note that the recent
39: SH0ES 2024 result (R24) H0 = 73.17 ± 0.86 km/s/Mpc [13] is still in 5 −6σ tension with Planck 2018,
40: while it has been cross-checked with the early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) subsamples from
41: SH0ES and CCHP.
42: In history, the Hubble tension has not emerged in the WMAP era of CMB before 2011, then manifested
43: itself at 2 −3σ since the ﬁrst Planck result in 2013, and ﬁnally reached > 5σ in December 2021 (R22).
44: Various independent probes, e.g. the Tip of the Red Giant Branch (TRGB), Mira variables, J-region
45: Asymptotic Giant Branch (JAGB) stars, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), strong gravitational lensing,
46: gravitational waves, water masers, have been considered in the past decade to this end, but the Hubble
47: tension has not been resolved to date. We refer to e.g. [1–10] for comprehensive reviews.
48: Many eﬀorts have been made in the literature. Of course, it is fairly reasonable to carefully check the
49: observational data, since there might be unresolved systematic errors in them. On the other hand, if all
50: the observational data are right, the Hubble tension suggests the need for non-trivial extensions to the
51: standard ΛCDM cosmology. There might be something new in the early, middle, late or local universes.
52: Although numerous theoretical solutions have been proposed in the literature (e.g. [1–10, 113–118] and
53: references therein), the Hubble tension is still a tough problem currently.
54: Here, we are interested in alleviating the Hubble tension with a local void. The key idea is to violate
55: the cosmological principle by assuming that we live in a locally underdense void centered nearby our
56: location. In this underdense region, one will feel a locally faster expansion rate compared to the cosmic
57: average. Noting that H0 ∼73 km/s/Mpc directly measured from the local Cepheids/SNIa is larger than
58: H0 ∼67 km/s/Mpc indirectly inferred from CMB assuming a background Friedmann-Robertson-Walker
59: (FRW) universe, the Hubble tension might be alleviated with a local void [1, 2, 7, 8].

62: sample has been examined for evidence of a local “ Hubble Bubble ” [17]. Later, various LTB void models
63: were used to explain the cosmic acceleration without invoking dark energy or modiﬁed gravity [18–41].
64: Notice that cosmological constant is not allowed to this end, since it is the simplest candidate of dark
65: energy as well known. Recently, the Hubble tension attracted a lot of attention. If the goal is no longer
66: to explain the cosmic acceleration, we can allow a non-zero cosmological constant Λ in the LTB model
67: and use the ΛLTB void model to alleviate the Hubble tension, while the cosmic acceleration is instead
68: driven by Λ̸ = 0. The role of LTB void has been changed in this case.

578: VI.
579: DISCUSSION
580: We have shown that a gigaparsec-scale local void has the potential to ease the so-called Hubble tension between the
581: local determinations involving SNe and Planck CMB observations. We also discussed implications of such a local void
582: for BAO observations. The depth of such a void and hence to what extent it can ease the tension are restricted by the
583: kSZ eﬀect. Taking this into account, assuming the Planck cosmology for the outside of the void, the internal Hubble
584: parameter can be raised by a few percent due to the presence of the void, thus potentially alleviating the Hubble
585: tension. The presence of such a large void is unexpected in minimal standard cosmological scenarios, but the presence
586: of such a void can be realized by multi-stream inﬂation.
587: Although the mechanism of multi-stream inﬂation is intuitive and it is known how to relate the early universe model
588: to late time observables, it is important to study multi-stream inﬂation in more details in the future by, for example, a
589: lattice simulation to study the details of the bubble proﬁle. Also, in the present work we have used a LTB metric with
590: an assumed density proﬁle. It is interesting to understand the density proﬁle from ﬁrst principles in multi-stream
591: inﬂation. With these understandings, we would obtain predictions on possible corrections of the distance-redshift
592: relation when the universe is inhomogeneous as a result of multi-stream inﬂation.
593: There can be eﬀects other than the kSZ eﬀect of a local void aﬀecting CMB observations. One eﬀect is the diﬀerence
594: in the angular diameter distance to the last scattering surface. We have checked that the diﬀerence is suﬃciently small
595: for the parameter space of a local void we consider, noting that the angular diameter distance in our void cosmology is
596: given by the metric function R in the LTB metric [33]. A local void can also induce CMB spectral distortions, but the
597: constraints from this eﬀect wouldn’t be as stringent as those from the kSZ eﬀect [65]. A local void in principle should
598: also aﬀect the CMB observations through the integrated Sachs-Wolfe eﬀect. But quantifying this eﬀect precisely in
599: void cosmology appears challenging partly because cosmological perturbation on an inhomogeneous background can be
600: very complicated [33, 66]. This would be particularly so for voids with a thick edge, whereas for voids with a sharp
601: edge we may ﬁnd approximate methods by treating the inside and outside diﬀerent FRW universes.
602: In this work we have assumed that we locate at the center of the void. In general, we should be located away from
603: the exact center of a local void, and there would be additional observational eﬀects associated with this [67, 68]. The
604: observations would also be aﬀected from deviations from spherical symmetry of a local void. These two eﬀects would
605: determine the amount of ﬁne-tuning associated with our scenario.
606: A few more comments are in order. It would also be interesting and important to investigate how the parameter
607: determinations of [3] are aﬀected by the presence of a local void. Our scenario would be tested by observations of
608: high-redshift SNe or galaxies, the redshift distribution of transients such as gamma-ray or gravitational-wave bursts,
609: and future CMB experiments due to the kSZ eﬀect.

1: A gigaparsec-scale local void and the Hubble tension
2: Qianhang Ding, Tomohiro Nakama, and Yi Wang
3: Department of Physics, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, P.R.China and
4: Jockey Club Institute for Advanced Study, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, P.R. China
5: We explore the possibility of using a gigaparsec-scale local void to reconcile the Hubble tension.
6: Such a gigaparsec-scale void can be produced by multi-stream inﬂation where diﬀerent parts of the
7: observable universe follow diﬀerent inﬂationary trajectories. The impact of such a void for cosmological
8: observations is studied, especially those involving supernovae, Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO)
9: and the kinetic Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (kSZ) eﬀect. As a benchmark model, a 1.7Gpc scale with
10: boundary width 0.7Gpc and density contrast -0.14 may ease the Hubble tension.
11: I.
12: INTRODUCTION
13: The value of the Hubble parameter is of central importance in modern cosmology. However, recent cosmological
14: observations do not seem to converge on the measurement of the Hubble parameter. Ref. [1] reported a local
15: value of the Hubble parameter H0 = 73.24 ± 1.74km s−1 Mpc−1, 3.4σ higher than the value from Planck [2]: H0 =
16: 66.93 ± 0.62km s−1 Mpc−1. Another independent determination by observations of multiply-imaged quasar systems
17: yielded the results consistent with the local determination: H0 = 71.9+2.4
18: −3.0km s−1 Mpc−1 [3]. See also [4–7] for relevant
19: discussions.
20: While this so-called Hubble tension could be caused by unrecognized systematic uncertainties associated with the
21: determinations of H0 [8, 9], it has invoked studies of scenarios which can potentially alleviate or solve the tension
22: by new physics. Such scenarios include early dark energy [10–13], dark radiation [1, 14], emerging spacial curvature
23: [15], evolving scalar ﬁelds [16–18], primordial non-Gaussianity [19], non-standard neutrino interactions (see [20] and
24: references therein), acoustic dark energy [21], neutrinos interacting with dark matter [22], emergent dark energy [23],
25: quintessence axion dark energy [24], a family of alternate dynamics of dark energy [25], massive dark vector ﬁelds [26]
26: and dissipative axion [27], and so on.
27: In addition, the Hubble tension could be explained a local void with radius ≃150 Mpc, but such a scenario was
28: shown to be inconsistent with the supernova (SN) luminosity-distance relation (see [28] and references therein. See
29: also [29, 30]). Here we explore a similar but diﬀerent possibility, which employs a Gpc-scale local void. If we are
30: located in the center of such a void, the Hubble tension could be alleviated, while evading the constraint of [28]. The
31: presence of such a large void is unlikely in standard cosmological scenarios, as can be understood from σ8 ≃0.81
32: [31], which indicates that inhomogeneities with large amplitudes on comoving scales much larger than 10 Mpc are
33: statistically unlikely for Gaussian primordial ﬂuctuations. However, such a large void can be realized in very early
34: universe scenarios such as multi-stream inﬂation [32].
35: There is a long history about theories in which we live at the center of a Gpc-scale void. In particular, this possibility
36: has been extensively discussed as an alternative to dark energy (see [33, 34] and references therein). Our proposal is
37: also related to this line of research, but the depth of the void we need to ease or address the recently-debated Hubble
38: tension is much smaller than that required for the void to be an alternative to dark energy.
39: Ultimately, whether introducing a large void really helps or not in resolving the Hubble tension should be determined
40: by testing such a hypothesis simultaneously against diﬀerent observations of e.g. supernovae (SNe), baryon acoustic
41: oscillations (BAO), large-scale structure and the cosmic microwave background (CMB), as was done in [33] in the
42: context of a void serving as an alternative to dark energy. However, we leave such a detailed analysis to a future work,
43: partly because cosmological perturbation theory on an inhomogeneous background can be much more complicated
44: than that for a homegeneous background. We instead, for simplicity and as a ﬁrst step, just show how the local Hubble
45: parameter behaves in a void cosmology, which would provide an indicator of how much the Hubble tension is eased as
46: discussed later. In addition, a large void and hence its capabilities to ease the Hubble tension can be constrained by
47: diﬀerent observational eﬀects of such a void, one of which is the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel’dovich (kSZ) eﬀect [35], and we
48: also show how a large void is strictly constrained by the kSZ eﬀect.
49: II.
50: A LARGE LOCAL VOID REALIZED IN MULTI-STREAM INFLATION
51: A gigaparsec-scale void with O(0.1) density contrast is exponentially unlikely to arise from rare random ﬂuctuations
52: of a minimal scenario of cosmic inﬂation. To better motivate our study, we show that such a void can be generated
53: by multi-stream inﬂation [32]. In multi-stream inﬂation, the inﬂationary trajectory bifurcates in multi-ﬁeld space by
54: encountering a barrier or waterfall type potential. Previously multi-stream inﬂation was also used to generate position

59: structures in the multiverse [38].
60: We illustrate the dynamics of multi-stream inﬂation in Fig. 1. If the inﬂaton trajectory gets split during inﬂation,
61: and further if the potential realizing such a situation is constructed in such a way that spatial regions corresponding to
62: one of the trajectories experience shorter inﬂation than the other regions corresponding to the other trajectory, then
63: such regions later show up as underdense regions or voids, where the matter energy density contrast is related to the
64: e-folding number diﬀerence by δρ/ρ ∼δN. The abundance and depth of such voids as well as the density proﬁle for
65: each void can be controlled by the potential shape realizing such a bifurcation of the inﬂaton trajectory.
66: If the bifurcation probability is small, it is possible that only one such void exists in the observable universe. In this
67: case, it is more likely that the void is of spherical shape. Because events with small chance, either rare tail of Gaussian
68: ﬂuctuations in the isocurvature ﬂuctuation or quantum tunneling, prefer spherical bubbles.
69: The width of the void boundary is determined by the e-folding number between the bifurcation and combination of

71: expanded again after combination. To get a void whose boundary is thick, we require that the bifurcation last only for

We present the most up-to-date constraints on axion early dark energy (AEDE) from cosmic
microwave background (CMB) and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements. In particular,
we assess the impact of data from ground-based CMB experiments, the South Pole Telescope (SPT)
and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT)—both with and without Planck—on constraints on
AEDE. We also highlight the impact that BAO information from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic
Instrument (DESI) has on these constraints. From CMB data alone, we do not find statistically
significant evidence for the presence of AEDE, and we find only moderate reduction in the Hubble
tension. From the latest SPT data alone, we find the maximal fractional contribution of AEDE to
the cosmic energy budget is fEDE < 0.12 at 95% confidence level (CL), and the Hubble tension
between the SPT and SH0ES results is reduced to the 2.3 σ level. When combining the latest SPT,
ACT, and Planck datasets, we find fEDE < 0.070 at 95% CL and the Hubble tension at the 3.6 σ
level. In contrast, adding DESI data to the CMB datasets results in mild preference for AEDE
and, in some cases, non-negligible reduction in the Hubble tension.

INTRODUCTION
In recent months, three major datasets have been
released that provide significant new constraints on
cosmological parameters.
These are the South Pole
Telescope’s third generation camera’s (SPT-3G) obser-
vations of the main field taken during 2019 and 2020
(SPT-3G D1) [1–3] , the Atacama Cosmology Telescope’s
sixth data release (ACT-DR6) [4–6], and the second
release of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument
(DESI-DR2) [7, 8]. SPT-3G D1 is the first in a series
of SPT releases;
following releases will improve the
constraints even further [9]. With this trio of datasets,
the time is auspicious to revisit one of the most promising
models to ease the Hubble tension:
axion early dark
energy (AEDE) [10–13].
As a reminder, the Hubble tension is a discrepancy
between cosmological model-dependent inferences of the
expansion rate today, H0, and those using the classical
distance ladder [14–21]. The latter method more directly
determines H0 and is much less sensitive to cosmological
model assumptions. The most precise model-dependent
inference of H0 comes from the CMB. Within ΛCDM,
the combination of SPT-3G D1, ACT-DR6, and Planck
results in H0 = 67.19 ± 0.38 km/s/Mpc [1].1
The
most precise result using the classical distance ladder is
from the “Supernovae, H0, for the Equation of State of
Dark Energy” (SH0ES) Collaboration, which finds H0 =
73.17 ± 0.86 km/s/Mpc [24]. This value is discrepant
with the CMB one mentioned above by 6.4 σ [1]. The
quest to solve this tension has resulted in a plentitude of
theoretical models [21, 25], of which AEDE is one of the
most promising solutions. It is therefore interesting to
update constraints on this model with the new datasets
and see whether it still relieves the Hubble tension.
In this work, which is a follow-up to the cosmological
constraints in [1], we present constraints on AEDE
from the datasets mentioned above.

1771: Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension, namely the
1772: discrepancy between the Hubble constants from the local observation of Type Ia supernova (SNIa) and
1773: the high-z observation of cosmic microwave background (CMB). Here, we are interested in alleviating
1774: the Hubble tension with a local void. The key idea is to violate the cosmological principle by assuming
1775: that we live in a locally underdense void centered nearby our location. In this underdense region, one will
1776: feel a locally faster expansion rate compared to the cosmic average. In the literature, it was found that a
1777: local void cannot satisfyingly alleviate the Hubble tension, since it is not preferred over the ΛCDM model
1778: by the observations such as the Pantheon SNIa sample, especially in terms of the information criteria
1779: AIC and BIC. In this work, we try to alleviate the Hubble tension with a local void and transitions of
1780: the absolute magnitude M, by using the Pantheon+ SNIa sample alone or jointly with the CMB data of
1781: Planck 2018. We ﬁnd that the Hubble tension can be satisfyingly alleviated, while the ΛLTB models are
1782: strongly preferred by the observations.

**Q1: Are statistical methods reliable?**

- The 5.6σ "declining trend" from 2606.12980 Fig. 11: The paper itself says bins are NOT statistically independent ("inferred H0 values across different redshift bins are not statistically independent: since distance is a cumulative quantity, this leads to intrinsic correlations among the estimates"). They apply PCA decorrelation (Huterer & Cooray 200). The 5.6σ is a trend significance, not a per-bin significance. The review does NOT state the covariance matrix used; the significance likely comes from a PCA-based trend test. So late_a's claim of "5.6σ for z>0.3" is a trend significance — but the paper does not say how it was computed (PCA eigenvalues?). This is a real concern: quoting it as if it's independent evidence alongside the 2.1σ six-bin result is double-counting since the six-bin grouping (Krishnan et al.) uses megamasers+CC+SNe+BAO, while the 5.6σ uses SNe+BAO+H(z) — likely overlapping Pantheon+ SNe.

- The 2.1σ (Krishnan et al., six bins of megamasers, CC, SNe, BAO) and 1.9σ (lensed quasars) are separate probes but the SNe component overlaps with the 5.6σ analysis.

- The Dainotti et al. fit: H0 = 73.493 ± 0.144 with α = 0.008 ± 0.006 — note α is consistent with 0 at 1.3σ. The "66% alleviation" comes from H0(z=1100) = 69.271 ± 2.815, which has a 2.8 error — that's a weak statement. The low-z H0 is essentially the SH0ES value with a tiny error bar (±0.144) which is suspiciously small for a binned fit.

- GP reconstruction (Hu & Wang): transition at z≈0.49, ~70% mitigation, consistent with H0LiCOW within 1σ. But the GP uses Ωm fixed to Planck — that's an assumption.

**Q2: What criteria for "resolution"?**

- 2310.16800 uses two criteria: ΔAIC < −6.91 AND QDMAP < 3σ. These are different things. ΔAIC measures improvement in fit relative to ΛCDM; QDMAP measures how much the SH0ES M_B prior degrades the fit. The authors themselves caution against overinterpreting ΔAIC when QDMAP indicates inconsistency.

1: # Panel transcript: is the Hubble tension new physics or a measurement problem?
2: 
3: ## Round 1, Judge
4: 
5: **Questions to settle:**
6: 1. Is the Hubble tension evidence of new physics beyond ΛCDM, or is it a measurement and analysis problem?
7: 2. Which assumptions underpinning the ΛCDM inference of H0 must break to resolve the tension? (cf. 2101.01372's 7 assumptions)
8: 3. Are early-universe solutions (EDE, modified recombination, self-interacting neutrinos) viable? Are late-universe solutions (local void, modified gravity, late dark energy) viable?
9: 
10: **Paper assignments:**
11: - **early_a** (early universe new physics): 2101.01372, 2212.04494, 2502.15541, 2507.23355
12: - **late_a** (late universe/local): 2202.12214, 2309.05749, 2504.13380, 2606.12980
13: - **skeptic_a** (measurement problem): 2211.00578, 2302.13671
14: - **skeptic_b** (tests resolutions against data): 2109.03263, 2310.16800
15: - **methods** (statistician): 2101.01372 (methods), 2606.12980 (statistics)
16: 
17: **Rules:** Each panelist appends one statement under `## Round 1, <name>`. Read all papers before speaking. Cite specific arXiv IDs. Be concise but substantive.
18: ## Round 1, late_a
19: 
20: **Position: the tension is a statement about the *local* expansion rate, not about the sound horizon. Late-universe and local physics — a local underdensity, and a mild late-time departure from ΛCDM — reproduce the data; nothing requires new early-universe microphysics.**
21: 
22: **1. The data already show a redshift-dependent H0, and that is the whole story.** With equal-width binning in ten redshift intervals, the H0(z) analysis compiled in 2606.12980 (Jia & Dai, Galaxies review) finds a declining trend significant at **5.6σ for z > 0.3**: H0 at low z matches SH0ES, and at high z converges to the CMB value (2606.12980 §, Fig. 11). Independent routes reproduce the same shape: six-bin grouping of megamasers, cosmic chronometers, SNe Ia and BAO gives the trend at **2.1σ** (Krishnan et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 7), and a Gaussian-process reconstruction of H(z) with no new cosmological model finds the transition at **z ≈ 0.49**, mitigating the tension by **~70%** and remaining consistent with H0LiCOW within 1σ (Hu & Wang, via 2606.12980 Fig. 9). A parametrisation H0(z) = H̃0(1+z)^α fitted in ΛCDM gives **H0 = 73.493 ± 0.144 km/s/Mpc** with **α = 0.008 ± 0.006** and **H0(z=1100) = 69.271 ± 2.815 km/s/Mpc**, alleviating the tension by **~66%** (Dainotti et al., 2606.12980). Lensed-quasar time delays show the same mild decline at **1.9σ**, softening to **1.7σ** with a new H0 measurement (2606.12980). Every one of these is a *late-universe* signal. The CMB's 67 km/s/Mpc is the value of H0 far outside our inhomogeneous neighbourhood; the ladder measures it inside. A discrepancy between those two statements is expected without any new field existing at z > 1100.
23: 
24: **2. DESI strengthens the late-time reading, and the void works quantitatively.** DESI BAO + Planck + SNe lifts the preference for w0waCDM over ΛCDM to **3.9σ** (2606.12980, citing DESI+DESY5), and DESI DR2 BAO + Pantheon+ reproduces the same declining H0(z) (2606.12980 Fig. 12). Void models with both **Gaussian and exponential** density profiles reproduce that decline and do so while keeping a *low background* H0 (Mazurenko et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 13). The best-fit void depth found there, δV ≈ **−0.48, −0.47, −0.47** for zcut = 0.2, 1.0, 2.0, gives Ωm,in = (1+δV)Ωm,out ≈ 0.2 — directly consistent with the loose cluster-counting constraint **Ωm = 0.20 ± 0.04 ± 0.09** quoted in 2504.13380. So a deep local void is not forbidden by large-scale structure.
25: 
26: **3. 2504.13380: the local void is strongly preferred once the CMB is in the fit.** Fitting Planck 2018 + Pantheon+ SNe (zcut = 0.2), the ΛLTB void models beat both fiducials overwhelmingly: **ΔBIC = −73.28 and ΔAIC = −91.28 vs ΛCDM_P18 with ln B = 25.36** (ΛLTB4M), and **ΔBIC = −70.81, ΔAIC = −84.81, ln B = 25.87** (ΛLTB3M), against fiducial best-fit χ²_tot,min = 938.769 (ΛCDM_F) and 943.827 (ΛCDM_P18). The ranking is stable: **ΛLTB3M ≫ ΛLTB2M**. The required depth, **δV = −0.45^{+0.05}_{−0.06}** (2M), **−0.44 ± 0.05** (3M), **−0.49 ± 0.06** (4M), i.e. δV ≲ −38%, "even <~−50%", and the transitions of the SN absolute magnitude at **~20 Mpc, ~129 Mpc and ~860–960 Mpc** are all significant far beyond 1σ (Tables IV, V). Crucially, the CMB scale is far outside the void, so Ωm,out = 0.3153 and H0,out = 67.36 km/s/Mpc are retained — the void changes the local number, not the global fit.
27: 
28: **4. Honest accounting of the two strongest objections, and why they do not close the case.**
29: 
30: *(a) "No-go for late-time solutions" (2202.12214, Cai et al.).* Their ΔBIC are real: **+5.3483** (PAge) and **+11.0470** (MAPAge) over ΛCDM for CC+BAO+SNe, strengthening to **ΔBIC > 10** (RSD 2018) and **> 8** (RSD 2021). But that result is about *homogeneous* late-time background parametrisations fitted to *background* data, and the paper says so: it concludes that if late-time solutions are invoked "then the modifications must go beyond the background level", and it explicitly excepts inhomogeneous solutions from its no-go. Two further facts cut my way. First, their own IDL fit gives **H0 = 70.1 ± 2.5 km/s/Mpc** (CC+BAO+SNe, ΛCDM) and **70.2 ± 2.5** with RSD 2018 — the late-universe data, unhelped, already sit ~3σ above Planck's 67.27 ± 0.60 and pull toward SH0ES. Second, that same analysis shows a second, independent H0 problem that is *not* about the sound horizon: with M_B fixed identically for both ladders, **H0^LDL ≈ 74 vs H0^IDL ≈ 68**, which is described as "the recent intriguing view on the H0 tension as the M_B tension". 145: early_a writes that skeptic_b's diagnosis of the SINU case "is right and I endorse it." That is correct as far as it goes. But early_a also writes, in the same paragraph, that a phase-shift fix "has not touched Assumption 7 at all." That is not established. 2101.01372's Assumption 7 is ∂ρ_x/∂z ≥ 0 for z < z*, and a neutrino self-interaction that is strong in the radiation era changes ρ_ν(z) in exactly that interval. Whether the model *satisfies* or *breaks* Assumption 7 depends on the sign of dρ_ν/dz over the relevant range, which is a calculation neither early_a nor skeptic_b has put in the transcript. 2109.03263's failure is well established on the numbers (r_s moves 0.29 Mpc), and I am not going to overturn that; but the panel should not record "SINU does not break Assumption 7" as established, because it is not, and early_a should either produce the sign of dρ_ν/dz or drop the clause.

3: Role: test every proposed resolution against CMB / BAO / DESI / matter-growth constraints. Quote exact numbers. Read papers in archive/papers/ (see archive/INDEX.txt).

7: Papers read: 2109.03263 (SINU), 2310.16800 (ADE/axion EDE), 2502.15541 (EDE after DESI), 2212.04494 (modified recombination), 2202.12214 (late-time no-go), 2309.05749 (void sample variance), 2504.13380 (void + M transitions), 2507.23355 (SPT-3G AEDE), 2606.12980 (late-universe review), 2101.01372 (7 assumptions).

9: ### Failure table (my own numbers, all quoted)
10: 1. **Self-interacting neutrinos (2109.03263)** — fails the *H0* constraint even with CMB help.
11:    - Planck+BAO (2015) SI mode 3c+0f: H0 = **69.47 ± 0.59** (2c+1f: **68.87 ± 0.58**); ΛCDM 67.90 ± 0.54.
12:    - So the best SINU does is move H0 ~1.5-2σ; the paper's own words: "**the SINU scenario cannot resolve the Hubble tension** when all laboratory and cosmological constraints are taken into consideration" (line 268-269).
13:    - Mechanism fail: the phase shift moves peaks, but r_s barely changes: 144.58 ± 0.32 (3c+0f) vs 144.87 ± 0.29 (ΛCDM) — ~0.9σ, "sub-dominant role" (line 220-222). So it does not break Assumption 7 in a way that shrinks r_d.
14:    - Laboratory fail: flavor-universal is "ruled out by laboratory constraints from meson decay, τ decay, and double beta decay" (line 48-49). Flavor-specific evades the lab bound but buys no H0 (68.87 < 69.47).
15: 2. **Acoustic EDE (ADE, 2310.16800)** — fails the SN Ωm constraint, i.e. the "Ω_m wall".
16:    - Pantheon+ alone prefers Ωm = **0.334 ± 0.018**; DESI Y1 BAO prefers Ωm = **0.295 ± 0.015** (2502.15541 line 116-118). 2.1σ BAO–SN disagreement in Ωm.
17:    - With Planck+ext-BAO+EFT+Pantheon+Mb: ADE H0 = **71.13 ± 0.73**, QDMAP = **3.6σ**; axion EDE H0 = **71.67 ± 0.77**, QDMAP = **2.5σ**. Both fail the QDMAP < 3σ criterion of 2101.01372-family requirement.
18:    - ADE best-fit Ωm = **0.3014** is 1.8σ below Pantheon+; χ²_Mb = **6.42**.
19:    - Note the direction: ADE needs HIGH ω_cdm to keep CMB damping tail flat; Pantheon+ wants high Ωm → high ω_cdm; but that suppresses the low-ℓ TT spectrum beyond what ADE can compensate (Fig. 3 residual). This is the structural fail.
20: 3. **Axion-like EDE** — survives at 2.5σ (2310.16800) but: SPT-3G+ACT CMB-only f_EDE < **0.068** (0.070 for CMB-SPA) with the tension still at **3.6σ** (2507.23355 lines 115-120, 494, 517, 630). Adding DESI drops it to 2.6σ, still "no strong statistical preference" (line 631). So CMB-only axion EDE is dead; it lives only when DESI BAO is added.
21: 4. **Modified recombination (2212.04494)** — fails BAO, and the failure grows as you add data.
22:    - Planck+SH0ES-only: H0 = **72.70 ± 0.57**, tension down to **0.29σ**, Δχ² = **−1.15**. Nice — and S8 also fixed (1.1σ from DES-Y3 0.776 ± 0.017).
