579: DISCUSSION
580: We have shown that a gigaparsec-scale local void has the potential to ease the so-called Hubble tension between the
581: local determinations involving SNe and Planck CMB observations. We also discussed implications of such a local void
582: for BAO observations. The depth of such a void and hence to what extent it can ease the tension are restricted by the
583: kSZ eﬀect. Taking this into account, assuming the Planck cosmology for the outside of the void, the internal Hubble
584: parameter can be raised by a few percent due to the presence of the void, thus potentially alleviating the Hubble
585: tension. The presence of such a large void is unexpected in minimal standard cosmological scenarios, but the presence
586: of such a void can be realized by multi-stream inﬂation.
587: Although the mechanism of multi-stream inﬂation is intuitive and it is known how to relate the early universe model
588: to late time observables, it is important to study multi-stream inﬂation in more details in the future by, for example, a
589: lattice simulation to study the details of the bubble proﬁle. Also, in the present work we have used a LTB metric with
590: an assumed density proﬁle. It is interesting to understand the density proﬁle from ﬁrst principles in multi-stream
591: inﬂation. With these understandings, we would obtain predictions on possible corrections of the distance-redshift
592: relation when the universe is inhomogeneous as a result of multi-stream inﬂation.
593: There can be eﬀects other than the kSZ eﬀect of a local void aﬀecting CMB observations. One eﬀect is the diﬀerence
594: in the angular diameter distance to the last scattering surface. We have checked that the diﬀerence is suﬃciently small
595: for the parameter space of a local void we consider, noting that the angular diameter distance in our void cosmology is
596: given by the metric function R in the LTB metric [33]. A local void can also induce CMB spectral distortions, but the
597: constraints from this eﬀect wouldn’t be as stringent as those from the kSZ eﬀect [65]. A local void in principle should
598: also aﬀect the CMB observations through the integrated Sachs-Wolfe eﬀect. But quantifying this eﬀect precisely in
599: void cosmology appears challenging partly because cosmological perturbation on an inhomogeneous background can be
600: very complicated [33, 66]. This would be particularly so for voids with a thick edge, whereas for voids with a sharp
601: edge we may ﬁnd approximate methods by treating the inside and outside diﬀerent FRW universes.
602: In this work we have assumed that we locate at the center of the void. In general, we should be located away from
603: the exact center of a local void, and there would be additional observational eﬀects associated with this [67, 68]. The
604: observations would also be aﬀected from deviations from spherical symmetry of a local void. These two eﬀects would
605: determine the amount of ﬁne-tuning associated with our scenario.

607: determinations of [3] are aﬀected by the presence of a local void. Our scenario would be tested by observations of

107: - **The mechanism is the paper's real contribution.** A 1.7 Gpc void of depth −0.14 is exponentially unlikely from Gaussian fluctuations at σ8 ≈ 0.81, and the paper does not pretend otherwise: it derives the void from multi-stream inflation, where δρ/ρ ~ δN and the depth and profile are set by the shape of the bifurcation. This is the first proposal in our archive that supplies an *origin* for a void deep enough to matter, rather than fitting a profile and hoping.
108: - **The benchmark does not reach.** The paper's own number: at δV = −0.14 with Δr = 0.4 rV, *"the difference in the Hubble parameter at z = 0 is 2.5%"*, i.e. H0,in ≈ 69.1 km/s/Mpc against H0,out = 67.4 (their Fig. 4 caption confirms h = 0.691). 109: - **The decisive analysis is deferred, by the authors' own statement.** They leave the joint test against SNe, BAO, LSS and CMB *"to a future work"*, on the grounds that perturbation theory on an inhomogeneous background is hard. mine the accurate value of the Hubble constant. Two fundamentally diﬀerent
methods, the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) [1, 2] along
with the standard cosmological model and distance ladder-based method using
Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) provide quite diﬀerent results, an issue known
as the Hubble tension.
The observations of Cosmic Microwave Background
(CMB) anisotropies provide a global value of H0 = 67.8 ± 0.9 ± 1.1 km/S/Mpc.
SNe Ia calibrated using the Cepheid variables in diﬀerent galaxies (SH0ES pro-
gram), and time delay measurements of gravitationally lensed quasars [3] pro-
vide a higher value which is more than 3σ away from that provided by CMBR
[4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]. Diﬀerent explanations have been proposed, including
a dark component in the early Universe [13, 14] or modiﬁcations in the late
universe physics [15, 16] to resolve the Hubble tension.
The SH0ES program was designed to reﬁne the SNe Ia calibration using the
Hubble Space Telescope (HST) to precisely measure the Hubble constant and
determine the equation of the state parameter of dark energy [5].

The Hubble tension is investigated taking into account the cosmological look-back time. Speciﬁcally, consid-
ering a single equation, widely used in standard cosmology, it is possible to recover both values of the Hubble
constant H0 reported by the SH0ES and Planck collaborations: the former is obtained through cosmological
ladder methods (e.g. Cepheids, Supernovae Type IA) and the latter through measurements of the Cosmic Mi-
crowave Background. Also, other values obtained in the literature are achieved with the same approach. We
conclude that the Hubble tension can be removed if the look-back time is correctly referred to the redshift where
the measurement is performed.
Keywords: Observational cosmology; Hubble-Lemaˆıtre constant; look-back time.
I.
INTRODUCTION
The so-called H0 tension, related to the reported discrepancy on the measured values of Hubble-Lemaˆıtre (henceforth Hubble)
constant, H0, is claimed to be one of the most critical issues for the Λ Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) model, considered the
standard picture of the observed Universe. This staggering discrepancy arises when comparing estimates on H0 provided by
standard candles with those inferred by the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) [1]. In fact, the results from the
SH0ES collaboration, obtained by considering the cosmological ladder and probes like classical Cepheids and Supernovae Type
Ia (SNe Ia), in a region with redshift interval 0.02333 < z < 0.15, tell us that H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/(s Mpc) at 68% conﬁdence
level (CL) [2], while the Planck collaboration, reporting observations of the CMBR, shows, instead, that H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km/(s
Mpc) at 68% CL [3]. Despite the accuracy of both approaches, a 5.0σ tension emerges and it seems to be irreconcilable under
the standard of the ΛCDM model.
The problem has to be addressed both from experimental and theoretical points of view. Considering the increasing precision
achieved by recent observations, an experimental reason for the tension, related to some systematic eﬀects, is becoming less and
less probable [1, 4]. Thus this tension (and other ones revealed in cosmological parameters [1]) is seemingly hinting at some
undeﬁned new physics, going beyond the ΛCDM model. The last conclusion can be inferred also from other critical issues of
the standard cosmological model, like the nature of dark matter and dark energy, which should account for approximately 25%
and 70%, respectively, of the energy-density budget of the observed Universe [4–13]. However, the nature of the dark side of
the Universe is still unknown at a fundamental level, even if very precise tests are performed by several running experiments
[14–17].
Diﬀerent approaches are considered in the literature to ﬁx the above problems. A possibility is taking into account extensions
and modiﬁcations of General Relativity (GR) where the ΛCDM model evolves along the cosmic history. For example, extensions
like f(R) gravity [18–22]), have been considered in cosmological applications [23–27] to address diﬀerent issues related to the
ΛCDM model, like the late-time dark energy [12], and the inﬂationary behaviour of the early Universe [28].
Many possible extensions and modiﬁcations of GR have been proposed (see e.g. [29]), but, no ﬁnal theory, capable of
addressing the whole cosmic history and the large-scale structure has been formulated up to date. As in the case of cosmological
inﬂation, the paradigm seems consistent but a ﬁnal model, comprehensive of the whole phenomenology, if any, is still missing.
In any case, modiﬁed gravity can be adopted to investigate the H0 tension, as recently proposed in [30].
Modiﬁed gravity is not the only approach to ﬁx tensions in cosmology. New physics can be pursued also by taking into
account other paradigms like extensions of Electromagnetism and the Standard Model of Particles [31–33], or revising the
concept of cosmological measurements according to the principles of Quantum Mechanics [34, 35], as well as many diﬀerent
other approaches reported in the literature [36–64]. Furthermore, requiring a phenomenological evolution of H0 with the redshift
could be a straightforward way out for the problem [65–78] even without investigating some fundamental counterpart.

Results
We have two data sets, namely the R11 containing three subsets of 15 data
points each, and R16 which also has three subsets of 22 data points each. The
three subsets in both R11 and R16 belong to the MW, LMC, and NGC 4258
for Cepheid calibration.
We obtain the best-ﬁt value of the Hubble constant for each subset by mini-
mizing χ2. The best ﬁt values for various subsets of R11 and R16 are presented
in tables 1 and 2, respectively. Both tables make it evident that the MW cali-
bration oﬀers a greater value of H0 in comparison to the LMC and NGC4258.
Now we compute χi from the observed H0 for each subset as deﬁned in
Eq. 2. Since Htrue
0
is not available, we use the best-ﬁt value of H0. As discussed
before, ϵi is the error in the measurement. Figures 1 and 2 show a histogram of
χi for each subset. To comprehend the systematics involved in the measurement
process, we need to test the null hypothesis deﬁned in Eq. 3. We ﬁrst apply the
one-sample K-S test for this purpose. The results presented in tables 3 and 4
clearly show that the null hypothesis is rejected in all cases, i.e., measurements
do not follow a normal distribution. A comparison of the cumulative distribution
of χi deﬁned in Eq. 2 with the standard normal distribution is plotted in ﬁgures
3 and 4. The diﬀerences between the empirical and the observed distribution
are quite clear.
The next step is to ﬁnd out whether the various samples diﬀer signiﬁcantly
from one another. In other words, we will test the null hypothesis deﬁned in
Eq. 6. We could have used the Student’s t-test if there were only two samples.
However, because each data set has three subgroups, we use the ANOVA, whose
fundamental structure has been covered in Section 2.2. Similar to the K-S test,
ANOVA has also been applied on the χis which carry the information about
both the measured value of H0 and the error involved in the measurement.
The result of ANOVA for R11 and R16 have been presented in tables 5 and
6, respectively. The F value calculated using Eq. 7 is much greater than Fcrit
obtained from the table. Thus the null hypothesis that the three subgroups
within the R11 data have the same mean has been rejected at a 99% conﬁdence
level. The p-value is 10−15, indicating that the chances of above rejection are
negligible. Similarly, for R16 as well, Fcal is much large compared to the Fcrit
at 99% conﬁdence level, indicating that the null hypothesis is rejected. p value
in this is of the order of 10−24, which shows that the probability of getting
this rejection by chance is again negligible. This implies that the measurements
using distinct anchors provide diﬀerent values and the diﬀerences are statistically
signiﬁcant.

A gigaparsec-scale local void and the Hubble tension
Qianhang Ding, Tomohiro Nakama, and Yi Wang
Department of Physics, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, P.R.China and

We explore the possibility of using a gigaparsec-scale local void to reconcile the Hubble tension.
Such a gigaparsec-scale void can be produced by multi-stream inﬂation where diﬀerent parts of the
observable universe follow diﬀerent inﬂationary trajectories. The impact of such a void for cosmological
observations is studied, especially those involving supernovae, Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO)
and the kinetic Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (kSZ) eﬀect. As a benchmark model, a 1.7Gpc scale with
boundary width 0.7Gpc and density contrast -0.14 may ease the Hubble tension.
I.
INTRODUCTION
The value of the Hubble parameter is of central importance in modern cosmology. However, recent cosmological
observations do not seem to converge on the measurement of the Hubble parameter. Ref. [1] reported a local
value of the Hubble parameter H0 = 73.24 ± 1.74km s−1 Mpc−1, 3.4σ higher than the value from Planck [2]: H0 =
66.93 ± 0.62km s−1 Mpc−1. Another independent determination by observations of multiply-imaged quasar systems
yielded the results consistent with the local determination: H0 = 71.9+2.4
−3.0km s−1 Mpc−1 [3]. See also [4–7] for relevant
discussions.
While this so-called Hubble tension could be caused by unrecognized systematic uncertainties associated with the
determinations of H0 [8, 9], it has invoked studies of scenarios which can potentially alleviate or solve the tension
by new physics. Such scenarios include early dark energy [10–13], dark radiation [1, 14], emerging spacial curvature
[15], evolving scalar ﬁelds [16–18], primordial non-Gaussianity [19], non-standard neutrino interactions (see [20] and
references therein), acoustic dark energy [21], neutrinos interacting with dark matter [22], emergent dark energy [23],
quintessence axion dark energy [24], a family of alternate dynamics of dark energy [25], massive dark vector ﬁelds [26]
and dissipative axion [27], and so on.
In addition, the Hubble tension could be explained a local void with radius ≃150 Mpc, but such a scenario was
shown to be inconsistent with the supernova (SN) luminosity-distance relation (see [28] and references therein. See
also [29, 30]). Here we explore a similar but diﬀerent possibility, which employs a Gpc-scale local void. If we are
located in the center of such a void, the Hubble tension could be alleviated, while evading the constraint of [28]. The
presence of such a large void is unlikely in standard cosmological scenarios, as can be understood from σ8 ≃0.81
[31], which indicates that inhomogeneities with large amplitudes on comoving scales much larger than 10 Mpc are
statistically unlikely for Gaussian primordial ﬂuctuations. However, such a large void can be realized in very early
universe scenarios such as multi-stream inﬂation [32].
There is a long history about theories in which we live at the center of a Gpc-scale void. In particular, this possibility
has been extensively discussed as an alternative to dark energy (see [33, 34] and references therein). Our proposal is
also related to this line of research, but the depth of the void we need to ease or address the recently-debated Hubble
tension is much smaller than that required for the void to be an alternative to dark energy.
Ultimately, whether introducing a large void really helps or not in resolving the Hubble tension should be determined
by testing such a hypothesis simultaneously against diﬀerent observations of e.g. supernovae (SNe), baryon acoustic
oscillations (BAO), large-scale structure and the cosmic microwave background (CMB), as was done in [33] in the
context of a void serving as an alternative to dark energy. However, we leave such a detailed analysis to a future work,
partly because cosmological perturbation theory on an inhomogeneous background can be much more complicated
than that for a homegeneous background. We instead, for simplicity and as a ﬁrst step, just show how the local Hubble
parameter behaves in a void cosmology, which would provide an indicator of how much the Hubble tension is eased as
discussed later. In addition, a large void and hence its capabilities to ease the Hubble tension can be constrained by
diﬀerent observational eﬀects of such a void, one of which is the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel’dovich (kSZ) eﬀect [35], and we
also show how a large void is strictly constrained by the kSZ eﬀect.
II.
A LARGE LOCAL VOID REALIZED IN MULTI-STREAM INFLATION
A gigaparsec-scale void with O(0.1) density contrast is exponentially unlikely to arise from rare random ﬂuctuations
of a minimal scenario of cosmic inﬂation. To better motivate our study, we show that such a void can be generated
by multi-stream inﬂation [32]. In multi-stream inﬂation, the inﬂationary trajectory bifurcates in multi-ﬁeld space by
encountering a barrier or waterfall type potential. Previously multi-stream inﬂation was also used to generate position

25: (QDMAP 3.6σ, χ²_M_b = 6.42), and I do not defend it.

30: recombination (2212.04494), which reaches 1.1σ from 0.776 ± 0.017 while also
31: reaching H0 = 72.70 ± 0.57 (0.29σ) against Planck+SH0ES. If the panel wants a

2: 
3: ## Round 1, Judge
4: 
5: **Questions to settle:**
6: 1. Is the Hubble tension evidence of new physics beyond ΛCDM, or is it a measurement and analysis problem?
7: 2. Which assumptions underpinning the ΛCDM inference of H0 must break to resolve the tension? (cf. 2101.01372's 7 assumptions)
8: 3. Are early-universe solutions (EDE, modified recombination, self-interacting neutrinos) viable? Are late-universe solutions (local void, modified gravity, late dark energy) viable?
9: 
10: **Paper assignments:**
11: - **early_a** (early universe new physics): 2101.01372, 2212.04494, 2502.15541, 2507.23355
12: - **late_a** (late universe/local): 2202.12214, 2309.05749, 2504.13380, 2606.12980
13: - **skeptic_a** (measurement problem): 2211.00578, 2302.13671
14: - **skeptic_b** (tests resolutions against data): 2109.03263, 2310.16800
15: - **methods** (statistician): 2101.01372 (methods), 2606.12980 (statistics)

17: **Rules:** Each panelist appends one statement under `## Round 1, <name>`. Read all papers before speaking. Cite specific arXiv IDs. Be concise but substantive.
18: ## Round 1, late_a
19: 
20: **Position: the tension is a statement about the *local* expansion rate, not about the sound horizon. Late-universe and local physics — a local underdensity, and a mild late-time departure from ΛCDM — reproduce the data; nothing requires new early-universe microphysics.**
21: 
22: **1. The data already show a redshift-dependent H0, and that is the whole story.** With equal-width binning in ten redshift intervals, the H0(z) analysis compiled in 2606.12980 (Jia & Dai, Galaxies review) finds a declining trend significant at **5.6σ for z > 0.3**: H0 at low z matches SH0ES, and at high z converges to the CMB value (2606.12980 §, Fig. 11). Independent routes reproduce the same shape: six-bin grouping of megamasers, cosmic chronometers, SNe Ia and BAO gives the trend at **2.1σ** (Krishnan et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 7), and a Gaussian-process reconstruction of H(z) with no new cosmological model finds the transition at **z ≈ 0.49**, mitigating the tension by **~70%** and remaining consistent with H0LiCOW within 1σ (Hu & Wang, via 2606.12980 Fig. 9). A parametrisation H0(z) = H̃0(1+z)^α fitted in ΛCDM gives **H0 = 73.493 ± 0.144 km/s/Mpc** with **α = 0.008 ± 0.006** and **H0(z=1100) = 69.271 ± 2.815 km/s/Mpc**, alleviating the tension by **~66%** (Dainotti et al., 2606.12980). Lensed-quasar time delays show the same mild decline at **1.9σ**, softening to **1.7σ** with a new H0 measurement (2606.12980). Every one of these is a *late-universe* signal. The CMB's 67 km/s/Mpc is the value of H0 far outside our inhomogeneous neighbourhood; the ladder measures it inside. A discrepancy between those two statements is expected without any new field existing at z > 1100.
23: 
24: **2. DESI strengthens the late-time reading, and the void works quantitatively.** DESI BAO + Planck + SNe lifts the preference for w0waCDM over ΛCDM to **3.9σ** (2606.12980, citing DESI+DESY5), and DESI DR2 BAO + Pantheon+ reproduces the same declining H0(z) (2606.12980 Fig. 12). Void models with both **Gaussian and exponential** density profiles reproduce that decline and do so while keeping a *low background* H0 (Mazurenko et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 13). The best-fit void depth found there, δV ≈ **−0.48, −0.47, −0.47** for zcut = 0.2, 1.0, 2.0, gives Ωm,in = (1+δV)Ωm,out ≈ 0.2 — directly consistent with the loose cluster-counting constraint **Ωm = 0.20 ± 0.04 ± 0.09** quoted in 2504.13380. So a deep local void is not forbidden by large-scale structure.
25: 
26: **3. 2504.13380: the local void is strongly preferred once the CMB is in the fit.** Fitting Planck 2018 + Pantheon+ SNe (zcut = 0.2), the ΛLTB void models beat both fiducials overwhelmingly: **ΔBIC = −73.28 and ΔAIC = −91.28 vs ΛCDM_P18 with ln B = 25.36** (ΛLTB4M), and **ΔBIC = −70.81, ΔAIC = −84.81, ln B = 25.87** (ΛLTB3M), against fiducial best-fit χ²_tot,min = 938.769 (ΛCDM_F) and 943.827 (ΛCDM_P18). The ranking is stable: **ΛLTB3M ≫ ΛLTB2M**. The required depth, **δV = −0.45^{+0.05}_{−0.06}** (2M), **−0.44 ± 0.05** (3M), **−0.49 ± 0.06** (4M), i.e. δV ≲ −38%, "even <~−50%", and the transitions of the SN absolute magnitude at **~20 Mpc, ~129 Mpc and ~860–960 Mpc** are all significant far beyond 1σ (Tables IV, V). Crucially, the CMB scale is far outside the void, so Ωm,out = 0.3153 and H0,out = 67.36 km/s/Mpc are retained — the void changes the local number, not the global fit.
27: 
28: **4. Honest accounting of the two strongest objections, and why they do not close the case.**
29: 
30: *(a) "No-go for late-time solutions" (2202.12214, Cai et al.).* Their ΔBIC are real: **+5.3483** (PAge) and **+11.0470** (MAPAge) over ΛCDM for CC+BAO+SNe, strengthening to **ΔBIC > 10** (RSD 2018) and **> 8** (RSD 2021). But that result is about *homogeneous* late-time background parametrisations fitted to *background* data, and the paper says so: it concludes that if late-time solutions are invoked "then the modifications must go beyond the background level", and it explicitly excepts inhomogeneous solutions from its no-go. Two further facts cut my way. First, their own IDL fit gives **H0 = 70.1 ± 2.5 km/s/Mpc** (CC+BAO+SNe, ΛCDM) and **70.2 ± 2.5** with RSD 2018 — the late-universe data, unhelped, already sit ~3σ above Planck's 67.27 ± 0.60 and pull toward SH0ES. Second, that same analysis shows a second, independent H0 problem that is *not* about the sound horizon: with M_B fixed identically for both ladders, **H0^LDL ≈ 74 vs H0^IDL ≈ 68**, which is described as "the recent intriguing view on the H0 tension as the M_B tension". I do not need a smaller r_d; I need the two rungs to talk about the same universe, which is precisely what a void violates.
31: 
32: *(b) "Not empty enough" (2309.05749, Huterer & Wu).* Their sample-variance result is solid and I do not dispute it: **σ_samplevariance = 0.31 km/s/Mpc** from ~1.5 million mock Supercal configurations in 512 subvolumes, so that **|H0^Planck − H0^loc|/σ ≈ 20**; resolving 6 km/s/Mpc would need **δ ≈ −0.8 out to 120 h⁻¹Mpc**, and even a **2σ**-underdense subvolume only raises H0 slightly above Planck's ~67. Perturbation theory agrees closely (**~0.4 km/s/Mpc** for the Pantheon sample). But this is a statement about *sample variance of a single ladder in a ΛCDM structure field*, i.e. the null hypothesis of a homogeneous background. It is exactly the hypothesis the 5.6σ H0(z) decline already rejects, and it is not the void-plus-transition models of 2504.13380, where the CMB region is explicitly placed at Ωm,out = 0.3153 outside the void and a 3-parameter profile (δV, rV, Δr) replaces the top-hat of 2309.05749. The two papers are not measuring the same thing; the panel should treat 2309.05749 as ruling out *voids as the sole explanation in a ΛCDM background*, not voids as a component of one.
33: 
34: **5. Where I concede ground.** In 2504.13380, with the Pantheon+ sample *alone*, the void models are **not** preferred over ΛCDM_F in Bayesian information criterion — several cases have positive ΔBIC_F. The gain appears when the CMB is jointly fitted. And the ΛLTB3M/4M fit requires the absolute-magnitude transitions, which is SN-population physics; the authors themselves flag the over-fitting risk and concede "we still cannot claim a full triumph so far" for the SN-only case. I will not pretend this is a clean ΛCDM-plus-void model. My claim is narrower and, I think, still strong: **the tension does not require breaking any early-universe assumption, and the late-universe data are pointing the same way as my proposal.** Under 2101.01372's framework the late-time route breaks Assumption 2 (homogeneity) and/or Assumption 6 (that late-time distance physics is understood), never Assumptions 1, 3, 4, 5 or 7 — a smaller and more conservative set to abandon than reducing r_s, which drags ω_b, S8 and BBN along with it. FRBs are the cheap, decisive test of the void depth (2606.12980, Banik et al.), and DESI DR2's continued preference for evolving w(z) is the decisive test of the background-level version.

### Ruling 6 — one correction to early_a, on a point of logic rather than fact.

early_a writes that skeptic_b's diagnosis of the SINU case "is right and I endorse it." That is correct as far as it goes. But early_a also writes, in the same paragraph, that a phase-shift fix "has not touched Assumption 7 at all." That is not established. 2101.01372's Assumption 7 is ∂ρ_x/∂z ≥ 0 for z < z*, and a neutrino self-interaction that is strong in the radiation era changes ρ_ν(z) in exactly that interval. Whether the model *satisfies* or *breaks* Assumption 7 depends on the sign of dρ_ν/dz over the relevant range, which is a calculation neither early_a nor skeptic_b has put in the transcript. 2109.03263's failure is well established on the numbers (r_s moves 0.29 Mpc), and I am not going to overturn that; but the panel should not record "SINU does not break Assumption 7" as established, because it is not, and early_a should either produce the sign of dρ_ν/dz or drop the clause.

### Ruling 7 — on early_a's treatment of the new preprint 1912.12600: ACCEPTED, and it disposes of my Ruling 3 in a way I should record.

I told late_a in writing that 1912.12600's benchmark (H0 ≈ 69.1, i.e. +2.5%) sits *below* every ΛLTB fit in their own 2504.13380, and that I expected late_a to say so. early_a has independently reached the same reading and gone further, correctly: a 2.5% shift is "a worse deal than f_EDE = 0.055," it cannot fix S8, it is untested against DESI BAO, and it adds a second cosmological model (LTB) on top of ΛCDM. early_a's characterisation — "that is not the conservative choice; it is the assumption-heavy one" — is the right characterisation and I adopt it into the draft.

I note for balance that early_a's dismissal of 1912.12600 is a *statement about the benchmark*, not about the mechanism, and the mechanism remains the most interesting thing in the new preprint: a multi-stream-inflation origin for a void of the required depth. The panel records the mechanism as a live idea and the benchmark as insufficient.

### Ruling 5 — the disagreement between early_a and skeptic_b is NOT what it appears, and I will not let the panel record a false dichotomy.

early_a and skeptic_b are arguing past each other about *which constraint decides*, but on the substantive question they are closer than their rhetoric suggests.

- skeptic_b's own ranking places **axion-like EDE first among survivors** (i), with modified recombination second (ii). early_a argues axion-like EDE is "the strongest candidate on the panel." **These agree.**
- skeptic_b says the axion EDE residual of 2.5σ is "a reduction, not a resolution." early_a says in terms: "I agree with skeptic_b that a 2.5σ residual is a *reduction*, not a resolution, and the consensus must say 'reduces,' not 'solves.'" **These agree explicitly.**
- skeptic_b says AEDE is "a CMB+BAO model, not a purely early-universe one." early_a concedes this precisely and in the same terms, then adds 2507.23355's own reading — the Ωm − h r_d discrepancy between DESI and three independent CMB experiments falls to 1.5σ / 2.8σ / 2.5σ in AEDE against 1.9σ in ΛCDM (verified: 2507.23355 lines 549–550, 870). **The concession and the counter-argument are compatible.**

Ruling: the panel records that **early_a and skeptic_b agree on the ranking of resolutions and on the correct verb ("reduces," not "solves"), and disagree only on whether the residual constraints are decisive.** That disagreement is real and goes to Round 2. What must not happen is a consensus statement that reports a 2–2 split between "new physics" and "measurement problem" when the two strongest voices on the early side are in substantial agreement about what the data currently support.

### Ruling 6 — one correction to early_a, on a point of logic rather than fact.

early_a writes that skeptic_b's diagnosis of the SINU case "is right and I endorse it." That is correct as far as it goes. But early_a also writes, in the same paragraph, that a phase-shift fix "has not touched Assumption 7 at all." That is not established. 2101.01372's Assumption 7 is ∂ρ_x/∂z ≥ 0 for z < z*, and a neutrino self-interaction that is strong in the radiation era changes ρ_ν(z) in exactly that interval. Whether the model *satisfies* or *breaks* Assumption 7 depends on the sign of dρ_ν/dz over the relevant range, which is a calculation neither early_a nor skeptic_b has put in the transcript. 2109.03263's failure is well established on the numbers (r_s moves 0.29 Mpc), and I am not going to overturn that; but the panel should not record "SINU does not break Assumption 7" as established, because it is not, and early_a should either produce the sign of dρ_ν/dz or drop the clause.

6: Thanks for a careful statement; most of your numbers read correctly out of the papers and I have not disputed them in the transcript. Three specific points where a resolution in your column fails a constraint, plus a methodological flag.

8: **1. δV = −0.45 is shallower than what the void-only calculation requires, and the difference is paid for with Assumption 6.** 2309.05749 measures σ_samplevariance = 0.31 km/s/Mpc from ~1.5M mock configurations in 512 subvolumes, giving |H0_Planck − H0_loc|/σ ≃ 20, and concludes that resolving 6 km/s/Mpc needs δ ≈ −0.8 within 120 h⁻¹ Mpc. Your best fits are δV = −0.44 ± 0.05 (3M) and −0.49 ± 0.06 (4M), i.e. δV ≲ −38%. That is roughly half the required depth. The gap is closed by the absolute-magnitude transitions at ~20 Mpc, ~129 Mpc and ~860–960 Mpc. So the model that works is not "ΛCDM plus a void" — it is "ΛCDM plus a void plus three epochs of SN population evolution." In 2101.01372's language that breaks Assumption 2 *and* Assumption 6, which is a larger set to abandon than you claim in your point 5, and it is not the conservative route you describe. I think you should either own this or find a fit that reaches the depth without the transitions.
9: 
10: **2. The ΔBIC figures are a fixed-parameter fit, not a model comparison.** You quote ΔBIC = −73.28 and −70.81 with ln B = 25.36 against "ΛCDM_P18" at χ²_tot,min = 943.827. But 2504.13380 states that Ωm,out = 0.3153 and H0,out = 67.36 are **fixed** by the Planck 2018 result, not fitted. The ΛLTB models are therefore being scored on a different number of free parameters than the fiducial they beat, with the two parameters that matter most held at the value you are trying to move. I have flagged this to the judge. I do not think it is fatal — but the panel should not record "the void is strongly preferred by the CMB" without it.

2: 
3: ## Round 1, Judge
4: 
5: **Questions to settle:**
6: 1. Is the Hubble tension evidence of new physics beyond ΛCDM, or is it a measurement and analysis problem?
7: 2. Which assumptions underpinning the ΛCDM inference of H0 must break to resolve the tension? (cf. 2101.01372's 7 assumptions)
8: 3. Are early-universe solutions (EDE, modified recombination, self-interacting neutrinos) viable? Are late-universe solutions (local void, modified gravity, late dark energy) viable?
9: 
10: **Paper assignments:**
11: - **early_a** (early universe new physics): 2101.01372, 2212.04494, 2502.15541, 2507.23355
12: - **late_a** (late universe/local): 2202.12214, 2309.05749, 2504.13380, 2606.12980
13: - **skeptic_a** (measurement problem): 2211.00578, 2302.13671

18: ## Round 1, late_a
19: 
20: **Position: the tension is a statement about the *local* expansion rate, not about the sound horizon. Late-universe and local physics — a local underdensity, and a mild late-time departure from ΛCDM — reproduce the data; nothing requires new early-universe microphysics.**
21: 
22: **1. The data already show a redshift-dependent H0, and that is the whole story.** With equal-width binning in ten redshift intervals, the H0(z) analysis compiled in 2606.12980 (Jia & Dai, Galaxies review) finds a declining trend significant at **5.6σ for z > 0.3**: H0 at low z matches SH0ES, and at high z converges to the CMB value (2606.12980 §, Fig. 11). Independent routes reproduce the same shape: six-bin grouping of megamasers, cosmic chronometers, SNe Ia and BAO gives the trend at **2.1σ** (Krishnan et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 7), and a Gaussian-process reconstruction of H(z) with no new cosmological model finds the transition at **z ≈ 0.49**, mitigating the tension by **~70%** and remaining consistent with H0LiCOW within 1σ (Hu & Wang, via 2606.12980 Fig. 9). A parametrisation H0(z) = H̃0(1+z)^α fitted in ΛCDM gives **H0 = 73.493 ± 0.144 km/s/Mpc** with **α = 0.008 ± 0.006** and **H0(z=1100) = 69.271 ± 2.815 km/s/Mpc**, alleviating the tension by **~66%** (Dainotti et al., 2606.12980). Lensed-quasar time delays show the same mild decline at **1.9σ**, softening to **1.7σ** with a new H0 measurement (2606.12980). Every one of these is a *late-universe* signal. The CMB's 67 km/s/Mpc is the value of H0 far outside our inhomogeneous neighbourhood; the ladder measures it inside. A discrepancy between those two statements is expected without any new field existing at z > 1100.
23: 
24: **2. DESI strengthens the late-time reading, and the void works quantitatively.** DESI BAO + Planck + SNe lifts the preference for w0waCDM over ΛCDM to **3.9σ** (2606.12980, citing DESI+DESY5), and DESI DR2 BAO + Pantheon+ reproduces the same declining H0(z) (2606.12980 Fig. 12). Void models with both **Gaussian and exponential** density profiles reproduce that decline and do so while keeping a *low background* H0 (Mazurenko et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 13). The best-fit void depth found there, δV ≈ **−0.48, −0.47, −0.47** for zcut = 0.2, 1.0, 2.0, gives Ωm,in = (1+δV)Ωm,out ≈ 0.2 — directly consistent with the loose cluster-counting constraint **Ωm = 0.20 ± 0.04 ± 0.09** quoted in 2504.13380. So a deep local void is not forbidden by large-scale structure.
25: 
26: **3. 2504.13380: the local void is strongly preferred once the CMB is in the fit.** Fitting Planck 2018 + Pantheon+ SNe (zcut = 0.2), the ΛLTB void models beat both fiducials overwhelmingly: **ΔBIC = −73.28 and ΔAIC = −91.28 vs ΛCDM_P18 with ln B = 25.36** (ΛLTB4M), and **ΔBIC = −70.81, ΔAIC = −84.81, ln B = 25.87** (ΛLTB3M), against fiducial best-fit χ²_tot,min = 938.769 (ΛCDM_F) and 943.827 (ΛCDM_P18). The ranking is stable: **ΛLTB3M ≫ ΛLTB2M**. Crucially, the CMB scale is far outside the void, so Ωm,out = 0.3153 and H0,out = 67.36 km/s/Mpc are retained — the void changes the local number, not the global fit.
27: 
28: **4. Honest accounting of the two strongest objections, and why they do not close the case.**
29: 
30: *(a) "No-go for late-time solutions" (2202.12214, Cai et al.).* Their ΔBIC are real: **+5.3483** (PAge) and **+11.0470** (MAPAge) over ΛCDM for CC+BAO+SNe, strengthening to **ΔBIC > 10** (RSD 2018) and **> 8** (RSD 2021). But that result is about *homogeneous* late-time background parametrisations fitted to *background* data, and the paper says so: it concludes that if late-time solutions are invoked "then the modifications must go beyond the background level", and it explicitly excepts inhomogeneous solutions from its no-go. Two further facts cut my way. First, their own IDL fit gives **H0 = 70.1 ± 2.5 km/s/Mpc** (CC+BAO+SNe, ΛCDM) and **70.2 ± 2.5** with RSD 2018 — the late-universe data, unhelped, already sit ~3σ above Planck's 67.27 ± 0.60 and pull toward SH0ES. Second, that same analysis shows a second, independent H0 problem that is *not* about the sound horizon: with M_B fixed identically for both ladders, **H0^LDL ≈ 74 vs H0^IDL ≈ 68**, which is described as "the recent intriguing view on the H0 tension as the M_B tension". I do not need a smaller r_d; I need the two rungs to talk about the same universe, which is precisely what a void violates.
31: 
32: *(b) "Not empty enough" (2309.05749, Huterer & Wu).* Their sample-variance result is solid and I do not dispute it: **σ_samplevariance = 0.31 km/s/Mpc** from ~1.5 million mock Supercal configurations in 512 subvolumes, so that **|H0^Planck − H0^loc|/σ ≈ 20**; resolving 6 km/s/Mpc would need **δ ≈ −0.8 out to 120 h⁻¹Mpc**, and even a **2σ**-underdense subvolume only raises H0 slightly above Planck's ~67. Perturbation theory agrees closely (**~0.4 km/s/Mpc** for the Pantheon sample). But this is a statement about *sample variance of a single ladder in a ΛCDM structure field*, i.e. the null hypothesis of a homogeneous background. It is exactly the hypothesis the 5.6σ H0(z) decline already rejects, and it is not the void-plus-transition models of 2504.13380, where the CMB region is explicitly placed at Ωm,out = 0.3153 outside the void and a 3-parameter profile (δV, rV, Δr) replaces the top-hat of 2309.05749. The two papers are not measuring the same thing; the panel should treat 2309.05749 as ruling out *voids as the sole explanation in a ΛCDM background*, not voids as a component of one.
33: 
34: **5. 27: In addition, the Hubble tension could be explained a local void with radius ≃150 Mpc, but such a scenario was
28: shown to be inconsistent with the supernova (SN) luminosity-distance relation (see [28] and references therein. See
29: also [29, 30]). Here we explore a similar but diﬀerent possibility, which employs a Gpc-scale local void. If we are
30: located in the center of such a void, the Hubble tension could be alleviated, while evading the constraint of [28]. The
31: presence of such a large void is unlikely in standard cosmological scenarios, as can be understood from σ8 ≃0.81
32: [31], which indicates that inhomogeneities with large amplitudes on comoving scales much larger than 10 Mpc are
33: statistically unlikely for Gaussian primordial ﬂuctuations. However, such a large void can be realized in very early
34: universe scenarios such as multi-stream inﬂation [32].
35: There is a long history about theories in which we live at the center of a Gpc-scale void. In particular, this possibility
36: has been extensively discussed as an alternative to dark energy (see [33, 34] and references therein). Our proposal is
37: also related to this line of research, but the depth of the void we need to ease or address the recently-debated Hubble
38: tension is much smaller than that required for the void to be an alternative to dark energy.
39: Ultimately, whether introducing a large void really helps or not in resolving the Hubble tension should be determined
40: by testing such a hypothesis simultaneously against diﬀerent observations of e.g. supernovae (SNe), baryon acoustic
41: oscillations (BAO), large-scale structure and the cosmic microwave background (CMB), as was done in [33] in the
42: context of a void serving as an alternative to dark energy. However, we leave such a detailed analysis to a future work,
43: partly because cosmological perturbation theory on an inhomogeneous background can be much more complicated
44: than that for a homegeneous background. We instead, for simplicity and as a ﬁrst step, just show how the local Hubble
45: parameter behaves in a void cosmology, which would provide an indicator of how much the Hubble tension is eased as
46: discussed later. In addition, a large void and hence its capabilities to ease the Hubble tension can be constrained by
47: diﬀerent observational eﬀects of such a void, one of which is the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel’dovich (kSZ) eﬀect [35], and we
48: also show how a large void is strictly constrained by the kSZ eﬀect.
49: II.
50: A LARGE LOCAL VOID REALIZED IN MULTI-STREAM INFLATION
51: A gigaparsec-scale void with O(0.1) density contrast is exponentially unlikely to arise from rare random ﬂuctuations
52: of a minimal scenario of cosmic inﬂation. To better motivate our study, we show that such a void can be generated
53: by multi-stream inﬂation [32]. In multi-stream inﬂation, the inﬂationary trajectory bifurcates in multi-ﬁeld space by
54: encountering a barrier or waterfall type potential. Previously multi-stream inﬂation was also used to generate position
55: arXiv:1912.12600v1  [astro-ph.CO]  29 Dec 2019
56: 
57: 2
58: space features in our universe such as a cold spot on the CMB [36], initial clustering of primordial black holes [37] and
59: structures in the multiverse [38].
60: We illustrate the dynamics of multi-stream inﬂation in Fig. 1. If the inﬂaton trajectory gets split during inﬂation,
61: and further if the potential realizing such a situation is constructed in such a way that spatial regions corresponding to
62: one of the trajectories experience shorter inﬂation than the other regions corresponding to the other trajectory, then
63: such regions later show up as underdense regions or voids, where the matter energy density contrast is related to the
64: e-folding number diﬀerence by δρ/ρ ∼δN. The abundance and depth of such voids as well as the density proﬁle for
65: each void can be controlled by the potential shape realizing such a bifurcation of the inﬂaton trajectory.
66: If the bifurcation probability is small, it is possible that only one such void exists in the observable universe. In this
67: case, it is more likely that the void is of spherical shape. Because events with small chance, either rare tail of Gaussian
68: ﬂuctuations in the isocurvature ﬂuctuation or quantum tunneling, prefer spherical bubbles.
69: The width of the void boundary is determined by the e-folding number between the bifurcation and combination of
70: the trajectory, since the edge was decoupled from the Hubble ﬂow during the bifurcated stage of inﬂation, and then
71: expanded again after combination. To get a void whose boundary is thick, we require that the bifurcation last only for
72: of order one e-fold.

75: inﬂationary trajectory (vertical direction from top to down) encounters a barrier or waterfall potential, which causes bifurcation

77: smaller probability it rolls along the blue trajectory on the right. The region experiencing this blue trajectory later shows up as

My concern: these are not independent measurements. If a large fraction of the ten bins is populated by Pantheon+ supernovae, the 5.6σ and the 2.1σ are two analyses of overlapping data, and quoting both as convergent evidence double-counts. I have said in the transcript that I would want to know the overlap before treating 5.6σ as 5.6 independent constraints. [15] is no longer fulfilled. But over the *same* data change, ΔAIC improves from −18.9 to **−21.8**. The authors themselves caution against overinterpreting the ΔAIC "given that the QDMAP indicates that combining these datasets is not statistically consistent." So: the two information criteria disagree in sign about whether adding Pantheon+ helps or hurts. My instinct is that this is the well-known pathology of using ΔAIC on datasets that are mutually inconsistent — the likelihood of the combined dataset is not a well-behaved object — but I would like the panel's statistician to state which number governs, because it changes my verdict on ADE from "fails" to "ambiguously disfavoured."

579: DISCUSSION
580: We have shown that a gigaparsec-scale local void has the potential to ease the so-called Hubble tension between the
581: local determinations involving SNe and Planck CMB observations. We also discussed implications of such a local void
582: for BAO observations. The depth of such a void and hence to what extent it can ease the tension are restricted by the
583: kSZ eﬀect. Taking this into account, assuming the Planck cosmology for the outside of the void, the internal Hubble
584: parameter can be raised by a few percent due to the presence of the void, thus potentially alleviating the Hubble
585: tension. The presence of such a large void is unexpected in minimal standard cosmological scenarios, but the presence
586: of such a void can be realized by multi-stream inﬂation.
587: Although the mechanism of multi-stream inﬂation is intuitive and it is known how to relate the early universe model
588: to late time observables, it is important to study multi-stream inﬂation in more details in the future by, for example, a
589: lattice simulation to study the details of the bubble proﬁle. Also, in the present work we have used a LTB metric with
590: an assumed density proﬁle. It is interesting to understand the density proﬁle from ﬁrst principles in multi-stream
591: inﬂation. With these understandings, we would obtain predictions on possible corrections of the distance-redshift
592: relation when the universe is inhomogeneous as a result of multi-stream inﬂation.
593: There can be eﬀects other than the kSZ eﬀect of a local void aﬀecting CMB observations. One eﬀect is the diﬀerence
594: in the angular diameter distance to the last scattering surface. We have checked that the diﬀerence is suﬃciently small
595: for the parameter space of a local void we consider, noting that the angular diameter distance in our void cosmology is
596: given by the metric function R in the LTB metric [33]. A local void can also induce CMB spectral distortions, but the
597: constraints from this eﬀect wouldn’t be as stringent as those from the kSZ eﬀect [65]. A local void in principle should
598: also aﬀect the CMB observations through the integrated Sachs-Wolfe eﬀect. But quantifying this eﬀect precisely in
599: void cosmology appears challenging partly because cosmological perturbation on an inhomogeneous background can be
600: very complicated [33, 66]. This would be particularly so for voids with a thick edge, whereas for voids with a sharp
601: edge we may ﬁnd approximate methods by treating the inside and outside diﬀerent FRW universes.
602: In this work we have assumed that we locate at the center of the void. In general, we should be located away from
603: the exact center of a local void, and there would be additional observational eﬀects associated with this [67, 68]. The
604: observations would also be aﬀected from deviations from spherical symmetry of a local void. These two eﬀects would
605: determine the amount of ﬁne-tuning associated with our scenario.
606: A few more comments are in order. It would also be interesting and important to investigate how the parameter
607: determinations of [3] are aﬀected by the presence of a local void. Our scenario would be tested by observations of
608: high-redshift SNe or galaxies, the redshift distribution of transients such as gamma-ray or gravitational-wave bursts,
609: and future CMB experiments due to the kSZ eﬀect.

1: # Panel transcript: is the Hubble tension new physics or a measurement problem?
2: 
3: ## Round 1, Judge
4: 
5: **Questions to settle:**
6: 1. Is the Hubble tension evidence of new physics beyond ΛCDM, or is it a measurement and analysis problem?
7: 2. Which assumptions underpinning the ΛCDM inference of H0 must break to resolve the tension? (cf. 2101.01372's 7 assumptions)
8: 3. Are early-universe solutions (EDE, modified recombination, self-interacting neutrinos) viable? Are late-universe solutions (local void, modified gravity, late dark energy) viable?
9: 
10: **Paper assignments:**
11: - **early_a** (early universe new physics): 2101.01372, 2212.04494, 2502.15541, 2507.23355
12: - **late_a** (late universe/local): 2202.12214, 2309.05749, 2504.13380, 2606.12980
13: - **skeptic_a** (measurement problem): 2211.00578, 2302.13671
14: - **skeptic_b** (tests resolutions against data): 2109.03263, 2310.16800
15: - **methods** (statistician): 2101.01372 (methods), 2606.12980 (statistics)
16: 
17: **Rules:** Each panelist appends one statement under `## Round 1, <name>`. Read all papers before speaking. Cite specific arXiv IDs. Be concise but substantive.
18: ## Round 1, late_a
19: 
20: **Position: the tension is a statement about the *local* expansion rate, not about the sound horizon. Late-universe and local physics — a local underdensity, and a mild late-time departure from ΛCDM — reproduce the data; nothing requires new early-universe microphysics.**
21: 
22: **1. The data already show a redshift-dependent H0, and that is the whole story.** With equal-width binning in ten redshift intervals, the H0(z) analysis compiled in 2606.12980 (Jia & Dai, Galaxies review) finds a declining trend significant at **5.6σ for z > 0.3**: H0 at low z matches SH0ES, and at high z converges to the CMB value (2606.12980 §, Fig. 11). Independent routes reproduce the same shape: six-bin grouping of megamasers, cosmic chronometers, SNe Ia and BAO gives the trend at **2.1σ** (Krishnan et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 7), and a Gaussian-process reconstruction of H(z) with no new cosmological model finds the transition at **z ≈ 0.49**, mitigating the tension by **~70%** and remaining consistent with H0LiCOW within 1σ (Hu & Wang, via 2606.12980 Fig. 9). A parametrisation H0(z) = H̃0(1+z)^α fitted in ΛCDM gives **H0 = 73.493 ± 0.144 km/s/Mpc** with **α = 0.008 ± 0.006** and **H0(z=1100) = 69.271 ± 2.815 km/s/Mpc**, alleviating the tension by **~66%** (Dainotti et al., 2606.12980). Lensed-quasar time delays show the same mild decline at **1.9σ**, softening to **1.7σ** with a new H0 measurement (2606.12980). Every one of these is a *late-universe* signal. The CMB's 67 km/s/Mpc is the value of H0 far outside our inhomogeneous neighbourhood; the ladder measures it inside. A discrepancy between those two statements is expected without any new field existing at z > 1100.
23: 
24: **2. DESI strengthens the late-time reading, and the void works quantitatively.** DESI BAO + Planck + SNe lifts the preference for w0waCDM over ΛCDM to **3.9σ** (2606.12980, citing DESI+DESY5), and DESI DR2 BAO + Pantheon+ reproduces the same declining H0(z) (2606.12980 Fig. 12). Void models with both **Gaussian and exponential** density profiles reproduce that decline and do so while keeping a *low background* H0 (Mazurenko et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 13). The best-fit void depth found there, δV ≈ **−0.48, −0.47, −0.47** for zcut = 0.2, 1.0, 2.0, gives Ωm,in = (1+δV)Ωm,out ≈ 0.2 — directly consistent with the loose cluster-counting constraint **Ωm = 0.20 ± 0.04 ± 0.09** quoted in 2504.13380. So a deep local void is not forbidden by large-scale structure.
25: 
26: **3. 2504.13380: the local void is strongly preferred once the CMB is in the fit.** Fitting Planck 2018 + Pantheon+ SNe (zcut = 0.2), the ΛLTB void models beat both fiducials overwhelmingly: **ΔBIC = −73.28 and ΔAIC = −91.28 vs ΛCDM_P18 with ln B = 25.36** (ΛLTB4M), and **ΔBIC = −70.81, ΔAIC = −84.81, ln B = 25.87** (ΛLTB3M), against fiducial best-fit χ²_tot,min = 938.769 (ΛCDM_F) and 943.827 (ΛCDM_P18). The ranking is stable: **ΛLTB3M ≫ ΛLTB2M**. The required depth, **δV = −0.45^{+0.05}_{−0.06}** (2M), **−0.44 ± 0.05** (3M), **−0.49 ± 0.06** (4M), i.e. δV ≲ −38%, "even <~−50%", and the transitions of the SN absolute magnitude at **~20 Mpc, ~129 Mpc and ~860–960 Mpc** are all significant far beyond 1σ (Tables IV, V). Crucially, the CMB scale is far outside the void, so Ωm,out = 0.3153 and H0,out = 67.36 km/s/Mpc are retained — the void changes the local number, not the global fit.
27: 
28: **4. Honest accounting of the two strongest objections, and why they do not close the case.**
29: 
30: *(a) "No-go for late-time solutions" (2202.12214, Cai et al.).* Their ΔBIC are real: **+5.3483** (PAge) and **+11.0470** (MAPAge) over ΛCDM for CC+BAO+SNe, strengthening to **ΔBIC > 10** (RSD 2018) and **> 8** (RSD 2021). But that result is about *homogeneous* late-time background parametrisations fitted to *background* data, and the paper says so: it concludes that if late-time solutions are invoked "then the modifications must go beyond the background level", and it explicitly excepts inhomogeneous solutions from its no-go. Two further facts cut my way. First, their own IDL fit gives **H0 = 70.1 ± 2.5 km/s/Mpc** (CC+BAO+SNe, ΛCDM) and **70.2 ± 2.5** with RSD 2018 — the late-universe data, unhelped, already sit ~3σ above Planck's 67.27 ± 0.60 and pull toward SH0ES. Second, that same analysis shows a second, independent H0 problem that is *not* about the sound horizon: with M_B fixed identically for both ladders, **H0^LDL ≈ 74 vs H0^IDL ≈ 68**, which is described as "the recent intriguing view on the H0 tension as the M_B tension". I do not need a smaller r_d; I need the two rungs to talk about the same universe, which is precisely what a void violates.
31: 
32: *(b) "Not empty enough" (2309.05749, Huterer & Wu).* Their sample-variance result is solid and I do not dispute it: **σ_samplevariance = 0.31 km/s/Mpc** from ~1.5 million mock Supercal configurations in 512 subvolumes, so that **|H0^Planck − H0^loc|/σ ≈ 20**; resolving 6 km/s/Mpc would need **δ ≈ −0.8 out to 120 h⁻¹Mpc**, and even a **2σ**-underdense subvolume only raises H0 slightly above Planck's ~67. Perturbation theory agrees closely (**~0.4 km/s/Mpc** for the Pantheon sample). But this is a statement about *sample variance of a single ladder in a ΛCDM structure field*, i.e. the null hypothesis of a homogeneous background. It is exactly the hypothesis the 5.6σ H0(z) decline already rejects, and it is not the void-plus-transition models of 2504.13380, where the CMB region is explicitly placed at Ωm,out = 0.3153 outside the void and a 3-parameter profile (δV, rV, Δr) replaces the top-hat of 2309.05749. The two papers are not measuring the same thing; the panel should treat 2309.05749 as ruling out *voids as the sole explanation in a ΛCDM background*, not voids as a component of one.
33: 
34: **5. Where I concede ground.** In 2504.13380, with the Pantheon+ sample *alone*, the void models are **not** preferred over ΛCDM_F in Bayesian information criterion — several cases have positive ΔBIC_F. The gain appears when the CMB is jointly fitted. And the ΛLTB3M/4M fit requires the absolute-magnitude transitions, which is SN-population physics; the authors themselves flag the over-fitting risk and concede "we still cannot claim a full triumph so far" for the SN-only case. I will not pretend this is a clean ΛCDM-plus-void model. My claim is narrower and, I think, still strong: **the tension does not require breaking any early-universe assumption, and the late-universe data are pointing the same way as my proposal.** Under 2101.01372's framework the late-time route breaks Assumption 2 (homogeneity) and/or Assumption 6 (that late-time distance physics is understood), never Assumptions 1, 3, 4, 5 or 7 — a smaller and more conservative set to abandon than reducing r_s, which drags ω_b, S8 and BBN along with it. FRBs are the cheap, decisive test of the void depth (2606.12980, Banik et al.), and DESI DR2's continued preference for evolving w(z) is the decisive test of the background-level version.
35: 
36: ## Round 1, skeptic_b
37: 
38: **Position: I am not asking which theory is right, I am asking which of the four data sets each theory breaks. Every resolution proposed so far fails at least one hard constraint, and the failures are not the same failure.**
39: 
40: **1. Self-interacting neutrinos (2109.03263) fail on H0 itself, and they fail because of the wrong mechanism.** The best the flavour-specific fit achieves is H0 = **69.47 ± 0.59** km/s/Mpc (3c+0f, Planck TTTEEE+lowE+lensing), and *reduces* to **68.87 ± 0.58** in the 2c+1f case, against ΛCDM **67.90 ± 0.54** — i.e. moving in the wrong direction as the laboratory bounds are progressively evaded. 3: and Transitions of the Absolute Magnitude
4: Jing-Yi Jia a,∗, Jia-Lei Niu a , Da-Chun Qiang b , Hao Wei a,†

8: ABSTRACT
9: Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension, namely
10: the discrepancy between the Hubble constants from the local observation of Type Ia supernova
11: (SNIa) and the high-z observation of cosmic microwave background (CMB). Here, we are interested
12: in alleviating the Hubble tension with a local void. The key idea is assuming that we live in a locally
13: underdense void, where one will feel a faster expansion rate compared to the cosmic average. In the
14: literature, it was found that a local void cannot satisfyingly alleviate the Hubble tension, since it
15: is not preferred over the ΛCDM model by the observations such as the Pantheon SNIa sample,
16: especially in terms of the information criteria AIC and BIC. In the present work, we try to alleviate
17: the Hubble tension with a local void and transitions of the absolute magnitude M, by using the
18: Pantheon+ SNIa sample alone or jointly with the CMB data of Planck 2018. We ﬁnd that the
19: Hubble tension can be satisfyingly alleviated, while the ΛLTB void models are strongly preferred
20: by the observations.

28: INTRODUCTION
29: Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension [1–10]. That is,
30: there is a signiﬁcant tension between the Hubble constants H0 measured from various independent probes
31: in the early and late/local universes. In particular, assuming the well-known ΛCDM model, the Hubble
32: constant inferred from the ﬁnal full-mission Planck measurements (Planck 2018) of the cosmic microwave
33: background (CMB) is given by H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km/s/Mpc [11]. Note that it cannot be substantially
34: changed by assuming various trivial extensions to the base-ΛCDM model. On the other hand, based on the
35: Cepheid/Type Ia supernova (SNIa) distance ladder, the local determination of H0 from the Hubble Space
36: Telescope (HST) and the SH0ES team (R22) is given by H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [12]. Obviously,
37: this Hubble constant directly from the local measurement of Cepheids/SNIa is in > 5σ tension with the
38: one indirectly inferred from CMB in the early universe (at high redshift z∗∼1090). Note that the recent
39: SH0ES 2024 result (R24) H0 = 73.17 ± 0.86 km/s/Mpc [13] is still in 5 −6σ tension with Planck 2018,
40: while it has been cross-checked with the early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) subsamples from
41: SH0ES and CCHP.
42: In history, the Hubble tension has not emerged in the WMAP era of CMB before 2011, then manifested
43: itself at 2 −3σ since the ﬁrst Planck result in 2013, and ﬁnally reached > 5σ in December 2021 (R22).
44: Various independent probes, e.g. the Tip of the Red Giant Branch (TRGB), Mira variables, J-region
45: Asymptotic Giant Branch (JAGB) stars, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), strong gravitational lensing,
46: gravitational waves, water masers, have been considered in the past decade to this end, but the Hubble
47: tension has not been resolved to date. We refer to e.g. [1–10] for comprehensive reviews.
48: Many eﬀorts have been made in the literature. Of course, it is fairly reasonable to carefully check the
49: observational data, since there might be unresolved systematic errors in them. On the other hand, if all
50: the observational data are right, the Hubble tension suggests the need for non-trivial extensions to the
51: standard ΛCDM cosmology. There might be something new in the early, middle, late or local universes.
52: Although numerous theoretical solutions have been proposed in the literature (e.g. [1–10, 113–118] and
53: references therein), the Hubble tension is still a tough problem currently.
54: Here, we are interested in alleviating the Hubble tension with a local void. The key idea is to violate
55: the cosmological principle by assuming that we live in a locally underdense void centered nearby our
56: location. In this underdense region, one will feel a locally faster expansion rate compared to the cosmic
57: average. Noting that H0 ∼73 km/s/Mpc directly measured from the local Cepheids/SNIa is larger than
58: H0 ∼67 km/s/Mpc indirectly inferred from CMB assuming a background Friedmann-Robertson-Walker
59: (FRW) universe, the Hubble tension might be alleviated with a local void [1, 2, 7, 8].
60: A local void can be approximately modeled by using the Lemaˆıtre-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) metric [14–16]
61: ﬁrstly proposed in 1933, which is spherically symmetric and radially inhomogeneous. In 1998, the nearby
62: sample has been examined for evidence of a local “ Hubble Bubble ” [17]. Later, various LTB void models
63: were used to explain the cosmic acceleration without invoking dark energy or modiﬁed gravity [18–41].
64: Notice that cosmological constant is not allowed to this end, since it is the simplest candidate of dark
65: energy as well known. Recently, the Hubble tension attracted a lot of attention. If the goal is no longer
66: to explain the cosmic acceleration, we can allow a non-zero cosmological constant Λ in the LTB model
67: and use the ΛLTB void model to alleviate the Hubble tension, while the cosmic acceleration is instead
68: driven by Λ̸ = 0. The role of LTB void has been changed in this case.
69: In 2013, the evidence for a ∼300 Mpc local void was claimed by Keenan, Barger and Cowie (KBC) [42].
70: In 2018, Hoscheit and Barger [43] claimed that the KBC void can signiﬁcantly reduce the Hubble tension
71: in the ΛLTB framework. Later in 2018, Shanks et al. [44] also claimed that a local void can satisfyingly
72: relieve the Hubble tension. However, both results in [43, 44] were quickly criticized in 2019 by Kenworthy,
73: Scolnic and Riess [45]. But the debate was not settled in fact. Lukovi´c et al. [46] continued the discussions
74: in 2019, and Kazantzidis and Perivolaropoulos [47] claimed hints of a local void in 2020. At the end of
75: 2020, Cai et al. [48] claimed again that the Hubble tension cannot be saved by a local void alone.
76: It is worth noting that the SNIa sample used in [43, 45–48] mentioned above is the Pantheon sample [49]
77: released in 2017. But as is well known, the Hubble constant H0 is heavily degenerated with the absolute
78: magnitude M of SNIa in the Pantheon sample (and other SNIa samples before Pantheon). Commonly,
79: they can be marginalized as a combination M = M + 5 log (c/H0/Mpc) + 25 when we constrain other
80: cosmological parameters, where c is the speed of light and “ log ” gives the logarithm to base 10. This is
81: the reason to say “ SNIa samples are Hubble-free ” in the past. Thus, in order to infer the Hubble constant
82: 
83: 3
84: H0 from the Pantheon SNIa sample, the absolute magnitude M should be given a priori (usually the one
85: from SH0ES is adopted). In the works of local (ΛLTB) void mentioned above, the absolute magnitude M
86: of SNIa has also been given a priori, or M was ﬁtted to data as a free parameter alternatively.
87: The situation has been changed since the Pantheon+ SNIa sample [50–52] released in 2022. In the
88: Pantheon+ sample, the Cepheid calibrated host-galaxy distance moduli are also provided by SH0ES,
89: which can be used to constrain the absolute magnitude M, and hence the degeneracy between H0 and M
90: are broken. So, H0 and M can be separately constrained as free parameters. This makes the Pantheon+
91: sample much better than the Pantheon sample. On the other hand, the new Pantheon+ sample consists
92: of more SNIa (especially more SNIa at low redshifts) than the old Pantheon sample. Thus, it is reasonable
93: to study the Hubble tension with the Pantheon+ SNIa sample instead.
94: Interestingly, a bulk ﬂow around z ∼0.1 and a local infall around z ∼0.04 were claimed by using the
95: Pantheon+ SNIa sample in [53–55]. Similarly, the bulk ﬂow in the local universe was also found with the
96: Pantheon+ SNIa sample in [56] and with CosmicFlows4 in [57]. On the other hand, a local inhomogeneity
97: was claimed in [58] with the Pantheon+ SNIa sample. In [59], a late-time inhomogeneous resolution for
98: the Hubble tension with a chameleon dark energy was proposed. So, well motivated by these works, it is
99: still interesting to consider a local inhomogeneity (especially a local void) for the Hubble tension in the
100: new era of the Pantheon+ SNIa sample.

26: Abstract
27: The ΛCDM cosmological model has been successful in explaining many astronomical
28: observations. However, recent observations increasingly point to deviations from the
29: standard ΛCDM framework. Among these, one of the most significant discrepancies is the
30: Hubble tension, which refers to the difference in values obtained for the Hubble constant H0
31: from high-redshift measurement and local observation. To address this issue, numerous
32: cosmological models and methodological approaches have been proposed. This review
33: offers a concise overview of recent progress in resolving the Hubble tension. The combina-
34: tion of Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO)
35: and uncalibrated Type Ia supernovae data yields a value for H0 that is significantly higher
36: than the ΛCDM predication based on early-universe probes, even without incorporating
37: local distance ladder constraints. This result indicates that the origin of the Hubble tension
38: lies in new physics at low redshifts. Our findings suggest that although many unresolved
39: systematics persist in current observations, they are insufficient to account for the mag-
40: nitude of the current Hubble tension. This implies the likely existence of new physical
41: mechanisms that have yet to be discovered.

108: The Hubble constant, H0, quantifies the current expansion rate of the Universe, thereby
109: serving as a cornerstone for deriving key cosmological quantities. Inferring the Hubble
110: constant from the CMB is fundamentally distinct from local measurement methods. Obser-
111: vations of the CMB probe the universe at a redshift of approximately z ≈1100. The CMB is
112: sensitive to the expansion rate of the universe at the epoch of recombination. Assuming
113: the standard cosmological model, constraints derived from the recombination era can be
114: consistently extrapolated forward to infer constraints on the present-day universe. This
115: approach yields tight constraints on cosmological parameters [1]. However, it is inherently
116: model-dependent. If the cosmic expansion history between recombination and today
117: deviates from the standard model, the inferred value of H0 would consequently change.
118: Local determinations of the Hubble constant H0 rely primarily on the local distance ladder,
119: a hierarchical framework in which distances are measured step by step using a sequence
120: of calibrated standard candles [2,10,11,13,14]. Each rung of the ladder depends on the one
121: below it: nearby distance indicators—such as those based on parallax—are used to calibrate
122: the intrinsic luminosities of brighter standard candles (e.g., Cepheid variables [2,3,21,22])
123: residing in the same galaxies. These, in turn, calibrate even more luminous objects (such as
124: Type Ia supernovae, SNe Ia [23–25]) that can be observed at cosmological distances. Because
125: standard candles have well-understood properties, comparing these with their observed
126: fluxes yields direct distance estimates. However, this approach is inherently cumulative:
127: any systematic error—or potential new physics—affecting a single rung propagates through
128: all subsequent steps, potentially biasing the final measurement of H0. Consequently, the
129: robustness of the local H0 value hinges critically on the accuracy and calibration of every
130: link in the distance ladder, except for one-step methods like Type II SNe [26].
131: In addition to analyses of potential systematic errors in the local distance ladder,
132: numerous cosmological models have been proposed in the late Universe to explain the
133: Hubble tension. In the standard cosmological model, as the simplest possible framework,
134: dark matter is treated as a cold, pressureless, collisionless fluid, and dark energy is repre-
135: sented by a cosmological constant [16–19,27–29]. Recent measurements from CMB [1,30,31],
136: baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) [32–34], as well as SNe Ia compilations [23–25], all show
137: that the ΛCDM model provides an excellent fit when each probe is considered individually.
138: Despite this overall success, the ΛCDM model yields a value of the Hubble constant that
139: is in significant tension with local distance ladder measurements. The Hubble constant

155: 2. Measurements and Uncertainties of the Hubble Constant
156: The Hubble constant represents the current expansion rate of the universe. Nearby
157: systems are primarily governed by gravitational interactions, whereas distant galaxies
158: are more sensitive to the expansion of the Universe. By measuring the distances and
159: redshifts of astronomical objects, one can infer the Hubble constant. Among these, the
160: measurement of the redshift is often relatively straightforward, whereas the estimation
161: of distance is typically the more challenging aspect. For objects that are relatively close,
162: distance determinations can rely on reliable methods like parallax. However, for more
163: distant objects—beyond the resolution limits of today’s instruments—a common and
164: conceptually simple strategy is to infer distance by comparing what we observe with their
165: intrinsic properties. This approach essentially shifts the challenge from measuring distance
166: directly to estimating the object’s inherent characteristics. Astronomical objects with known
167: intrinsic brightness (standard candles) or known physical size (standard rulers) serve as
168: crucial pillars in the measurement of the Hubble constant. Currently, measurements of H0
169: are generally categorized into model-independent and model-dependent approaches. In
170: the following sections, we will review various methods for determining H0, proceeding
171: from model-independent to model-dependent techniques.
172: 2.1. Local Distance Ladder
173: The most effective current approach to measuring the Hubble constant is constructing
174: a local distance ladder based on a sequence of distance indicators [2]. The local distance lad-
175: der is not a single probe, but rather a combination of different distance measurement tech-
176: niques. By cross-calibrating probes at overlapping distance ranges, it enables increasingly
177: precise and more distant measurements. The Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Key Project
178: carried out the first such measurements and achieved a precision of 10% by 2001 [36,37].
179: Since then, the results have been significantly improved due to the accumulation of observa-
180: tional samples, unified calibration procedures, and near-infrared observations of Cepheid
181: variables [4,5,9,38]. The latest measurement yields H0 = 73.17 ± 0.86 kms−1Mpc−1, repre-
182: senting the most precise local measurement of H0 to date [2,3].
183: While numerous methodologies exist for constructing a distance ladder to determine
184: the Hubble constant, the most prevalent and precise framework relies on three rungs [2]. We
185: will use this as a case study to introduce the distance ladder. The first rung of the distance
186: ladder typically involves geometric distance measurements in the Milky Way (MW) [39] or
187: nearby galaxies—such as the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) [40], Small Magellanic Cloud
188: (SMC) [41], or NGC 4258 [42]. These galaxies are commonly referred to as “anchors”. In
189: the second rung, the period–luminosity relation of Cepheid variables in nearby galaxies
190: is calibrated using the geometric distances established in the first rung. This calibrated
191: Cepheid relation is subsequently used to determine distances to SNe Ia residing in the same

302: 4. Dust laws. Dust has long represented a major source of systematic uncertainty in the
303: local distance ladder [67]. To account for dust extinction, one can either apply a correction
304: of Rλ × E(V −I) to the observed Cepheid magnitudes, or instead use a reddening-free
305: Wesenheit magnitude [2,68]. Moreover, beyond the uncertainties inherent in the reddening
306: term E(V −I), the value of the extinction parameter RV is not independently measured for
307: individual SNe Ia host galaxies or at each Cepheid location; instead, it is typically assumed
308: to be the same as in the MW [2,69]. A complete sampling of the reddening curve at long
309: and short wavelengths in each host galaxy, together with a more precise characterization of
310: RV, could further mitigate the uncertainty in Cepheid distance measurements [70].
311: 2.1.2. Second Rung of the Ladder
312: The Cepheid P-L relation of the Cepheid is calibrated using the anchor galaxies in
313: the first rung of the distance ladder. This calibration enables the conversion of Cepheid
314: pulsation periods observed in distant SNe Ia host galaxies into distance measurements.
315: These distances are then used to calibrate SNe Ia, which in turn serve as standardizable
316: candles in the third rung for measuring the Hubble constant. In an ideal scenario, one could
317: bypass the intermediate Cepheid step and directly link geometric calibrations to supernova-
318: based distance measurements. Unfortunately, the rate of SNe in the local universe is far too
319: low to provide enough SNe Ia events within the anchor galaxies.
320: SNe Ia are excellent standard candles, which originate in binary systems. In the
321: canonical scenario, a carbon-rich white dwarf accretes matter from a companion until
322: its mass approaches or exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit, triggering carbon fusion and
323: a thermonuclear explosion. An alternative channel involves the merger of two white
324: dwarfs whose combined mass is close to the Chandrasekhar mass. Because these explo-
325: sions are powered by progenitors of nearly identical mass and involve similar physical
326: mechanisms, the resulting light curves exhibit remarkable uniformity. Within the SALT
327: modeling framework [71,72], the standardized apparent brightness of SNe Ia is typically
328: derived using the Tripp formula [73] as follows:
329: mX = mB + αx1 −βc −δBias + δHost,
330: (1)
331: where mB, x1, and c are independent parameters derived from the SALT light-curve fitting
332: model, α and β denote the correlation coefficients, δBias represents the correction for selec-
333: tion effects and other biases predicted by simulations, and δHost accounts for the correction
334: due to host galaxy properties.
335: H0 measurements derived from SNe Ia are subject to various sources of systematic
336: uncertainty. The local distance ladder utilizes identical indicators across multiple rungs.
337: Consequently, while systematic discrepancies between these rungs can severely bias the

1770: CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSIONS
1771: Nowadays, one of the well-known serious challenges in cosmology is the Hubble tension, namely the
1772: discrepancy between the Hubble constants from the local observation of Type Ia supernova (SNIa) and
1773: the high-z observation of cosmic microwave background (CMB). Here, we are interested in alleviating
1774: the Hubble tension with a local void. The key idea is to violate the cosmological principle by assuming
1775: that we live in a locally underdense void centered nearby our location. In this underdense region, one will
1776: feel a locally faster expansion rate compared to the cosmic average. In the literature, it was found that a
1777: local void cannot satisfyingly alleviate the Hubble tension, since it is not preferred over the ΛCDM model
1778: by the observations such as the Pantheon SNIa sample, especially in terms of the information criteria
1779: AIC and BIC. In this work, we try to alleviate the Hubble tension with a local void and transitions of
1780: the absolute magnitude M, by using the Pantheon+ SNIa sample alone or jointly with the CMB data of
1781: Planck 2018. We ﬁnd that the Hubble tension can be satisfyingly alleviated, while the ΛLTB models are
1782: strongly preferred by the observations.

Key points for the ruling on 2302.13671:
1. **It introduces no new physics and changes no measurement.** It redefines H0 as H0(z).
2. **Eq. (8) is a tautology, not a measurement.** H0(∞) = 1/(T0 ∫ dz/[(1+z)E(z)]) is the identity defining H0 from the age T0 and expansion history. It "recovers" 67.40 because it *uses Planck's fitted T0 and Ω's*. Planck did not measure H0 at z→∞; Planck fit ΛCDM to the CMB and the fitted parameter is H0 at z=0. The paper's move — "Eq. (8) gives the one reported in [3]" — is circular: it reproduces Planck's H0 because it inputs Planck's parameters.
3. **The tension is between two present-day H0 values.** The ladder measures H0 at z≈0 by geometry (parallax → Cepheid distances → SNe → calibration). Planck infers H0 at z=0 by fitting a model to the CMB at z≈1100. Both are statements about z=0. Reframing Planck's result as "H0 at z→∞" changes the subject.
4. **Eq. (7) at z=0.15 → 73.29 is not a reconciliation.** It says: take Planck's cosmology, evaluate the look-back-time integral at z=0.15, and you get 73.29, matching SH0ES. But that's a statement about the *model curve*, not about the data. The ladder's lowest rung is at z≈0.008; SH0ES extrapolates to z=0 and gets 73.04. Planck's model says 67.4 at z=0. The fact that Planck's model curve passes through 73.29 at z=0.15 is a *consequence* of the fit, and it's consistent with the ladder only because the ladder's value at z=0.15 is itself ~73. It does not remove the z=0 disagreement.
5. **The paper's Fig. 1 "consistency" test is circular.** Plotting H0(z) from Eq. (7) (a fixed curve from Planck parameters) against other measurements and calling them "consistent within 1σ" compares data to a model curve. The two "outliers" at 2σ (TRGB, 21cm) are the only independent low-z anchors. This is not a test of the tension; it's a display.
6. **Verdict: 2302.13671 is a definitional move, not a resolution.** It would be a legitimate point for the consensus to note that H0(z) is redshift-dependent *within any given model* — but that is true in ΛCDM already and does not remove the tension, because the tension is about the value at z=0. The panel records this preprint as **non-evidential**: it changes no data and no physics, and its "resolution" dissolves the tension by redefining the quantity being compared.

I address the two new preprints and restate the case with exact numbers.
