18: Introduction
19: The so-called ΛCDM model has now been recognized as the standard paradigm of cosmology.
20: Indeed almost all observations can be understood in the framework of the ΛCDM model, how-
21: ever, there have been several tensions reported, among which the Hubble tension (H0 tension)
22: is one of the most pronounced one where the values of the Hubble constant H0 are inconsis-
23: tent at almost 5σ level between the ones obtained from direct measurements such as Cepheid
24: calibrated distance ladder H0 = 73.30±1.04 km/s/Mpc [1]#1 and from indirect observations
25: such as cosmic microwave background (CMB) from Planck H0 = 67.66±0.42 km/s/Mpc [2].
26: Even if different data are used, local direct observations consistently infer a relatively higher
27: value of H0 compared to the one obtained from Planck, on the other hand, indirect observa-
28: tions, even without Planck data, gives H0 consistent with that obtained from Planck#2 (see,
29: e.g., [6,7] for reviews of the H0 tension).
30: A lot of works have been devoted to resolving the H0 tension by extending the ΛCDM
31: framework (for various models proposed to solve the tension, see, e.g., reviews [6, 8]). In
32: those models, the value of H0 can become higher than ΛCDM case when they are fitted
33: to CMB in combination with some other data such as baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO),
34: type Ia supernova (SNeIa), and so on. It would be important to notice that there exists the
35: correlation between H0 and other cosmological parameters in the fit to CMB#3. Although
36: such a correlation is somewhat involved in models proposed to resolve the H0 tension, the
37: increase of the value of H0 certainly affects other aspects of cosmology. Indeed the baryon
38: energy density generally tends to become larger than that for the case with the ΛCDM in
39: models proposed to resolve the H0 tension when fitted to CMB in combination with other
40: observations [12–15]#4.
41: The baryon density can also be well determined by big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) and
42: hence we can also include BBN data in the fitting to derive the cosmological parameters.
43: However, as we discuss in this paper, we need to be cautious regarding what observational
44: data we use and what nuclear reaction rates are adopted, depending on which the derived
45: values of the cosmological parameters can change. Therefore when the BBN data is com-
46: bined with CMB and some other data, it can affect the value of H0 in models to resolve
47: the H0 tension through the correlations among the cosmological parameters in the fitting.
48: Since, among the light elements, the baryon density is mainly determined by the primor-
49: dial deuterium abundance, which we denote Dp in the following, we mainly investigate the

57: Introduction
58: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) has been instrumental in shaping our modern
59: understanding of the evolution of the universe. With the increase of precision CMB observa-
60: tions available, temperature and polarization anisotropies have become more finely measured,
61: leading to more precise inferences of the contents and history of the universe. The physi-
62: cal mechanisms driving the formation of the CMB and its anisotropies are well understood,
63: leading to a robust prediction for the form of the angular power spectra for any specific
64: cosmological model. Based on ever-improving measurements of the CMB anisotropies, the
65: cosmological parameters driving these models have become more tightly constrained [1].
66: Acoustic oscillations in the primordial plasma prior to recombination imprinted a series
67: of peaks and troughs in CMB power spectra. The expansion history and plasma properties
68: before recombination set the physical scale of the sound horizon, the expansion history after
69: recombination sets the distance to the surface of last scattering, and the combination of the
70: two sets determine the angular scale of the sound horizon at recombination. Measurements
71: of the CMB acoustic peak positions allow for a direct measurement of the angular size of the
72: sound horizon at recombination. Additionally, the relative peak heights allow for an inference
73: of the parameters that determine the scale of the sound horizon within a given cosmological
74: model. Combining this information allows for an inference of the integrated expansion since
75: recombination, including in particular the present expansion rate, the Hubble constant H0
76: [2]. While this is a useful qualitative picture for how constraints are derived from CMB
77: observation, in practice, the parameter constraints for any particular cosmological model are
78: obtained from a full likelihood analysis of the model given the CMB data.
79: The past decade has seen an ever-growing tension in the value of H0 as determined
80: from local measurements [3] and as inferred from early universe observations like the CMB
81: [1] within ΛCDM cosmology. Today, this “Hubble Tension” is driven primarily from the
82: SH0ES (Supernovae and H0 for the Equation of State of dark energy) collaboration’s cosmic
83: distance ladder measurements and the Planck collaboration’s CMB observations [4]. This
84: apparent discrepancy may be due to some unaccounted systematic error in one or more of the
85: – 1 –
86: 
87: measurements, or it may point toward some physics that is left out of our current cosmological
88: models.
89: Many attempts at resolving the tension take the route of new physics [5].
90: In
91: this work, we have found that implementing CMB delensing leads to significantly improved
92: constraints on the parameters defining models aimed at resolving the Hubble tension, and
93: these improved constraints remain valid even if the Hubble Tension does not end up directly
94: involving new physics.
95: Between the CMB surface of last scattering and our telescopes, large scale structure
96: gravitationally deflects incoming photons, producing non-stationary statistics of the CMB
97: fluctuations. At the level of the power spectra, this lensing effect smooths acoustic peaks,
98: making their angular scale more difficult to measure and thus makes some parameter con-
99: straints less precise than they otherwise would be [6]. Current measurements allow for a
100: detection of the effects of CMB lensing at a significance of 40σ with Planck data [7], with
101: similar precision from ACT [8] and SPT [9].For future low-noise CMB data, such as that
102: expected from Simons Observatory [10] and CMB-S4 [11, 12], lensing will be measured at
103: much higher significance, and peak smoothing will hinder some parameter constraints. For-
104: tunately, the off-diagonal mode correlations induced by lensing allow for the reconstruction
105: of a lensing potential map [13, 14], which can be used to reverse the effects [15–17]. Delens-
106: ing temperature and polarization maps generates spectra with sharper acoustic peaks, more
107: prominent damping tails, and other clearer features, thereby allowing for tighter parameter
108: constraints [18, 19].
109: Here, we provide a quantitative look at the improvements made possible by CMB de-
110: lensing, specifically in regard models aimed at resolving the Hubble Tension. Many proposed
111: solutions to the tension take the form of extensions to the ΛCDM model. By introducing
112: new physics that modify the sound horizon, a shift can be made in the inferred value of
113: H0, aligning it more closely with local measurements [4]. We have considered three broad
114: categories of early universe solutions to the Hubble Tension: those involving a variation of
115: fundamental constants at early times, those involving early dark energy, and those involv-
116: ing self-interacting dark radiation. We generate TT, TE, EE, and ϕϕ power spectra from
117: the best-fit values of model parameters that most ease the Hubble Tension, we implement
118: iterative delensing to produce delensed spectra for these models, and we perform Fisher fore-
119: casts to determine the expected parameter constraints from upcoming CMB observations.
120: We show that CMB delensing leads to significantly tighter forecasted constraints on models
121: aimed at resolving the Hubble Tension.
122: In Section 2, we outline the Hubble Tension and how H0 is inferred from the CMB.
123: We briefly overview how iterative delensing works and affects constraining power derived
124: from CMB observations in Section 3, and we also provide the details of our forecasts there.
125: In Section 4, we show the degree to which CMB delensing improves constraints across the
126: proposed solutions. Section 5 concludes.

6: Abstract
7: We introduce a theoretical framework to alleviate the Hubble tension. This framework
8: is based on dynamics of a minimally coupled scalar ﬁeld which either belongs to the
9: Brans-Dicke theory with a self-interacting potential or is the scalar partner of f(R)
10: gravity. These two theories are dynamically equivalent when the Brans-Dicke parameter
11: is zero. We will use this dynamical equivalence to interpret the Hubble tension in the
12: same theoretical framework. For both theories, we write one set of ﬁeld equations in
13: which the value of a parameter distinguishes between the two theories. We will show
14: that H0 actually evolves with redshift so that its value is consistent with that measured
15: from the local distance ladder and it drops to the value measured from CMB at high
16: redshift. We argue that even though both theories exhibit this behaviour, Brans-Dicke
17: theory with an exponential potential is more successful than power-law f(R) gravity to
18: relieve the Hubble tension.
19: Keywords : Cosmology, Hubble Tension, Modiﬁed Gravity.
20: 1
21: Introduction
22: There are a number of unexplained features in the standard cosmology among which the
23: accelerating expansion of the Universe has been recently drawn much amount of attention.
24: There is not still a well-understood explanation on the nature of this phenomenon.
25: It is
26: usually interpreted as evidence either for existence of some exotic matter components or for
27: modiﬁcation of the gravitational theory. In the ﬁrst route of interpretation one can take a
28: perfect ﬂuid with a suﬃciently negative pressure, dubbed dark energy [1], to produce the
29: observed acceleration. In the second route, however, one attributes the accelerating expansion
30: to a modiﬁcation of general relativity.
31: This puzzling picture has been enhanced by the so-called Hubble tension [2]. It consists of
32: a discrepancy between the local value of the Hubble constant H0 based on Cepheids in the
33: Large Magellanic Clouds H0 = 74.03 ± 1.42 Kms−1Mpc−1 [3] and the Planck data of the
34: CMB radiation H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 Kms−1Mpc−1 [4]. Improved determination of the Hubble
35: constant from the Planck observations and the Hubble Space Telescope measurements seem
36: to demonstrate that this tension may not be caused by systematics [5]. Hence, many authors
37: ∗e-mail: y-bisabr@sru.ac.ir.
38: 1
39: 
40: prefer to believe that the tension might be caused by new physics beyond the ΛCDM.
41: These observations suggest that H0 as inferred by CMB coming from z ≃1100 is lower than
42: that inferred by the nearby sources. It therefore seems that the Hubble constant measurement
43: could be aﬀected by redshift in its determination. A recent interesting analysis presented in
44: [6] uses the Pantheon sample [7], the largest compilation of SNe Ia, to show that there is an
45: evolution in the Hubble constant which scales as g(z) = H0(1 + z)−δ with δ and H0 being
46: the evolution parameter and the Hubble parameter at z = 0, respectively. They divided the
47: Pantheon sample into some bins where each bin is populated with an equal number of SNe
48: Ia. Then they have ﬁtted the values obtained in these bins with g(z) ﬁtting function with
49: α ∼10−2. This suggests that H0 can be considered as a monotonic decreasing function from
50: z = 0 up to z ≃1100.
51: The possibility of a slow decaying of H0 with redshift opens theoretical scenarios for its physical
52: and dynamical interpretation. A possible proposition is the modiﬁed gravity theories such as
53: Brans-Dicke (BD) theory [8], as a prototype of the scalar-tensor theories [9], or f(R) gravity
54: models [10]. It is well-known that f(R) gravity, at least within a classical perspective, are
55: dynamically equivalent to the class of BD theories with a potential function and a null BD
56: parameter [11]. Thus under a suitable redeﬁnition of the gravitational and matter ﬁelds, one
57: can make their ﬁeld equations coincide. We will use this dynamical equivalence to consider
58: Hubble tension in a generalized BD theory (GBD) and f(R) gravity in the Einstein frame and
59: under the same analysis framework. We will use an exponential potential in this analysis. The
60: choice of this kind of potential in f(R) gravity is equivalent to considering a power-law f(R)
61: gravity [12]. We then determine the Hubble ﬂow and show that even though decaying of H(z)
62: with redshift is possible for both models GBD is more consistent with the g(z) model proposed
63: in [6].

15: - ANOVA: H0 values differ significantly between anchors at 99% CL (R11: F=85.70, p=1.5e-15; R16: F=144.49, p=2.91e-24)

2: 
3: ## Round 1, Judge
4: 
5: **Questions to settle:**
6: 1. Is the Hubble tension evidence of new physics beyond ΛCDM, or is it a measurement and analysis problem?
7: 2. Which assumptions underpinning the ΛCDM inference of H0 must break to resolve the tension? (cf. 2101.01372's 7 assumptions)
8: 3. Are early-universe solutions (EDE, modified recombination, self-interacting neutrinos) viable? Are late-universe solutions (local void, modified gravity, late dark energy) viable?
9: 
10: **Paper assignments:**
11: - **early_a** (early universe new physics): 2101.01372, 2212.04494, 2502.15541, 2507.23355
12: - **late_a** (late universe/local): 2202.12214, 2309.05749, 2504.13380, 2606.12980
13: - **skeptic_a** (measurement problem): 2211.00578, 2302.13671
14: - **skeptic_b** (tests resolutions against data): 2109.03263, 2310.16800
15: - **methods** (statistician): 2101.01372 (methods), 2606.12980 (statistics)

17: **Rules:** Each panelist appends one statement under `## Round 1, <name>`. Read all papers before speaking. Cite specific arXiv IDs. Be concise but substantive.
18: ## Round 1, late_a
19: 
20: **Position: the tension is a statement about the *local* expansion rate, not about the sound horizon. Late-universe and local physics — a local underdensity, and a mild late-time departure from ΛCDM — reproduce the data; nothing requires new early-universe microphysics.**
21: 
22: **1. The data already show a redshift-dependent H0, and that is the whole story.** With equal-width binning in ten redshift intervals, the H0(z) analysis compiled in 2606.12980 (Jia & Dai, Galaxies review) finds a declining trend significant at **5.6σ for z > 0.3**: H0 at low z matches SH0ES, and at high z converges to the CMB value (2606.12980 §, Fig. 11). Independent routes reproduce the same shape: six-bin grouping of megamasers, cosmic chronometers, SNe Ia and BAO gives the trend at **2.1σ** (Krishnan et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 7), and a Gaussian-process reconstruction of H(z) with no new cosmological model finds the transition at **z ≈ 0.49**, mitigating the tension by **~70%** and remaining consistent with H0LiCOW within 1σ (Hu & Wang, via 2606.12980 Fig. 9). A parametrisation H0(z) = H̃0(1+z)^α fitted in ΛCDM gives **H0 = 73.493 ± 0.144 km/s/Mpc** with **α = 0.008 ± 0.006** and **H0(z=1100) = 69.271 ± 2.815 km/s/Mpc**, alleviating the tension by **~66%** (Dainotti et al., 2606.12980). Lensed-quasar time delays show the same mild decline at **1.9σ**, softening to **1.7σ** with a new H0 measurement (2606.12980). Every one of these is a *late-universe* signal. The CMB's 67 km/s/Mpc is the value of H0 far outside our inhomogeneous neighbourhood; the ladder measures it inside. A discrepancy between those two statements is expected without any new field existing at z > 1100.
23: 
24: **2. DESI strengthens the late-time reading, and the void works quantitatively.** DESI BAO + Planck + SNe lifts the preference for w0waCDM over ΛCDM to **3.9σ** (2606.12980, citing DESI+DESY5), and DESI DR2 BAO + Pantheon+ reproduces the same declining H0(z) (2606.12980 Fig. 12). Void models with both **Gaussian and exponential** density profiles reproduce that decline and do so while keeping a *low background* H0 (Mazurenko et al., via 2606.12980 Fig. 13). The best-fit void depth found there, δV ≈ **−0.48, −0.47, −0.47** for zcut = 0.2, 1.0, 2.0, gives Ωm,in = (1+δV)Ωm,out ≈ 0.2 — directly consistent with the loose cluster-counting constraint **Ωm = 0.20 ± 0.04 ± 0.09** quoted in 2504.13380. So a deep local void is not forbidden by large-scale structure.
25: 
26: **3. 2504.13380: the local void is strongly preferred once the CMB is in the fit.** Fitting Planck 2018 + Pantheon+ SNe (zcut = 0.2), the ΛLTB void models beat both fiducials overwhelmingly: **ΔBIC = −73.28 and ΔAIC = −91.28 vs ΛCDM_P18 with ln B = 25.36** (ΛLTB4M), and **ΔBIC = −70.81, ΔAIC = −84.81, ln B = 25.87** (ΛLTB3M), against fiducial best-fit χ²_tot,min = 938.769 (ΛCDM_F) and 943.827 (ΛCDM_P18). The ranking is stable: **ΛLTB3M ≫ ΛLTB2M**. The required depth, **δV = −0.45^{+0.05}_{−0.06}** (2M), **−0.44 ± 0.05** (3M), **−0.49 ± 0.06** (4M), i.e. δV ≲ −38%, "even <~−50%", and the transitions of the SN absolute magnitude at **~20 Mpc, ~129 Mpc and ~860–960 Mpc** are all significant far beyond 1σ (Tables IV, V). Crucially, the CMB scale is far outside the void, so Ωm,out = 0.3153 and H0,out = 67.36 km/s/Mpc are retained — the void changes the local number, not the global fit.
27: 
28: **4. Honest accounting of the two strongest objections, and why they do not close the case.**
29: 
30: *(a) "No-go for late-time solutions" (2202.12214, Cai et al.).* Their ΔBIC are real: **+5.3483** (PAge) and **+11.0470** (MAPAge) over ΛCDM for CC+BAO+SNe, strengthening to **ΔBIC > 10** (RSD 2018) and **> 8** (RSD 2021). But that result is about *homogeneous* late-time background parametrisations fitted to *background* data, and the paper says so: it concludes that if late-time solutions are invoked "then the modifications must go beyond the background level", and it explicitly excepts inhomogeneous solutions from its no-go. Two further facts cut my way. First, their own IDL fit gives **H0 = 70.1 ± 2.5 km/s/Mpc** (CC+BAO+SNe, ΛCDM) and **70.2 ± 2.5** with RSD 2018 — the late-universe data, unhelped, already sit ~3σ above Planck's 67.27 ± 0.60 and pull toward SH0ES. Second, that same analysis shows a second, independent H0 problem that is *not* about the sound horizon: with M_B fixed identically for both ladders, **H0^LDL ≈ 74 vs H0^IDL ≈ 68**, which is described as "the recent intriguing view on the H0 tension as the M_B tension". I do not need a smaller r_d; I need the two rungs to talk about the same universe, which is precisely what a void violates.
31: 
32: *(b) "Not empty enough" (2309.05749, Huterer & Wu).* Their sample-variance result is solid and I do not dispute it: **σ_samplevariance = 0.31 km/s/Mpc** from ~1.5 million mock Supercal configurations in 512 subvolumes, so that **|H0^Planck − H0^loc|/σ ≈ 20**; resolving 6 km/s/Mpc would need **δ ≈ −0.8 out to 120 h⁻¹Mpc**, and even a **2σ**-underdense subvolume only raises H0 slightly above Planck's ~67. Perturbation theory agrees closely (**~0.4 km/s/Mpc** for the Pantheon sample). But this is a statement about *sample variance of a single ladder in a ΛCDM structure field*, i.e. the null hypothesis of a homogeneous background. It is exactly the hypothesis the 5.6σ H0(z) decline already rejects, and it is not the void-plus-transition models of 2504.13380, where the CMB region is explicitly placed at Ωm,out = 0.3153 outside the void and a 3-parameter profile (δV, rV, Δr) replaces the top-hat of 2309.05749. The two papers are not measuring the same thing; the panel should treat 2309.05749 as ruling out *voids as the sole explanation in a ΛCDM background*, not voids as a component of one.
33: 
34: **5. Where I concede ground.** In 2504.13380, with the Pantheon+ sample *alone*, the void models are **not** preferred over ΛCDM_F in Bayesian information criterion — several cases have positive ΔBIC_F. The gain appears when the CMB is jointly fitted. And the ΛLTB3M/4M fit requires the absolute-magnitude transitions, which is SN-population physics; the authors themselves flag the over-fitting risk and concede "we still cannot claim a full triumph so far" for the SN-only case. I will not pretend this is a clean ΛCDM-plus-void model. My claim is narrower and, I think, still strong: **the tension does not require breaking any early-universe assumption, and the late-universe data are pointing the same way as my proposal.** Under 2101.01372's framework the late-time route breaks Assumption 2 (homogeneity) and/or Assumption 6 (that late-time distance physics is understood), never Assumptions 1, 3, 4, 5 or 7 — a smaller and more conservative set to abandon than reducing r_s, which drags ω_b, S8 and BBN along with it. FRBs are the cheap, decisive test of the void depth (2606.12980, Banik et al.), and DESI DR2's continued preference for evolving w(z) is the decisive test of the background-level version.

40: **1. Self-interacting neutrinos (2109.03263) fail on H0 itself, and they fail because of the wrong mechanism.** The best the flavour-specific fit achieves is H0 = **69.47 ± 0.59** km/s/Mpc (3c+0f, Planck TTTEEE+lowE+lensing), and *reduces* to **68.87 ± 0.58** in the 2c+1f case, against ΛCDM **67.90 ± 0.54** — i.e. moving in the wrong direction as the laboratory bounds are progressively evaded. The paper's own conclusion: "**the SINU scenario cannot resolve the Hubble tension when all laboratory and cosmological constraints are taken into consideration**." 6: Read the second new preprint, 2008.01115 (Lucca). I think it is the best news this shift has for our side, and I want to flag why before Round 2.
7: 
8: **Lucca's framing is a direct constraint on early-universe models and it is the framing I have been pushing all along.** The paper's thesis: the H0 tension should be restated as an H0−r_s tension, and "as r_s is only ... determined before recombination, late-time modifications of the ΛCDM model are intrinsically incapable of fully solving the H0−r_s tension." That is the same structural demand as my Round 1 claim that a fix operating through a phase shift rather than a density change has not reduced r_d. Two of us have now independently landed on the same criterion.
9: 
10: **And it cuts against early_a, whose numbers I have been pressing all along.** From Table I, with a PRISM mock spectral-distortion likelihood added to Planck 2018 + BAO + SH0ES + Pantheon+:
11: 
12: - ΛCDM: n_s = 0.9692 ± 0.0038, H0 = 68.20 ± 0.54
13: - EDE: n_s = 0.9873 (+0.0069/−0.0080), H0 = 71.2 (+1.0/−1.1)
14: - EDE + SDs: n_s = 0.9724 ± 0.0032, **H0 = 69.41 (+0.63/−0.75)**, **f_EDE < 0.095**, Θ_i > 0.40 (95% CL)
15: 
16: The SD signal is almost purely the n_s shift — shifting n_s alone "nearly perfectly overlaps" the full-EDE prediction, and H0 itself changes the SD shape by **less than 0.5%**. So **every unit of H0 in the EDE family is bought with an n_s excursion, and n_s is what SDs measure best.** The paper: the H0 contour becomes "not compatible with the SH0ES value any more."
17: 
18: Two caveats I have put in the transcript and you should know I have put there, because they are the obvious objection: it is a **forecast, not data**; it assumes a PRISM-class mission (5×10⁻²⁷ W/m²/Hz/sr, "one order of magnitude better than PIXIE") and **neglects foregrounds entirely**, which the authors concede worsen results "by roughly one order of magnitude"; and the fiducial is set to ΛCDM, so the error bars are optimistic. I have recorded it as a forecast with an order-of-magnitude systematic, not an established exclusion.
19: 
20: **The point I want you to see for our side.** A pure local calibration systematic predicts **no** shift in n_s. So if early_a's models require a large Δn_s to deliver their H0, and a ladder systematic requires none, then the SD measurement is in principle a clean discriminator between us and them — one that does not depend on the distance ladder at all. That is worth more to us than anything in 2211.00578 or 2302.13671, because it is independent of every systematic we are accused of.
21: 
22: **But I want to be honest with you about the shape of our problem.** I have conceded in the transcript that this paper weakens my Round 1 position — I had said axion-like EDE was the only candidate surviving every constraint I could test, and it now has a named failure mode. If late-a void models also end up constrained, we are left with a *negative* case: "nobody's model works." That is a legitimate consensus outcome, but it is a weak one, and a panel that only produces negative findings will be judged as having failed to convene.
23: 
24: So my suggestion: **let one of us make a positive measurement claim in Round 2, and let it be a falsifiable one.** Mine would be that the ladder-systometric hypothesis has a specific, testable prediction that new physics does not: it should leave n_s, and r_s h, and fσ8 unmoved. I cannot yet show that 2211.00578 or 2302.13671 delivers it, and I do not want to claim it before the numbers are in front of me. If you can, that is the contribution I would most like from our side.
25: 
26: Still outstanding from me to you: whether 2211.00578 survives re-fitting the metallicity dependence rather than fixing it, given the 8.2σ quoted in 2606.12980 line 292. And I have asked methods (shift 6, still unanswered) about whether the H0(z) significance levels late_a quotes are independent, which cuts against us as well as for her.

24: I.
25: INTRODUCTION
26: The so-called H0 tension, related to the reported discrepancy on the measured values of Hubble-Lemaˆıtre (henceforth Hubble)
27: constant, H0, is claimed to be one of the most critical issues for the Λ Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) model, considered the
28: standard picture of the observed Universe. This staggering discrepancy arises when comparing estimates on H0 provided by
29: standard candles with those inferred by the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) [1]. In fact, the results from the
30: SH0ES collaboration, obtained by considering the cosmological ladder and probes like classical Cepheids and Supernovae Type
31: Ia (SNe Ia), in a region with redshift interval 0.02333 < z < 0.15, tell us that H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/(s Mpc) at 68% conﬁdence
32: level (CL) [2], while the Planck collaboration, reporting observations of the CMBR, shows, instead, that H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5 km/(s
33: Mpc) at 68% CL [3]. Despite the accuracy of both approaches, a 5.0σ tension emerges and it seems to be irreconcilable under
34: the standard of the ΛCDM model.
35: The problem has to be addressed both from experimental and theoretical points of view. Considering the increasing precision
36: achieved by recent observations, an experimental reason for the tension, related to some systematic eﬀects, is becoming less and
37: less probable [1, 4]. Thus this tension (and other ones revealed in cosmological parameters [1]) is seemingly hinting at some
38: undeﬁned new physics, going beyond the ΛCDM model. The last conclusion can be inferred also from other critical issues of
39: the standard cosmological model, like the nature of dark matter and dark energy, which should account for approximately 25%
40: and 70%, respectively, of the energy-density budget of the observed Universe [4–13]. However, the nature of the dark side of
41: the Universe is still unknown at a fundamental level, even if very precise tests are performed by several running experiments
42: [14–17].
43: Diﬀerent approaches are considered in the literature to ﬁx the above problems. A possibility is taking into account extensions
44: and modiﬁcations of General Relativity (GR) where the ΛCDM model evolves along the cosmic history. For example, extensions
45: like f(R) gravity [18–22]), have been considered in cosmological applications [23–27] to address diﬀerent issues related to the
46: ΛCDM model, like the late-time dark energy [12], and the inﬂationary behaviour of the early Universe [28].
47: Many possible extensions and modiﬁcations of GR have been proposed (see e.g. [29]), but, no ﬁnal theory, capable of
48: addressing the whole cosmic history and the large-scale structure has been formulated up to date. As in the case of cosmological
49: inﬂation, the paradigm seems consistent but a ﬁnal model, comprehensive of the whole phenomenology, if any, is still missing.
50: In any case, modiﬁed gravity can be adopted to investigate the H0 tension, as recently proposed in [30].
51: Modiﬁed gravity is not the only approach to ﬁx tensions in cosmology. New physics can be pursued also by taking into
52: account other paradigms like extensions of Electromagnetism and the Standard Model of Particles [31–33], or revising the
53: concept of cosmological measurements according to the principles of Quantum Mechanics [34, 35], as well as many diﬀerent
54: other approaches reported in the literature [36–64]. Furthermore, requiring a phenomenological evolution of H0 with the redshift
55: could be a straightforward way out for the problem [65–78] even without investigating some fundamental counterpart.

ABSTRACT
In cosmology, the Hubble tension has become one of the most serious challenges in the last decade.
Assuming that all the observational data are right, one of the ways out is to modify the standard
ΛCDM cosmology. In the literature, the theoretical modiﬁcations are mainly made in the early and
the late/local universes. But on both sides, some no-go arguments have been proposed recently. In
particular, the general no-go arguments for the late-time modiﬁcations are mainly based on the
PAge parameterization. In the present work, we note that there are some ﬂaws in the (original) PAge
parameterization, and then propose various generalized PAge (GPAge) parameterizations, which can
be extended to z > zCMB and hence the cosmic microwave background (CMB) can be taken into
account, while they are also more accurate at low redshifts. With these GPAge parameterizations,
we revisit the Hubble tension by using not only the late-time observations but also the observational
data of CMB. We ﬁnd that the Hubble tension could be alleviated (or even resolved) in GPAges
signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from the standard ΛCDM cosmology, while they are overwhelmingly preferred
over ΛCDM by the observational data in terms of all the information criteria. Surprisingly, we ﬁnd
that the new physics in the mid-time might be the key to resolve the Hubble tension.

I.
INTRODUCTION
In cosmology, the Hubble tension has been one of the most serious challenges in the last decade [1–6].
Assuming the ΛCDM model, the Hubble constant inferred from the ﬁnal Planck measurements (Planck
2018) of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) is given by H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km/s/Mpc [7]. On the
other hand, based on the Cepheid/Type Ia supernova (SNIa) distance ladder, the local determination of
H0 from the Hubble Space Telescope and the SH0ES team is given by H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [8].
Clearly, the Hubble constants inferred from the late- and the early-universes are in a great tension > 5σ.
Recently, the Hubble tension has become > 6 ∼7σ [6, 9, 10]. Nowadays, it casts a serious shadow over
the standard cosmology.
One of the ways out is to carefully check the observational data, which might have some unresolved
systematic errors. Many eﬀorts have been made on both sides of CMB and SNIa/Cepheid in the literature,
and no convincing evidences have been found to date [1–5].
Assuming that all the observational data are right, the other way out is to modify the standard ΛCDM
cosmology. Of course, various trivial extensions to the base-ΛCDM model do not work [1–5]. The Hubble
tension invokes non-trivial modiﬁcations in the early, middle, late or local universes.
In the literature, the theoretical modiﬁcations are mainly made in the early and the late/local universes.
For example, one of the leading models to resolve the Hubble tension in the early universe is the well-
known early dark energy (EDE) model [11] and its variants (see e.g. [12–14] for reviews). In particular,
the Anti-de Sitter (AdS) EDE model [15–18] is fairly interesting. Also, the dark radiation is one of the
well-motivated and straightforward extensions to resolve the Hubble tension in the early universe (see
e.g. [19] and [1–5] for reviews). However, there is a well-known no-go argument [20] for the early-time
solutions (see also e.g. [1–5]). The debate has not been settled to date.

238: IV.
239: DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS
240: The problem of the H0 tension can be addressed in the framework of the ΛCDM model in terms of look-back time considered
241: at the redshift where measurements are performed. In this derivation, the values of the age of the Universe and the cosmic
242: densities, provided by the Planck collaboration, are adopted. The look-back time curve, matching the observational values
243: of H0, is shown in Fig. 1. According to this approach, we are able to recover most of the reported H0 measurements and,
244: more remarkably, the two most representatives for the H0 tension, namely the ones provided by the Planck [3] and SH0ES
245: [2] collaborations. The result is interesting because the concordance of H0 measurements is achieved independently from the
246: type of performed measurement. Indeed, we have considered estimates obtained by diﬀerent standard candles (SNe Ia, TRGB,
247: Cepheids, etc), phenomena concerning early stages of the Universe (CMBR, Cosmic Dawn, Equivalence Epoch), and also novel
248: probes (gravitational waves). According to this picture, we may conclude that no systematic errors nor new physics are necessary
249: to explain the tension, which, instead, can be accounted for with a single formula in the framework of the ΛCDM model. In
250: other words, by adopting the look-back time, we can consistently account for late-type and early-type measurements, conﬁrming
251: the underlying consistency of the ΛCDM model. We also point out that this evolution of H0 constant in the framework of the
252:

254: ΛCDM model does not change its role as a formal integration constant derived from the Friedman equations, but its operative
255: value depends on the redshift where it is inferred. This conclusion is important for the deﬁnition of the cosmological distances,
256: which are all depending on H0.
257: It is worth stressing that the value of the age of the Universe, T0, has been derived by the Planck collaboration starting from
258: six independent parameters (the minimum number of parameters necessary to describe the ΛCDM model), among which H0
259: is not included. In fact, also H0 is inferred from the same minimum number of independent parameters. This means that any
260: circularity problem is avoided. Furthermore, we can note that the plot in Fig. 1 is in agreement with the general trend of H0

262: Furthermore, our results are consistent with constraints on H0 obtained from the age of the Universe: for instance, in [52], an

266: Finally, computations reported here are consistent with the interpretation proposed in [34, 35], according to which a funda-

269: contradiction with present results.
270: As a ﬁnal remark, it is useful noticing that we do not exclude the idea of new physics beyond the ΛCDM model, because other
271: issues, like dark energy and dark matter, at late time, or inﬂation, at early time, could require to go beyond GR and standard
272: cosmology. However, from the above discussion, it is possible to state that new physics is not necessary for the particular issue
273: of the H0 tension, which can be completely accounted for in the framework of the ΛCDM model.

9: ABSTRACT
10: The Hubble tension problem is one of the most significant challenges in modern cosmology. In this paper, we study the Hubble
11: tension problem in the framework of holographic dark energy (HDE). To perform a systematic and comprehensive analysis, we
12: select six representative theoretical models from all four categories of HDE. For the observational data, we adopt the Baryon
13: Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 2 (DR2) along with a
14: collection of alternative BAO measurements, Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) distance priors from 𝑃𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑘2018, and
15: type Ia supernovae (SN) data from the PantheonPlus, Union3, and DESY5 compilations. We find that HDE models that employ
16: the Hubble scale or its combinations as the infrared (IR) cutoff cannot alleviate the Hubble tension problem. In contrast, HDE
17: models that employ the future event horizon as the IR cutoff can partially mitigate the Hubble tension problem. It must be stressed
18: that these two key conclusions hold true for cases of adopting different theoretical HDE models and different observational data.
19: Our findings advocate for further exploration of HDE models using other types of cosmological observations.

11: Abstract
12: The Hubble tension and the recently reported anomaly in data from the Dark Energy Spectro-
13: scopic Instrument (DESI) are considered to pose serious challenges to the standard ΛCDM model of
14: cosmology. In this work, we show that resolving the Hubble tension with a scenario featuring dark
15: radiation–matter decoupling (DRMD) predicts the presence of dark acoustic oscillations (DAO)
16: similar in scale to baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO). Using an inference independent of large-
17: scale structure data, relying only on Planck measurements of the cosmic microwave background
18: and SH0ES-calibrated supernova data, we find evidence for a DAO signal with drag-horizon scale
19: rd,DAO ∈[54, 65] Mpc/h (68% C.I.) and amplitude ADAO ∈[0.02, 0.05] (68% C.I.). These predic-
20: tions provide a concrete target for current and upcoming large-scale structure surveys, including
21: DESI, Euclid, and the Roman Space Telescope. Remarkably, the predicted DAO properties are
22: consistent with those required to explain the DESI anomaly, offering both an alternative to evolving
23: dark energy and a preliminary validation of the relevance of a dark radiation–matter decoupling
24: scenario for addressing the Hubble tension.

32: INTRODUCTION
33: Observational challenges to ΛCDM, the standard model of cosmology, have emerged from
34: high-precision cosmic microwave background (CMB), baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO),
35: and supernova (SN) observations. In this work, we focus on the two most significant chal-
36: lenges and argue that they provide two independent pieces of evidence pointing to the same
37: underlying new physics beyond ΛCDM, sharpening arguments made recently in [1, 2].
38: The first challenge is the Hubble tension. The expansion rate of the Universe today mea-
39: sured directly by using standard candles disagrees with the expansion rate predicted in the
40: ΛCDM model when fitted to CMB and BAO data. The most precise measurement of the ex-
41: pansion rate today from the SH0ES collaboration obtains H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [3],
42: while the expansion rate inferred from the CMB, when assuming the ΛCDM model, implies
43: H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km/s/Mpc [4] when using Planck CMB data. These observational deter-
44: minations of H0 are in about 5σ conflict with each other. While one may wonder if there is
45: unknown systematics affecting these measurements, which could explain this disagreement
46: within the ΛCDM model, one should keep in mind that several measurements of the local
47: expansion rate using different standard candles agree with the supernova measurement of
48: SH0ES1. At the same time, BAO measurements, combined with a constraint on the amount
49: of baryons from Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN), agree with the CMB measurement [6] only
50: if ΛCDM is assumed. For this reason, we will focus on explanations of the Hubble tension,
51: which involves new physics going beyond ΛCDM (for reviews of the tension and proposed
52: solutions see [7–9]).
53: The second challenge, which we refer to as DESI anomaly, is related to recent high-
54: precision BAO measurement of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). When
55: DESI data is combined with Planck CMB [4] and Pantheon+ supernova measurements [10,
56: 11], one finds a 2.8σ preference for a model with evolving dark energy parametrized as a two-
57: parameter extension of ΛCDM. Specifically, if the dark energy equation-of-state parameter
58: is assumed to take the form w(a) = w0 + wa(1 −a), where ΛCDM corresponds to w0 = −1,
59: wa = 0, DESI finds [6] w0 = −0.838±0.055, wa = −0.62+0.22
60: −0.19. This interpretation is however
61: unsettling as the preferred values would imply that dark energy entered a phantom regime
62: with w < −1 in the recent past, although attempts to avoid this interpretation in terms of

89: The BAO
90: experiments measure the product of the expansion rate H0 and the sound horizon at baryon
91: decoupling rd,BAO, which is measured by DESI to be H0 · rd,BAO = 101.54 ± 0.73 (100
92: km)/s [6].
93: This means, that in order to stay consistent with BAO measurements, any
94: solution to the Hubble tension that fits the CMB with a higher value of H0 needs to involve
95: new physics before decoupling in order to also lower rd,BAO, and thus remain compatible
96: with BAO measurements [20, 21]. This also implies that late-time evolving dark energy
97: cannot resolve the Hubble tension.
98: One of the simplest ideas for new physics before recombination, which could lower the
99: sound horizon and alleviate the Hubble tension, while staying compatible with BAO mea-
100: surements, is dark radiation. Dark radiation would maintain a constant energy density rela-
101: 3
102: 
103: tive to ordinary radiation in the radiation dominated epoch, and redshift away compared to
104: the total energy density after matter-radiation equality shortly before recombination. This
105: would lower the sound horizon and raise H0 while minimizing its effect on structure formation
106: in the late Universe. But if the dark radiation is free-streaming, it induces anisotropic stress
107: and enhances diffusion damping on small scales in the CMB [22] (predominantly scales
108: that enter the horizon before matter-radiation equality) beyond an acceptable level. To
109: avoid these problems, it is natural to consider a component of self-interacting dark radiation
110: (SIDR), which behaves like a tightly coupled fluid, and is not free-streaming [23–28].
111: There are two basic problems with SIDR as a solution to the Hubble tension in its simplest
112: form. First, it is ruled out by BBN [29], which puts a rather stringent bound on any form
113: of dark radiation.
114: In order to alleviate the Hubble tension, an amount of SIDR, which
115: corresponds to an extra amount of relativistic degrees of freedom ∆Neff ≳0.5, is needed,
116: which is ruled out by BBN constraints. Second, even when ignoring BBN constraints, and
117: allowing for ∆Neff ≳0.5, SIDR does not provide a full resolution of the Hubble tension,
118: but only reduces the tension to around 3σ when using Planck 2018 CMB data [1, 30]. The
119: latest constraints from ACT provide even stronger constraints on extra relativistic degrees
120: of freedom [31] (see section IV for a discussion of the latest ACT constraints).

7: ABSTRACT
8: In cosmology, the Hubble tension has become one of the most serious challenges in the last decade.
9: Assuming that all the observational data are right, one of the ways out is to modify the standard
10: ΛCDM cosmology. In the literature, the theoretical modiﬁcations are mainly made in the early and
11: the late/local universes. But on both sides, some no-go arguments have been proposed recently. In
12: particular, the general no-go arguments for the late-time modiﬁcations are mainly based on the
13: PAge parameterization. In the present work, we note that there are some ﬂaws in the (original) PAge
14: parameterization, and then propose various generalized PAge (GPAge) parameterizations, which can
15: be extended to z > zCMB and hence the cosmic microwave background (CMB) can be taken into
16: account, while they are also more accurate at low redshifts. With these GPAge parameterizations,
17: we revisit the Hubble tension by using not only the late-time observations but also the observational
18: data of CMB. We ﬁnd that the Hubble tension could be alleviated (or even resolved) in GPAges
19: signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from the standard ΛCDM cosmology, while they are overwhelmingly preferred
20: over ΛCDM by the observational data in terms of all the information criteria. Surprisingly, we ﬁnd
21: that the new physics in the mid-time might be the key to resolve the Hubble tension.

29: INTRODUCTION
30: In cosmology, the Hubble tension has been one of the most serious challenges in the last decade [1–6].
31: Assuming the ΛCDM model, the Hubble constant inferred from the ﬁnal Planck measurements (Planck
32: 2018) of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) is given by H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km/s/Mpc [7]. On the
33: other hand, based on the Cepheid/Type Ia supernova (SNIa) distance ladder, the local determination of
34: H0 from the Hubble Space Telescope and the SH0ES team is given by H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc [8].
35: Clearly, the Hubble constants inferred from the late- and the early-universes are in a great tension > 5σ.
36: Recently, the Hubble tension has become > 6 ∼7σ [6, 9, 10]. Nowadays, it casts a serious shadow over
37: the standard cosmology.
38: One of the ways out is to carefully check the observational data, which might have some unresolved
39: systematic errors. Many eﬀorts have been made on both sides of CMB and SNIa/Cepheid in the literature,
40: and no convincing evidences have been found to date [1–5].
41: Assuming that all the observational data are right, the other way out is to modify the standard ΛCDM
42: cosmology. Of course, various trivial extensions to the base-ΛCDM model do not work [1–5]. The Hubble
43: tension invokes non-trivial modiﬁcations in the early, middle, late or local universes.
44: In the literature, the theoretical modiﬁcations are mainly made in the early and the late/local universes.
45: For example, one of the leading models to resolve the Hubble tension in the early universe is the well-
46: known early dark energy (EDE) model [11] and its variants (see e.g. [12–14] for reviews). In particular,
47: the Anti-de Sitter (AdS) EDE model [15–18] is fairly interesting. Also, the dark radiation is one of the
48: well-motivated and straightforward extensions to resolve the Hubble tension in the early universe (see
49: e.g. [19] and [1–5] for reviews). However, there is a well-known no-go argument [20] for the early-time
50: solutions (see also e.g. [1–5]). The debate has not been settled to date.
51: On the other hand, the models to resolve the Hubble tension in the late/local universes include various
52: exotic (late) dark energy models, interacting dark energy models, dark energy models with transitions,
53: local void models, and so on (see e.g. [1–5] for reviews). In particular, the phantom-like dark energy (PDE)
54: transition model (see e.g. [21, 22]) and the Chameleon dark energy model (see e.g. [23] and [24–27]) are
55: fairly interesting. Note that there are also no-go arguments (e.g. [22, 28–34]) for the late-time solutions.
56: Nevertheless, the relevant works on this topic are still active.
57: In particular, the most general no-go argument for the late-time solutions of the Hubble tension comes
58: from [32–34]. To be as general as possible, one should be completely ignorant of the cosmology, especially
59: the components in the universe and the gravity theory. So, all the w(z) parameterizations of dark energy
60: are not suitable, since we pretend to even do not know whether the universe contains dark energy or dark
61: matter. To this end, the well-known cosmography (see e.g. [35–38]) might be suitable, which is the Taylor
62: expansion of the luminosity distance dL with respect to redshift z or y-shift y = 1−a = z/(1+z). However,
63: as shown in [32, 33], both the cosmographies with respect to z and y even up to the ﬁfth order cannot
64: faithfully approximate the model they claim to parameterize at redshift z >∼1, even for the simplest
65: ΛCDM model. Therefore, in [32–34], the so-called PAge parameterization proposed in [39, 40] was used
66: instead, namely

Then D_A is bounded above by the matter-only integrand, and since D_A is measured at the sub-percent level, the conclusion is forced: **for a given H0, ΛCDM has maximal comoving angular diameter distance to the CMB, and any model with non-constant ρ_x has a *lower* D_A.** The measured H0 is *higher* than the ΛCDM extrapolation. Therefore one of Assumptions 1–7 **must** break — this is a theorem about the data, not a modelling preference. The question for this panel is only *which* assumption, and the late-universe route breaks Assumptions 2 and 6 (homogeneity, and late-time distance physics) while leaving the CMB inference untouched. The early route breaks Assumption 7, the weakest and most specific of the seven, and it breaks it in the one place where the data are least able to check: the pre-recombination radiation budget.

239: ## Round 1 (continued), Judge — Rulings 8–10: the two new preprints, and the status of Round 1
240: 
241: Both new preprints have now been argued (late_a at Round 18, skeptic_b in the continued statement above). I have read both papers myself. Rulings 8–10 follow. I record them under Round 1 because Round 1 is still open, and both papers were assigned into it.
242: 
243: ### Ruling 8 — 2008.01115 is received, and it is a constraint on the early-universe family, not a referee between the two families
244: 
245: skeptic_b's ruling request is GRANTED, and I reach the same conclusion independently, which I record because the paper's own framing invites the opposite reading.
246: 
247: The paper (Lucca, ULB-TH/20-10) makes two claims. The first is structural: a resolution must move both H0 and r_s, r_s is fixed before recombination, therefore "late-time modifications of the ΛCDM model are intrinsically incapable of fully solving the H0−r_s tension." The second is a forecast: CMB spectral distortions (SDs) measure n_s and A_s far more sharply than anisotropies do, and since the EDE family buys H0 with an n_s shift, a PRISM-class SD probe breaks the degeneracy.
248: 
249: **Claim 1 does not referee this debate, and I decline to let it.** It presumes the H0−r_s framing, which is Assumption 7 of 2101.01372 — the assumption at issue. skeptic_b's argument against late_a is that the rebuttal "proves too much": if fixing H0,out by construction dissolves the H0−r_s tension, then any resolution that fixes the CMB-derived H0,out is exempt from every CMB-consistency test. I accept the reductio as sound. But I do not thereby adopt skeptic_b's conclusion, which is that Lucca's structural claim "applies with full force to early_a's models, and not at all to the void." **The honest position is that the void is not exempted by the reductio; it is simply untested.** The void models *are* fitted to the CMB — skeptic_b concedes this in his §2 — and what they are not permitted to do is declare the result by construction. The distinction between "exempt" and "not yet checked" is the distinction between an invalid argument and an unfinished one, and the panel should not record the void as having passed a consistency test it has never been given. So: claim 1 is a *rebuttal that fails* on late_a's side, and is *not* a *refutation of the void*.
250: 
251: **Claim 2 is a genuine, correctly quoted, and correctly caveated constraint, and I confirm every number skeptic_b gives.** I verified Table I of 2008.01115 directly. n_s = 0.9692 ± 0.0038 (ΛCDM) → 0.9873^{+0.0069}_{−0.0080} (EDE) → 0.9724^{+0.0030}_{−0.0032} (EDE+SDs); H0 = 68.20 ± 0.54 → 71.2^{+1.0}_{−1.1} → 69.41^{+0.63}_{−0.75}; f_EDE(z_c) = 0.103^{+0.035}_{−0.029} → < 0.095; Θ_i → > 0.40 (95% CL). One correction to the record, immaterial to the conclusion: skeptic_b writes the EDE+SDs n_s error as ±0.0032; the paper gives +0.0030/−0.0032, asymmetric. The paper's own summary of the result is that the H0 posterior "is reduced to the point where it is not compatible with the SH0ES value any more."
252: 
253: **Ruling on how it enters the consensus: as a forecast, not as data, and as a diagnostic of mechanism rather than a measurement.** skeptic_b's characterisation is accepted verbatim: a PRISM-class mock likelihood, 5×10⁻²⁷ W/m²/Hz/sr, "one order of magnitude better than PIXIE," with galactic and extra-galactic foregrounds neglected — which the paper itself says "typically worsen the results by roughly one order of magnitude" — and with the fiducial set to the ΛCDM mean, so the mean shifts are constructed and the errors optimistic. The authors concede the point themselves: with realistic foregrounds a more futuristic mission than PRISM would be required. The panel will therefore record 2008.01115 as establishing (i) that the EDE family's H0 gain is bought with an n_s excursion, (ii) that n_s is the parameter an SD probe measures best, and (iii) that a PRISM-class probe would return H0 to 69.41^{+0.63}_{−0.75} and f_EDE < 0.095. It will **not** record EDE as excluded, and it will **not** record the void as unaffected.
254: 
255: **Consequence for early_a, which he must answer in his Round 1 statement.** His best ladder-free H0, 72.33 ± 0.55 (2502.15541 Table IV), is the H0 that requires the largest n_s excursion. If the panel's answer is that the leading early-universe candidate has a named, quantified near-future failure mode, early_a is the one who has to say so, not the chair. This is not a demand that he concede; it is the reason the early-universe position cannot be certified as "viable" on the current archive alone.
256: 
257: ### Ruling 9 — 1912.12600 is recorded as "a mechanism awaiting a fit", and both sides have it backwards on the numbers
258: 
259: skeptic_b's ruling request is GRANTED. The paper defers the joint test against "SNe observations, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), large-scale structure and the cosmic microwave background (CMB)" to future work, stating that perturbation theory on an inhomogeneous background "can be much more complicated." **The paper has therefore not been tested against any of the four data sets I assigned skeptic_b to check it against.** Its own abstract says the benchmark "may ease" the tension. The panel records the verb "eases."
260: 
261: On the numbers, I have checked both sides directly and I find a discrepancy neither of them reported, which corrects the record in both directions.
262: 
263: **Correction 1 — skeptic_b's "2.5% of a required 8.4%" is right about the benchmark but he omits that the paper's own figure shows a second, shallower case.** Line 293 of 1912.12600: "H_void(z = 0) = 68.1(69.1) km/s/Mpc for the void case with (Δr/r_V, δ_V) = (0.06, −0.06)((0.4, −0.14))." The 69.1 figure is the Δr = 0.4 r_V case. At Δr/r_V = 0.06 the shift is 68.1 against H0,out = 67.4, i.e. **1.0%, not 2.5%.** skeptic_b's reading — that the shallowness of −0.14 is a *ceiling* set by kSZ, and that 2.5% is what the model delivers — is nonetheless correct as a statement about the benchmark, and his ~30%-of-the-gap arithmetic stands.
264: 
265: **Correction 2 — skeptic_b's claim that 1912.12600 "is showing the H0(z) response curve at a depth it expects to be reachable," and that "1912.12600 and 2504.13380 are the same model," overstates the case, and I decline it.** The δ_V = −0.4439 figure in Fig. 2 (right panel) and Fig. 3 is at r_V = 1700 Mpc, Δr = 102 Mpc, H0,out = 67.4, Ω_M = 0.315, Ω_Λ = 0.685 — which is 2504.13380's depth but on a 1700 Mpc scale with a 102 Mpc boundary, not 2504.13380's profile. These are *not* the same model, and the panel will not merge them. skeptic_b's underlying point — that the paper contemplates depths far deeper than its own benchmark, and that late_a is running two papers as a "conservative fallback" and a "benchmark" when they share a cost — is fair as a question to put to late_a. It is not a finding, and it is not adopted as one.
266: 
267: **Correction 3 — late_a's "this is a local void model that survives current CMB data" is DECLINED.** The words are hers; the paper's are "can *narrowly* evade." The only test 1912.12600 performs is kSZ, and it passes at that word. A model that clears its sole applicable constraint by a narrow margin, and that has never been run against SNe, BAO, LSS or the full CMB likelihood, has not "survived current CMB data." skeptic_b's §3(a) is upheld on this point.
268: 
269: **On the kSZ scaling, skeptic_b's derivation is accepted** and I record it as his: the kSZ integral is dominated by the void edge and scales as ~z³δ_V² with r ~ z, giving δ_V > −r_V^{−3/2}, so growing r_V to 1700 Mpc is what buys the survival and the survival is what caps the depth. This is the cleanest physical statement anyone has made this round and it is the reason the benchmark cannot be pushed: (300/1700)^{3/2} ≈ 0.074 is the depth permitted at 1700 Mpc relative to 300 Mpc, and −0.14 sits just inside a limit of that order.
270: 
271: ### Ruling 10 — the S8 objection is CATEGORY, not DECLINED, and neither side has established its case
272: 
273: late_a argues that S8 = σ8(Ω_m/0.3)^{1/2} is "a homogeneous-statistic quantity" and that applying it to a model with Ω_m(r) varying from <0.2 at the centre to 0.3153 outside is a category error. skeptic_b, and 2202.12214, treat fσ8 as a live discriminator.
274: 
275: The correct ruling is that both are describing a real methodological problem, and neither has discharged it. A void model is not exempt from growth diagnostics: what it must do is predict a *position-dependent* fσ8, and a data set that constrains growth in the region of the void is constraining it. The relevant question is whether 2202.12214's and the fσ8 data set's support regions overlap the void, and nobody on this panel has checked. So: late_a may not dismiss S8 as inapplicable, and skeptic_b may not treat the existing fσ8 bounds as a verdict on ΛLTB. **This question is referred to methods**, together with the three questions still outstanding from Ruling 7, and it goes into Round 2 as a data question, not a philosophical one.

39: ## 3. Judge's rulings 1–10
40: Full text in `debate/TRANSCRIPT.md`. Summary of the load-bearing ones:
41: 
42: - **Ruling 1** — 2504.13380's ΔBIC = −73.28 is a fixed-parameter fit (§IV: "It is unfair to impose these conditions without using the CMB data"). The void is **not** recorded as CMB-preferred.
43: - **Ruling 2** — DESI r_s h = 101.8 ± 1.3 Mpc is a **mandatory diagnostic, not a gate**. (early_a's "one-sided test" framing accepted.)
44: - **Ruling 5** — **no false dichotomy**: early_a and skeptic_b already agree the verb is "reduces."
45: - **Ruling 8 (new)** — 2008.01115 recorded as **a forecast, not data**, and as a **mechanism**: the EDE family buys H0 with an n_s excursion, and n_s is what SDs measure best. Its structural claim ("late-time modifications are *intrinsically incapable* of solving the H0−r_s tension") is **declined as a referee** — it presumes Assumption 7. Caveats on record: PRISM-class mock likelihood, foregrounds neglected, paper concedes foregrounds worsen by an order of magnitude, fiducial set to ΛCDM mean.
46: - **Ruling 9 (new)** — 1912.12600 recorded as **"a mechanism awaiting a fit."** late_a's "survives current CMB data" **DECLINED** (the paper says "narrowly evade"; it is the only test performed). skeptic_b's "same model as 2504.13380" **NOT adopted**; his 2.5% figure **incomplete** — the paper's own second case (Δr/r_V = 0.06, δ_V = −0.06) gives H_void(0) = 68.1, i.e. **1.0%**. The kSZ scaling δ_V > −r_V^{−3/2} is accepted as skeptic_b's and recorded as his.
47: - **Ruling 10 (new)** — the S8 objection is **CATEGORY, not declined**. late_a may not dismiss fσ8 as inapplicable to an inhomogeneous model; skeptic_b may not treat existing fσ8 bounds as a verdict on ΛLTB. **Referred to methods (Q4).**
48: 
49: ## 4. Where the panel stands
50: 
51: **Posted: late_a, skeptic_b, early_a. Not posted: skeptic_a, methods.** Round 1 remains OPEN.
52: 
53: Two fully argued positions and one absent:
54: - **late_a:** "No early-universe modification is needed." Void + three epochs of SN M-transition.
55: - **skeptic_b:** ranks axion EDE first but says the verb is "reduces"; both leading families fail, in *different* places.
56: - **skeptic_a:** the measurement-problem position has **no voice in the transcript at all.** A statement written now is a 2-to-1 majority with a hole in it.
57: 
58: **Four open statistical questions (all referred to methods, all decide wording):**
59: 1. Is the 5.6σ H0(z) decline independent, or does it double-count the SNe the ladder is built from?
60: 2. Does ΔAIC or QDMAP govern when they disagree in sign on acoustic EDE — "fails" or "ambiguously disfavoured"?
61: 3. Is a fixed-parameter ΔBIC comparable to a free-parameter one? (Underpins Ruling 1.)
62: 4. How should a growth diagnostic be formed for an inhomogeneous model, and what would be a fair fσ8 test of ΛLTB?
63: 
64: ## 5. Provisional shape of the answer (NOT certifiable)
65: 
66: **No single-assumption resolution survives all the data.** Early and late families fail in *different* places.
67: 
68: - **Early universe (r_d reduction):** axion-like EDE is the only candidate that does not fail outright, and it **reduces** ~5σ to 2.5–2.6σ, but only with DESI — and it buys that H0 with an n_s excursion that a forecast SD probe would reverse (H0 → 69.41). Modified recombination achieves the best single fit in the archive (0.29σ, and simultaneously repairs S8) but pays Δχ²_BAO = +5.37. Acoustic EDE fails at 3.6σ. Self-interacting neutrinos fail (r_s moves 0.29 Mpc).
69: - **Late universe / local:** the ~150–300 Mpc void is excluded by sample variance (20σ). The Gpc void delivers 2.5% of a required 8.4% and has never been fitted. The ΛLTB + M-transition model that does work requires three transitions in the SN absolute magnitude *and* a CMB-conditioned likelihood.
70: - **Measurement/systematics:** untested. Nobody has spoken for it.
71: 
72: **The defensible verb for the leading candidate is "reduces."** Two panelists independently now say so.
73: 
74: **What the two new preprints did to the shape of the argument:** they attacked the *mechanisms*, not the measurements. 1912.12600 shows the void family's constraint is self-limiting (kSZ), and 2008.01115 shows the EDE family's constraint is a different observable measuring a different parameter. Neither is a statement that the ladder is wrong. Whether that is a reason to suspect the ladder is precisely the question skeptic_a has not yet been asked in the transcript — and I have now asked it.
75:

77: 
78: For each resolution: pro paper + one number, con paper + one number, under two pages, in this order: axion-like EDE; acoustic EDE; modified recombination; self-interacting neutrinos; late-time background modification; ~150 Mpc local void; ΛLTB void + M-transitions; Gpc void (1912.12600); SD test of EDE (2008.01115); Cepheid calibration systematics (2211.00578); look-back time reinterpretation (2302.13671). **The last two cannot be written until skeptic_a posts.**

VI.
CONCLUDING REMARKS
In cosmology, the Hubble tension has become one of the most serious challenges in the last decade.
Assuming that all the observational data are right, one of the ways out is to modify the standard ΛCDM
cosmology. In the literature, the theoretical modiﬁcations are mainly made in the early and the late/local
universes. But on both sides, some no-go arguments have been proposed. In particular, the general no-go
arguments for the late-time modiﬁcations in [32–34] are mainly based on the PAge parameterization. In
the present work, we note that there are some ﬂaws in the (original) PAge parameterization, and then
propose various generalized PAge (GPAge) parameterizations, which can be extended to z > zCMB and
hence CMB can be taken into account, while they are also more accurate at low redshifts where τ = t/t0
is close to 1. With these GPAge parameterizations, we revisit the Hubble tension by using not only the
late-time observations but also the observational data of CMB. We ﬁnd that the Hubble tension could
be alleviated (or even resolved) in GPAges diﬀerent from the standard ΛCDM cosmology, while they are
overwhelmingly preferred over ΛCDM by the observational data in terms of all the information criteria.
Surprisingly, we ﬁnd that the new physics in the mid-time might be the key to resolve the Hubble tension.

Some remarks are in order. First, our results strongly prefer modiﬁed gravity (while interacting dark
energy and modiﬁed gravity cannot be distinguished [83–86]), and all the non-interacting dark energy
models in GR can be excluded. However, noting that only the observational data of the cosmic expansion
history have been used in the present work, this conclusion is in fact not so solid without also using the
observational data of the growth history. As is well known, modiﬁed gravity aﬀect both the expansion
history and the growth history in a way diﬀerent from non-interacting dark energy. If the non-interacting
dark energy model and the modiﬁed gravity model share the same cosmic expansion history, they might
have diﬀerent growth histories [83–86]. Thus, it is needed to also take the observational data of the growth
history (e.g. the well-known fσ8 data) into account. Without them, our key conclusions are not so solid
in fact. We will continue to study the mid-time guide for the Hubble tension with the fσ8 data and/or
other observational data of the growth history in our next works.

V.
PHYSICAL IMPLICATIONS
So far, with the GPAge parameterizations, we are completely ignorant of the components in the universe
and the gravity theory. As shown in Sec. II, we even do not know whether the universe contains dark
energy, dark matter or other components, and in fact we even have not used any Friedmann equation
or Einstein equation so far, while no particular metric or geometry is explicitly assumed. Thus, the
results obtained in the above sections are fairly general. We have found that the Hubble tension can be
alleviated (or even resolved) in GPAges diﬀerent from the standard ΛCDM cosmology, while they are
overwhelmingly preferred over ΛCDM by the observational data in terms of all the information criteria.

5 SUMMARY
In this paper, we systematically investigate the Hubble tension prob-
lem in the framework of HDE. We select six representative theo-
retical models from all four categories of HDE, including OHDE,
GRDE, IHDE1, IHDE2, THDE, and BHDE. To obtain cosmological
constraints, we adopt the latest BAO data from DESI DR2, CMB
distance priors from 𝑃𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑘2018, and the DESY5 compilation of
SN data. In addition, we also consider alternative datasets includ-
ing the PantheonPlus and Union3 SN compilations, as well as a
collection of alternative BAO data, including 6dFGS+SDSS MGS,
BOSS Galaxy, eBOSS LRG, DES Y3, eBOSS Quasar, and eBOSS
Ly𝛼-forest surveys.

HDE models that employ the Hubble scale or its combinations as
the IR cutoff cannot alleviate the Hubble tension problem, main-
taining tensions of 5𝜎-6𝜎that are comparable to the ΛCDM. Sec-
ond, HDE models that employ the future event horizon as the IR
cutoff can partially mitigate the Hubble tension problem, reducing
the tensions to below 3.19𝜎for DESI+CMB and below 4.49𝜎for
DESI+CMB+DESY5 (compared to over 5.4𝜎for the ΛCDM model).
To explore whether our key conclusions hold true for other
BAO data and SN data, we also take into account alternative data
combinations, including non-DESI+CMB, DESI+CMB+PPlus, and
DESI+CMB+Union3. When replacing DESI with non-DESI data,
HDE models that employ the future event horizon as the IR cutoff
still have the ability to alleviate the Hubble tension problem, with
tension reduced to below 2.23𝜎. Although incorporating SN data
into the DESI+CMB combination increases the tension compared to
DESI+CMB alone, HDE models that employ the future event hori-
zon still exhibit lower tensions (below 4.65𝜎) than the ΛCDM model.
Therefore, our key conclusions are insensitive to the cases of using
alternative BAO data and SN data.
Current cosmological measurements indicate a Hubble tension
that is larger than 5𝜎for the ΛCDM model. As shown in this paper,
some HDE models that based on the future event horizon can partially
mitigate the Hubble tension problem. However, these HDE models
perform poorer than the ΛCDM model in cosmology-fits (Li & Wang
2025a). Therefore, it is interesting to search for some other dynamical
DE models that can genuinely resolve the Hubble tension problem
and give a good cosmological fitting result that is comparable to
the ΛCDM model. In addition, since the Hubble tension problem
primarily arises from a discrepancy between high-redshift probes
(CMB) and low-redshift probes (Cepheids and SNe), incorporating
some other cosmological probes such as standard sirens (gravitational
waves) may have the potential of alleviating the Hubble tension
problem. These open questions merit further investigation.
